article_title: The GED Writing Skills Test Essay Teacher Training Manual.
citation: Coombs, Lucinda H. (1987). The GED Writing Skills Test Essay Teacher Training Manual. Maine Dept. of Educational and Cultural Services / University of Maine. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED324536
title: Design writing assignments around topics students care about and can substantively respond to
description: The manual instructs teachers to offer a choice of topics because, as it states, "Unless a writer is interested in the topic, has an opinion about it, and hasthe knowledge to write a substantive response, the writing is not going to be good." Topics should be generally familiar, worth writing about, clearly stated, and require evaluation rather than recitation of facts. Assignments should foster success and be calibrated carefully to avoid overestimating or underestimating student ability.
requirements: Topics must be familiar, clearly stated, and require the same critical thinking skills as the GED essay
constraints: Overestimating ability undermines confidence; underestimating causes frustration and limits progress
target_learners: Adult GED preparation students
target_learning_goals: Write substantive, well-supported expository responses
examples: The manual ranks the personal narrative as the easiest writing type and suggests starting there before moving students toward the essay
key_sources: Coombs, Lucinda H. (1987). The GED Writing Skills Test Essay Teacher Training Manual. Maine Dept. of Educational and Cultural Services / University of Maine. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED324536

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Zearn Math
citation: Zearn Math evidence review. (2024). https://zearn.org
title: Pair supplemental digital math programs with dedicated implementation support including professional development, coaching, and dosage monitoring
description: The review indicates that significant positive results occurred where Zearn Math was implemented with "accompanying professional development and coaching support for school leaders", which helps schools "establish dedicated time in the schedule for usage, build effective routines, and use data to ensure students reach the recommended dosage of three digital lessons per week". Support includes regular coach check-ins and motivational strategies such as classroom-based challenges to promote consistent lesson completion.
requirements: Dedicated scheduled time for program usage
Professional development and coaching for school leaders
Data-based progress monitoring toward the recommended dosage
Designated school or district points of contact for onboarding and rostering setup
constraints: The pilot implementation without full implementation support found no significant differences, suggesting support may be a boundary condition for effects.
target_learners: Students in grades K-8 in elementary and middle schools
target_learning_goals: Grade-level mathematics proficiency
examples: Treatment schools in the Texas RCT received dedicated implementation support including professional development, coaching, and progress monitoring; the Louisiana study likewise provided dedicated implementation support.
key_sources: Zearn Math evidence review. (2024). https://zearn.org

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Develop a culture of data use among all levels of district staff
description: The brief's first key recommendation is that districts should "Develop a culture of data use among all levels of staff." It frames effective data use as an organizational capacity issue rather than a purely technical one, arguing that strategic use of data to inform education policy and improve instruction depends on staff at every level engaging with data. The recommendation is one of four the brief offers to districts building data-use capacity.
requirements: Districts must have essential data systems and supports in place before strategic use challenges can be addressed
target_learners: school district staff and administrators
target_learning_goals: strategic use of data to inform education policy and improve instruction
examples: The brief draws data and supporting examples from work conducted as part of the evaluation of strategic data use initiatives
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Secure and dedicate resources to conduct analyses and interpret findings
description: The brief's fourth key recommendation is to "Secure and dedicate resources to conduct analyses and interpret findings." It treats analytic and interpretive work as requiring committed resources rather than residual staff effort, making resourcing a precondition for the other recommendations. The recommendation is drawn from the brief's work with districts in strategic data use initiatives.
requirements: Districts must allocate dedicated resources for conducting analyses and interpreting findings
target_learners: school district leaders and administrators
target_learning_goals: building organizational capacity for data analysis and interpretation
examples: The brief suggests ways districts can overcome challenges associated with this recommendation
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: Supporting Effective Data Use (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Supporting Effective Data Use (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data
description: The brief endorses data-informed decision making across every level of the education system, stating that "decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data." It presents this as a broadly shared goal that its recommendations aim to make operational in practice.
requirements: Good data must be available and usable by decision makers at each level of the education system.
constraints: The brief notes that in practice data can leave educators unmoved or drown them in extraneous information, so informing decisions with data is not automatic.
target_learners: Educators and decision makers at classroom, district, and state education agency levels
target_learning_goals: Improving classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement through data-informed decisions
examples: The brief series offers recommendations and strategies for state officials, district-level staff, and system developers to promote effective data use.
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Supporting Effective Data Use (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/supporting-effective-data-use

article_title: Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program
citation: Jeffrey Capizzano, Kendra Bischoff, Nicola Woodroffe, Duncan Chaplin. (2007). Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Describe the specific elements of an effective program so it can be replicated
description: After an intervention is shown effective, document its specific program elements so practitioners can replicate it. This paper follows that approach: given positive random-assignment results, "this new paper describes the specific elements of the successful program so it can be replicated." The elements documented are those present in the successful BELL summer program.
requirements: A prior evaluation establishing the program as effective, so that the documented elements come from a demonstrably successful program
constraints: The authors state they cannot distinguish which elements caused the positive impacts, so documented elements are of potential rather than proven importance
target_learners: Elementary school students in summer learning programs
target_learning_goals: Literacy and academic skill retention over the summer
examples: The paper describes the elements of the BELL Accelerated Learning Summer Program, which a prior random-assignment evaluation had found effective.
key_sources: Jeffrey Capizzano, Kendra Bischoff, Nicola Woodroffe, Duncan Chaplin. (2007). Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ingredients-of-a-successful-summer-learning-program-a-case-study-of-the-building-educated-leaders-for-life-bell-accelerated-learning-summer-program

article_title: The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2020). The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 13, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design the choice architecture of school choice websites deliberately, because small display manipulations shift which schools parents choose
description: This principle holds that how school information is displayed on choice websites — default ordering, icon versus graph versus number formats, and concise versus detailed summaries — is itself a design decision that shapes parental choices. The article's experiment shows that "a small design manipulation... induced meaningful changes in the types of schools selected," so website designers should treat display choices as consequential rather than neutral.
requirements: A school choice website presenting school information to parents, with measurable academic performance data to display
constraints: Evidence comes from a hypothetical school district choice task with low-income parents; the article reports trade-offs, e.g. graphs maximized satisfaction at the expense of understanding
target_learners: low-income parents of school-aged children choosing schools
target_learning_goals: informed school selection based on academic performance information
examples: In the experiment, changing the default order in which schools were presented and swapping graphs or numbers for icons changed the types of schools parents selected
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2020). The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 13, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-choice-architecture-of-school-choice-websites

article_title: Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters
citation: John Deke. (2016). Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters. Evaluation Review, vol. 40, issue 5. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/design-and-analysis-considerations-for-cluster-randomized-controlled-trials-that-have-a-small-number-of-clusters
title: Design small cluster randomized trials deliberately: use blocked randomization, Type I error-safe analysis, and corrected power calculations
description: The article offers best practices for designing and analyzing cluster randomized controlled trials with ten or fewer clusters, contexts where it says meaningful effects may still be detectable. Its stated objective is "to offer recommendations for best practices in design and analysis for small CRCTs," grounded in simulations of alternative approaches. The practices cover analytic choice, blocking, power estimation, and cluster-count planning.
requirements: Researchers must examine which analytic approaches control Type I errors and which design choices yield the most power, as the simulations did
constraints: Small effects remain very difficult to detect with just four clusters
Covariate adjustment for blocking depends on whether precision gains offset degrees of freedom loss
target_learners: Researchers and evaluators designing education and human services studies
target_learning_goals: Valid estimation of intervention effects in small-scale cluster randomized evaluations
examples: The author used simulations to examine which analytic approaches control Type I errors, which designs yield the most power, the design effect of spurious correlations, and scenarios under which impacts of different sizes can be detected with high probability
key_sources: John Deke. (2016). Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters. Evaluation Review, vol. 40, issue 5. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/design-and-analysis-considerations-for-cluster-randomized-controlled-trials-that-have-a-small-number

article_title: Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data
title: Decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data
description: The brief endorses data-informed decision making across every level of the education system. It observes that "Most agree that decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data", framing good data as an input to decisions at classroom, district, and state levels alike, while acknowledging that achieving this in practice is difficult.
requirements: Good data must be available to decision makers at classroom, central office, and state education agency levels
constraints: In practice, data often fails to move decision makers or overwhelms them with extraneous information
target_learners: classroom educators
central office staff
state education agency staff
target_learning_goals: making data-informed decisions to improve instruction and student achievement
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data

article_title: Using Demographic Data as Predictor Variables: a Questionable Choice
citation: Baker, R. S., Esbenshade, L., Vitale, J., & Karumbaiah, S. (2023). Using Demographic Data as Predictor Variables: a Questionable Choice. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 15(2). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/
title: Use demographic variables to validate fairness across groups rather than as predictors within at-risk models
description: The article's central recommendation is that demographic data serve model validation rather than prediction. The authors conclude that "there are greater benefits to fairness if demographic variables are used to validate fai rness rather than as predictors within models". In practice this means analyzing a model's goodness of fit broken down by demographic group to ensure comparable model quality across groups, while keeping actionable, malleable variables as predictors. This preserves the ability to detect group-level disparities without embedding immutable characteristics in individual predictions.
requirements: Models should be checked for fairness and equal accuracy across demographic groups as part of validation
constraints: The authors scope this argument to at-risk prediction models in education; they discuss alternate uses such as cost-sensitive classification separately
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students subject to at-risk or dropout prediction models
target_learning_goals: Fair and accurate prediction of student outcomes such as dropout or graduation risk
examples: The article notes commercial systems such as BrightBytes and Infinite Campus adopt the validation approach, analyzing model fit broken down by demographic group
key_sources: Baker, R. S., Esbenshade, L., Vitale, J., & Karumbaiah, S. (2023). Using Demographic Data as Predictor Variables: a Questionable Choice. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 15(2). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/619

article_title: 2023 Pace of Learning Report
citation: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/
title: Deploy high-impact teachers to more students via incentives, since better teachers derive more learning
description: The brief recommends shifting students' pace of learning upward by ensuring higher-quality instruction, arguing "better teachers derive more learning from their students than their peers." One deployment approach offers more effective teachers additional pay or sabbatical/training credit for taking on additional students, so each student drawn from the lower portion of the POL distribution receives "a high quality teacher and higher performing peers, both of which stimulate student performance."
requirements: Use qualitative and quantitative information, including multi-cohort test-based impact estimates strengthened by principal and peer assessments, to identify teachers with outsized impacts
constraints: The brief flags open questions: whether expanded classes taught by top teachers produce the expected gains for added students is listed among the things yet to learn
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those in the lower portion of the POL distribution
target_learning_goals: Increasing students' rate of learning through higher-quality instruction
examples: The brief suggests offering more effective teachers additional pay for taking on additional students, or credit toward later sabbatical or special training
key_sources: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/

article_title: The Information Content of Employee Awards
citation: Signaling effects of merit awards: Evidence from school principals in Chicago. (2023). Economics of Education Review. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/economics-of-education-review
title: Design merit award programs to reduce the loss of more effective school leaders
description: Because merit awards can signal effectiveness to outside employers and increase exit among winners, award programs should be modified to retain the leaders they identify. The article states the findings "highlight the importance of program modifications that reduce the loss of more effective school leaders." Program design should therefore anticipate labor-market signaling consequences alongside incentive benefits.
requirements: An award program with an explicit effectiveness threshold whose winners can be observed by outside employers
constraints: The recommendation rests on evidence from one merit award program for Chicago principals
target_learners: school principals
district policymakers
target_learning_goals: retaining effective school leaders while maintaining incentive effects
examples: The Chicago principal merit award program, whose incentives increased achievement while award winners exited at over twice the rate of near-threshold non-winners
key_sources: Signaling effects of merit awards: Evidence from school principals in Chicago. (2023). Economics of Education Review. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/economics-of-education-review

article_title: If Small Is Not Enough...?
citation: W. David Stevens. (2008). If Small Is Not Enough . . . ? The Characteristics of Successful Small High Schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Developmental practices: sustained, collective teacher work on shared instructional issues
description: Developmental practices are the report's term for improvement activities in which teachers engage in "regular group interactions focused on common instructional issues." To be coded as developmental, an activity had to be unrelated to external test preparation and meet three criteria: a focus on a specific and shared instructional issue, involvement of teachers in group work or discussion about that issue, and collaboration sustained over time through consistent meetings. Examples from the fieldwork included aligning curricula to state standards, improving student assessments, implementing differentiated instruction, and developing outcome-based learning goals.
requirements: Activities must meet the report's three criteria: shared instructional focus, group work or discussion, and sustained collaboration over time
constraints: The report distinguishes developmental practices from supportive practices, which exchange advice between pairs of teachers and address individual concerns but do not necessarily improve instruction school-wide
target_learners: high school teachers working in small schools
target_learning_goals: improving instructional quality and student course performance through collective teacher learning
examples: Paulina High's iterative development of grade-level performance expectations and Adams High's teacher-led creation of interim assessments given four times a year both met the developmental-practice criteria.
key_sources: W. David Stevens. (2008). If Small Is Not Enough . . . ? The Characteristics of Successful Small High Schools in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/if-small-not-enough-characteristics-successful-small-high-schools-chicago

article_title: Arguing about the effectiveness of assessments for the classroom
citation: Garron Gianopulos. (2021). Arguing about the effectiveness of assessments for the classroom. The Journal of Mathematical Behavior, 61. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/the-journal-of-mathematical-behavior
title: Design and evaluate classroom assessments around the problem, or 'job-to-be-done,' the intended test user needs solved
description: This principle holds that classroom assessment design and evaluation should start from the important problem faced by intended test users, treating score use as part of a potential solution to that problem rather than as an endpoint of validity evidence alone. The article argues that "this lack fails to reflect the ultimate purpose of a test score—to help solve an important problem faced by intended test users" and urges a shift from validity to effectiveness.
requirements: Designers must identify the important problem faced by intended test users and articulate an effectiveness argument linking score use to solving it.
constraints: The article scopes this conceptualization to classroom assessments based on complex constructs, such as learning progressions in math and science.
target_learners: K-12 students assessed through classroom and interim assessments in math and science
target_learning_goals: using interim and classroom assessment scores to support instructional decisions within learning progressions
examples: The article contrasts effectiveness arguments for interim assessments based on a conventional test blueprint versus a test blueprint augmented with learning progressions.
key_sources: Garron Gianopulos. (2021). Arguing about the effectiveness of assessments for the classroom. The Journal of Mathematical Behavior, 61. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/the-journal-of-mathematical-behavior

article_title: Defining Computational Thinking for a District: Inclusive Computing Pathways in Indian Prairie School District
citation: Digital Promise. (2021). Defining computational thinking for a district: Inclusive computing pathways in Indian Prairie School District. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/131
title: Define computational thinking at the outset of a district CT initiative and use the definition to guide scope, sequence, and integration
description: IPSD's reflection concludes that the definition of CT matters and can overwhelm teachers, and the district was glad it "taken the time to define CT from the beginning" and focused on competencies and integration throughout. The recommended actions are to understand CT, apply it to a scope and sequence, and leverage competencies to enhance disciplinary learning rather than only identifying CT in existing practice.
requirements: Time for the leadership team to examine existing CT definitions and build shared understanding before rollout
target_learners: District curriculum leaders and K-12 teachers
target_learning_goals: Shared district-wide understanding of computational thinking and its integration
examples: IPSD examined existing CT definitions, identified six competencies, and mapped them to the K-12 CS Framework before launching professional learning
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2021). Defining computational thinking for a district: Inclusive computing pathways in Indian Prairie School District. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/131

article_title: Partnerships that Work: Tapping Research to Address Learner Variability in Young Readers
citation: Tare, M., Nobles, S., & Xiao, W. (2018). Partnerships that work: Tapping research to address learner variability in young readers. Washington, DC: Digital Promise Global. https://www.digitalpromise.org/
title: Design features to the edges of learner variability to support all students
description: The report's key takeaway is that designing features to the edges of learner variability actually supports all students. Teachers felt all students can benefit from optional supports such as audio, not just readers who struggle, because teachers are attuned to the varying needs of all their students and welcome the ability to easily provide optional supports. Use of these tools also serves classroom cohesion, allowing all students to discuss together after completing an individual activity online.
requirements: Supports should be optional and easy for teachers to provide so they can be matched to varying needs
target_learners: All learners in inclusive K-3 classrooms, including struggling readers and advanced readers
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and participation in shared classroom discussion
examples: Teachers provided the audio option to all students, reporting benefits for below-grade-level readers hearing fluent reading and above-grade-level readers encountering new words
key_sources: Tare, M., Nobles, S., & Xiao, W. (2018). Partnerships that work: Tapping research to address learner variability in young readers. Washington, DC: Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/e59c6e47-4209-4187-a0ef-b8da08283ec6

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Reading Partners
citation: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: House school-based tutoring programs in a dedicated in-school reading center managed by a full-time coordinator
description: Reading Partners requires partner schools to provide infrastructure for consistent delivery: "Reading Partners requires partner schools to have a dedicated space for a reading center, usually a classroom," and "Reading Partners then provides a full-time site coordinator to manage the program and recruits community volunteers as tutors." A fixed space plus dedicated coordination supports reliable volunteer recruitment, training, and session delivery within the school day.
requirements: A dedicated space for a reading center, usually a classroom, with an internet connection
A full-time site coordinator to manage the program
target_learners: Elementary students in grades 2-4 reading below grade level
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and foundational reading skills
examples: A classroom converted to a reading center with an internet connection, staffed by a full-time site coordinator
key_sources: Reading Partners: Program Description and Evidence Rating. (2013). https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Navigating Research Approvals for EdTech Research and Evaluation: A Practical Guide
citation: Younger, J. (2026, September). Navigating research approvals for edtech research and evaluation: A practical guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/318
title: Design the de-identified data architecture before data collection begins
description: Because external evidence goals often emerge after a product ships, the guide urges teams to decide up front whether researchers will ever touch identifiable data. It states that "If there is a realistic possibility that the project will become research, design the data architecture before data collection begins," since de-identifying after analysis is fundamentally different from never granting access. Early architecture decisions preserve the option of an NHSR pathway and avoid costly retrofits.
requirements: Identifiers must be permanently removed or firewalled before researchers can view or analyze data
Role separation between those who link identifiable records and those who analyze research data
constraints: Retrofitting an operational product evaluation into publishable research after collection is described as much harder than designing it appropriately beforehand
target_learners: K-12 students whose platform usage data may support external efficacy evidence
target_learning_goals: Building external evidence and meeting procurement or ESSA evidence-tier standards
examples: The guide contrasts retrospective log analysis with prospective co-designed A/B testing using randomized system-generated IDs and a firewalled analytics interface
key_sources: Younger, J. (2026, September). Navigating research approvals for edtech research and evaluation: A practical guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/318

article_title: Privacy in LA Research: Understanding the Field to Improve the Practice
citation: Olga Viberg, Chantal Mutimukwe, Åke Grönlund. (2022). Privacy in LA Research: Understanding the Field to Improve the Practice. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 169–182. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7751
title: Define privacy explicitly in LA research and practice to enable responsible use of student data
description: The article's central design recommendation is that privacy must be explicitly defined before privacy-protecting models and tools can be built, because "poorly implemented frameworks for privacy protection may negatively impact LA outcomes and undermine trust in the discipline." Defining privacy in principle is not enough: specific situations must be operationalized through specifications of information content, flows, and access. The Smith et al. framework provides common ground for such situation-specific discussions.
requirements: A clear definition of privacy in the targeted study setting before designing privacy mechanisms
constraints: Privacy is not a simple checklist but concerns data handling in depth and detail; what privacy means differs across stakeholders and contexts
target_learners: learning analytics researchers
educational institutions
LA system developers
target_learning_goals: responsible, trust-preserving use of student data for analysis and decision-making
examples: The review shows 74% of LA articles omit definitions; the authors argue this gap slows effective data-driven decision-making in education
key_sources: Olga Viberg, Chantal Mutimukwe, Åke Grönlund. (2022). Privacy in LA Research: Understanding the Field to Improve the Practice. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 169–182. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7751

article_title: Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies
citation: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Defense of learning as a Portrait of a Graduate assessment
description: A defense of learning is a presentation in which students use selected artifacts to demonstrate and defend readiness for a next step such as promotion or graduation, scored by a trained panel using a rubric. In Shelby County Public Schools, students defend their learning in 5th, 8th, and 12th grades, and the defense serves as a graduation requirement for seniors. The report describes it as powerful for students, teachers, caregivers, and community members, and notes Shelby holds calibration sessions to increase score reliability.
requirements: Trained panels, rubrics, and calibration sessions to achieve score reliability
constraints: Like performance tasks, defenses of learning face challenges achieving score reliability
target_learners: students in grades 5, 8, and 12 presenting defenses of learning
target_learning_goals: Portrait of a Graduate skills, competencies, and dispositions
examples: Shelby County Public Schools students collect artifacts across time and explain how the collection demonstrates they have met a specific level of competency on each Portrait skill
key_sources: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/0a2c7a9e-634b-4ec1-ba5d-3c8bfa19e696

article_title: Potholes on the Road to College
citation: Roderick, M., Coca, V., & Nagaoka, J. (2011). Potholes on the Road to College: High School Effects in Shaping Urban Students' Participation in College Application, Four-year College Enrollment, and College Match. Sociology of Education, 84(3), 178-211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0038040711411280
title: Urban high schools should develop organizational norms and structures that guide students through the college application process to convert aspirations into four-year enrollment
description: The article argues that student qualifications and college aspirations alone are insufficient to produce four-year college enrollment; high schools must actively create norms, expectations, and concrete supports that guide students through planning, applying, gaining acceptance, and enrolling. This includes ensuring teachers hold high expectations, provide assistance outside class time, and embed college preparation across the curriculum rather than delegating it solely to counselors.
requirements: School-wide teacher buy-in and shared goals that all students can go to college
Concrete guidance on applications and financial aid
Organizational structures embedded in the academic program rather than isolated in the guidance department
constraints: The evidence is associational (HGLM with observational data), not causal; proxy measures of climate may partially reflect student composition rather than school practice
target_learners: Low-income urban high school seniors
First-generation college aspirants
target_learning_goals: Timely college application
FAFSA completion
Four-year college enrollment
College match
examples: The article's HGLM models found teacher assessment of college-going climate significantly associated with each enrollment step even after controlling for student qualifications and demographics
key_sources: Roderick, M., Coca, V., & Nagaoka, J. (2011). Potholes on the Road to College: High School Effects in Shaping Urban Students' Participation in College Application, Four-year College Enrollment, and College Match. Sociology of Education, 84(3), 178-211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0038040711411280

article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471
title: Universalizing college preparatory course work is unlikely to succeed without professional development, school-community support, and extra support for low-ability students
description: Drawing on the detracking literature, the article argues that a policy of universalizing college preparatory courses needs accompanying organizational supports. As the authors write, "a policy of universalizing college preparatory courses may have little chance of success if it does not address such issues as professional development around instruction, widespread support for the policy among the school community (teachers and parents), and extra support for low-ability students." Schools that detracked successfully shared staff belief in diversity, inclusive pedagogy from professional development, and supports such as extra support courses.
requirements: Professional development around instruction, widespread support among teachers and parents, and extra support courses for struggling students
constraints: Successful detracking schools' characteristics "seem to be exceptional"; resistance from parents, technical difficulties of teaching heterogeneous classrooms, and teachers' low expectations are common difficulties
target_learners: Ninth graders in comprehensive high schools, including low-ability students previously served by remedial tracks
target_learning_goals: Success in college preparatory course work in algebra and English
examples: Chicago's 1997 mandate ended remedial courses without the accompanying instructional supports the detracking literature identifies, and outcomes showed increased failure rates and no test-score gains
key_sources: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471

Schools that successfully detracked shared staff belief in diversity, inclusive pedagogy, and supports for struggling students. The Chicago evaluation's mixed outcomes illustrate the limits of a mandate without these accompanying conditions.

Widespread support for the policy among teachers and parents
Extra support for low-ability students
constraints: Schools face resistance from parents, technical difficulties of teaching heterogeneous classrooms, and low teacher expectations

article_title: Opportunity Gaps: Findings from Initial Analysis of Student Performance in Early Literacy in Massachusetts
citation: Lemke, M., Murphy, D., Soo Ping Chow, A., Spencer, H., & Zhang, A. (2023). Opportunity Gaps: Findings From Initial Analysis of Student Performance in Early Literacy in Massachusetts. WestEd. https://profiles.doe.mass.edu/
title: Massachusetts DESE grantee early literacy screening assessment dataset
description: A statewide observational dataset of K–3 literacy screener results collected by the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education beginning with the 2020/21 school year from schools and districts participating in certain state grants. It covers "More than 35,000 students" — about 10 percent of the state's K–3 population — across "43 districts and 159 schools," with scores from approved screening assessments including Acadience Reading, DIBELS 8th Edition, and MAP Growth. Schools selected assessments from a state-approved list and typically administered them at least three times per year (fall, winter, spring).
requirements: Districts and schools had to participate in qualifying state grants and use assessments from the state-approved screener list
constraints: The sample includes more English learner, Hispanic, and economically disadvantaged students than the state as a whole because of grantee selection criteria
Quartile data are not shown for two racial/ethnic groups due to small numbers

target_learning_goals: Early literacy and reading readiness benchmark performance

article_title: Supporting Students Early: Findings from Initial Analysis of Student Progress in Early Literacy in Massachusetts
citation: Lemke, M., Murphy, D., Soo Ping Chow, A., Spencer, H., & Zhang, A. (2023). Supporting students early: Findings from initial analysis of student progress in early literacy in Massachusetts. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Massachusetts DESE early literacy screening assessment dataset
description: A multi-year dataset of early literacy screener scores collected by the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education beginning with the 2020/21 school year from schools and districts participating in certain state grants. It covers "More than 35,000 students" across 43 districts and 159 schools, about 10 percent of the state's K–3 population, with scores from multiple state-approved commercial screeners such as Acadience Reading, DIBELS 8th Edition, and MAP Reading Fluency. The brief uses benchmark classifications to describe student progress within and across grade levels.
requirements: Districts select screening assessments from a list of state-approved, commercially available literacy screener products, typically administered at least three times per year (BOY, MOY, EOY)
constraints: Initial data are described as somewhat limited; cross-year analyses rest on a small subsample of students with matched scores in both years
target_learners: K–3 students in Massachusetts grantee districts
target_learning_goals: early literacy and reading readiness
examples: The brief analyzes BOY, MOY, and EOY benchmark classifications from 2020/21 and 2021/22 to track risk status within and across grade levels

article_title: The Arc of Dual Enrollment: Access, Struggle, and What Makes Success Possible
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Blanchard, A., & Roldan-Rueda, D. (2026). The arc of dual enrollment: Access, struggle, and what makes success possible. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Dual Enrollment Equity Pathway (DEEP) framework of four equity-oriented practice areas
description: The Dual Enrollment Equity Pathway (DEEP) framework, developed by the Community College Research Center, organizes what distinguishes equity-oriented dual enrollment programs from conventional ones. The brief states it "identifies four practice areas": "outreach to underserved students; alignment of dual enrollment coursework to postsecondary pathways; advising and exploration; and, most relevant here, high-quality instruction and academic support that responds quickly when students are struggling." The framework shifts focus from eligibility to supports in place, which the authors present as consistent with their findings.
requirements: Programs must invest in support infrastructure, which the authors say should be treated as a core program cost rather than an optional enhancement
constraints: The framework is attributed to Fink et al. (2023) and CCRC; the brief endorses it as consistent with its findings rather than testing it
target_learners: High school students in dual enrollment, especially students from low-income and first-generation backgrounds
target_learning_goals: College enrollment and success in college-level coursework during high school
examples: The brief cites research on high-performing programs identifying scaffolding coursework, quick response to struggling students, and structured academic support as the practices that improve outcomes

article_title: Declining Enrollment in America's Public Schools: How States Can Respond Strategically
citation: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://www.bellwether.org
title: Treat enrollment decline as an opportunity for strategic investment and system redesign rather than simply reducing spending, to avoid a vicious cycle of opt-out and disinvestment
description: The brief argues that how policymakers interpret declining enrollment shapes whether systems shrink haphazardly or strengthen. Viewing decline merely as a chance to reduce spending "risks exacerbating fiscal instability and undermining quality", prompting more families to opt out and creating a vicious cycle of eroding enrollment, resources, and public trust. Instead, state leaders should treat the moment as an opportunity for strategic, sustained investments that align spending with student and community needs, potentially enabling more personalized learning environments and reallocation toward evidence-based strategies.
requirements: State leaders must act proactively, mapping responses to long-range enrollment forecasts and evolving student needs rather than temporary downturns
constraints: The brief warns that without clear and consistent messaging, enrollment declines risk being framed solely as a crisis, which could undermine trust and make it harder for local leaders to act
target_learners: Students in K–12 public school systems experiencing sustained enrollment decline
target_learning_goals: Strengthening system quality, resilience, and public confidence so districts can continue serving students effectively through demographic transition
examples: The brief recommends states spotlight districts adopting promising new school designs, facility plans, staffing models, or cross-sector partnerships amid shrinking enrollment, and encourage innovation such as personalized learning models, expanded career pathways, and flexible scheduling
key_sources: Hahnel, C. & Willis, J. (2026). Declining enrollment in America's public schools: How states can respond strategically. Bellwether; WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681594

article_title: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom
citation: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Deeper Learning framework of six competency categories
description: The article presents Deeper Learning as "an umbrella term for the skills, understandings, and mindsets students must possess to succeed in today's jobs and civic life." The framework comprises "six categories of strategies that are essential for students to achieve at high levels": mastering core academic content, thinking critically and solving complex problems, working collaboratively, communicating effectively, learning how to learn, and developing academic mindsets. Each category is elaborated with observable student behaviors, such as transferring knowledge of core facts and concepts to a novel context and persisting and adjusting when an approach is not working.
requirements: Each competency is defined by observable student behaviors that can be demonstrated and assessed
target_learners: all K-12 students
target_learning_goals: mastering academic content, critical thinking and problem solving, collaboration, communication, self-directed learning, and academic mindsets
examples: The framework's six categories structure the 40 Deeper Learning micro-credentials described in the article
key_sources: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception
citation: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://lvp.digitalpromiseglobal.org/
title: Treat classroom challenges as design problems, not student problems, by starting from the assumption of learner variability
description: The paper argues that understanding learner variability informs design: if educators start from the assumption that there is a lot of variability among learners in each classroom, different decisions are made about how to create optimal environments to support learning. Combined with digital technology's flexibility and precision, this reframing makes classroom challenges "a design problem, not a student problem."
requirements: Start with the assumption that there is a lot of variability among learners in each classroom
constraints: The paper notes that gains have been slow to come in schools nationwide, with one-size-fits-all models continuing to under-serve nearly all students
target_learners: all K-12 learners in traditional school systems
target_learning_goals: creating optimal environments that support learning for each learner
examples: Digital Promise built the LVP systems to support teachers and edtech developers in addressing learner variability, putting evidence-based resources at their fingertips
key_sources: Pape, B. (2018). Learner Variability Is the Rule, Not the Exception. Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/b7b14506-0b46-4279-9f9e-675c694b06a6

article_title: Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners
citation: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Define HLS purposes and intended uses explicitly, including what the survey is not for, before designing questions
description: Session participants agreed the HLS serves three purposes: identifying potential members of a protected class under federal law, identifying who should be assessed with an English language proficiency screener, and better understanding students' language environments and use. The paper recommends that "The purposes and intended uses of the HLS should be made explicit to those administering and those completing the survey," and that states specify what the survey is not for, such as determining immigration status. Clear purposes then guide construct identification and more precise question wording.
requirements: Purposes and uses must be stated explicitly to administrators and respondents, and the HLS must be clearly distinguished from other questions when embedded in a larger intake form
constraints: The paper notes the HLS is not intended to measure English proficiency and should not pre-determine educational services or immigration status
target_learners: K-12 students potentially identified as English learners and their parents/guardians
target_learning_goals: Correct routing of potentially EL students to English language proficiency screening
examples: New York City's tiered intake form separates essential HLS questions (Tier 1) from instructional-planning questions (Tier 2) and parent communication preferences (Tier 3)
key_sources: Robert Linquanti and Alison L. Bailey. (2014). Reprising the Home Language Survey: Summary of a National Working Session on Policies, Practices, and Tools for Identifying Potential English Learners. CCSSO. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED565756

article_title: Moving toward Instructional Coherence: How Four Popular Student-Centered Approaches Deepen Identity, Agency, Equity, and Community
citation: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Deeper learning as real-world, transferable competency development across academic content, critical thinking, collaboration, self-direction, and mindsets
description: The paper describes deeper learning as a broad term for learning experiences building the skills, dispositions, and knowledge students need for 21st century jobs and civic life. It states that 'Compelling, real-world content and skills in deeper learning tasks enable transferability and application of knowledge across contexts (Honig & Rainey, 2015).' It lists five core competencies attributed to the Hewlett Foundation: mastering academic content, critical thinking and problem-solving, collaboration and communication, self-directed learning, and adaptive academic mindsets. Instructional strategies include interdisciplinary projects, work-based learning, and project-based learning.
requirements: Clear goals and expectations for what students should know and be able to do
Challenges connected to real-life tasks that students work on collaboratively
constraints: Opportunities for students to demonstrate their learning are typically summative in nature
target_learners: Secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and problem-solving
collaboration and communication
transfer of knowledge across contexts
self-directed learning
examples: Student-led conferences, portfolios, capstone projects, advisories, and employer-based mentorship assessments are common in deeper learning settings

article_title: National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report: Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress
citation: Cook, G., Linquanti, R., Chinen, M., & Jung, H. (2012). National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report—Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress. American Institutes for Research, Washington, DC. http://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/index.html
title: Set ELP performance standards through a deliberative process combining empirical analyses with informed, trained expert judges rather than empirical data alone
description: The report's foundational principle is that standard setting for EL accountability criteria is "not merely an empirical procedure" but requires empirical information plus informed judges in a rational, coherent, transparent deliberative process. Empirical methods ground policy deliberations and clarify implications of options, while qualified, trained panelists make the final judgment. The report applies this by pairing the analytic methods of Chapters II–IV with guidelines drawn from standard-setting best practices.
requirements: Panelists must be selected and trained, with appropriate qualifications and no vested interest in the standards set
A clear, sequential, documented process and a mechanism to validate decisions must be in place
constraints: No one empirical method gives a complete picture; methods seldom provide definitive answers and data are almost always imperfect, with missing cases common in AMAO analyses
target_learners: English Learners (ELs) in K–12 state assessment and accountability systems
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency and academic content proficiency in English language arts and mathematics
examples: The report applies decision consistency, logistic regression, and box plot methods to authentic state and district data sets in three states as worked examples supporting deliberative standard setting

National Evaluation of Title III Implementation Supplemental Report—Exploring Approaches to Setting English Language Proficiency Performance Criteria and Monitoring English Learner Progress. article_title: Taking Deeper Learning to Scale
citation: Noguera, P. (2017). Taking deeper learning to scale. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/deeper-learning-to-scale
title: Deeper learning as a reform framework of higher-order competencies
description: The report frames deeper learning as a set of learning experiences and capacities that schools should make available to all students, particularly the disadvantaged. It defines deeper learning as "the utilization of higher order thinking capacities and learning experiences that include critical thinking, problem solving, independent research, evaluation, comparative analysis, and the opportunity to acquire the skills needed for college and career readiness." It links this to Common Core goals of flexible content understanding, collaboration, effective communication, and learning how to learn, and uses the framework to analyze three school-improvement cases.
requirements: Schools must create fewer, higher and deeper curriculum goals and build teacher and school capacity rather than relying on accountability pressure alone
constraints: The report states these learning goals are currently not available in many schools, particularly to the most disadvantaged students
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly economically disadvantaged and historically underperforming students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
problem solving
collaboration
communication
college and career readiness
examples: Brockton High School adopted deeper learning as its high-leverage improvement strategy through a schoolwide literacy program

article_title: Building School Communities for Students Living in Deep Poverty
citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Building school communities for students living in deep poverty. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/121.698
title: Deep poverty–responsive schooling framework: funding adequacy, community schools, and whole child culture
description: The report extends Richard Milner and colleagues' "poverty-responsive" framework to deep poverty, organizing school reform around three strategies: "1. Begin with funding adequacy and equity. 2. Develop community schools and partnerships. 3. Develop a whole child teaching and learning culture." It argues the framework requires shifting "deficit-based conceptions of students in poverty to those that are asset-based", developing community partnerships, and creating schools students living in poverty can depend on because many are "school dependent". The framework targets structural reform of funding, school organization, and pedagogy rather than fixing students.
requirements: Adequate and equitable school funding as the foundation for all other strategies
Partnerships with community agencies to respond to out-of-school issues
Asset-based educator mindsets that build on students' strengths
constraints: Education alone cannot eliminate childhood deep poverty; the report states a suite of policies including housing, health care, and employment is required
target_learners: Students living in deep poverty in the United States
Students in communities of concentrated poverty
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement and graduation
Social-emotional well-being and healing from trauma
Equality of educational opportunity
examples: The report addresses Milner's three steps in reverse order, beginning with funding because money matters, then community schools, then whole child culture
key_sources: Cookson, P. W., Jr., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Building school communities for students living in deep poverty. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/121.698

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Design teams and student advisory committees for student voice in decision-making
description: As part of increasing student voice in decision-making and strategic-planning forums, Long Beach Unified implemented two participatory structures. The report describes how "Design teams (groups of staff, family members, and students who identify equity challenges and potential solutions) and student advisory committees (students from various pathways who advise their principal on school climate topics) enabled a wide range of students to share their perspectives and take an active role in school improvements." These structures institutionalize diverse student representation in school governance and improvement processes.
requirements: Staff, family members, and students willing to serve together on design teams
Principals open to receiving student advisory input on school climate
target_learners: High school students from various pathways
School principals and staff
target_learning_goals: Student voice in school decision-making
Identifying and addressing equity challenges
examples: Student advisory committees drew students from various pathways to advise principals on school climate topics

article_title: Design Principles for Teacher Preparation: Enacting the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Rushing, J.). (2025). Design principles for teacher preparation: Enacting the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/115.854
title: Develop the skills, habits, and mindsets of an equitable educator
description: Because students learn best when school connects to their cultural contexts and their identities are affirmed, the report argues that EPPs must be designed to develop educators with mindsets that support all students well and equitably. Program faculty should model empathy, demonstrate social and emotional learning and cultural competence, and prepare educators to use restorative practices. This includes strengthening candidates' understanding of how to create environments of trust and belonging and build partnerships with families, community members, and other educators.
requirements: Faculty who model empathy, social and emotional learning, and cultural competence
Support for candidates to understand how contextual realities impact students' experiences and social identities
target_learners: Teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: Creating environments of trust and belonging
Negotiating school policies toward equitable ends
examples: Programs should prepare educators who understand how contextual realities impact the experiences of their students and their perceptions of social identities

article_title: Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named
citation: Nama, R. (2026). Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named. Author's accepted manuscript, AI and Ethics (Springer Nature). https://arxiv.org/
title: Treat user literacy as a first-class design objective, because design defaults are literacy interventions
description: The paper argues that engineers must recognize that "design defaults are literacy interventions whether or not they are intended as such": the single undifferentiated permission grant, the invisible action log, and execute-first reporting for irreversible actions each decide whether users develop capacity to govern agents. It recommends transparency-by-design embedding literacy into agent interactions, AI tutoring simulating agentic scenarios, and contextual micro-learning at the point of risk.
requirements: These capabilities require treating user literacy as a first-class design objective rather than features emerging from roadmaps optimized for task completion.
constraints: The author notes these features do not emerge organically from product roadmaps optimized for task completion.
target_learners: users of agentic AI platforms across healthcare, financial services, and workplace contexts
target_learning_goals: capacity to see, constrain, and contest agent actions
examples: The paper describes current defaults: a single 'Allow' button with no scope granularity, no explanation, and no visible revocation mechanism.
key_sources: Nama, R. (2026). Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named. Author's accepted manuscript, AI and Ethics (Springer Nature). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27396

article_title: Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning
citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543
title: Design agentic AI for intentional instructional friction rather than friction-free interfaces
description: The article recommends that rather than aiming for seamless, friction-free interfaces, AI systems should be intentionally designed to withhold answers and support. By engineering strategic "instructional friction," agents can force the critical thinking and active inquiry necessary to cement knowledge, ensuring the learner remains the primary driver of the intellectual journey. Examples include an AI that asks the student to explain how their hobby relates to a new topic rather than explaining for them, and an AI that pauses the interface when it detects rapid clicking or superficial answers.
requirements: Agents must be able to detect when support is being over-used (e.g., rapid clicking or superficial answers) to time friction appropriately
constraints: The article presents this as a design recommendation grounded in pedagogical literature, not as a tested intervention
target_learners: students learning with proactive AI tutors
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, active inquiry, productive struggle
examples: The PBL agent refuses to provide a direct solution pathway when students are stuck, offering clues about where to look instead
key_sources: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543

article_title: Can AI-Assisted Inquiry Enhance Students' Decision-Making Skills in Socio-Scientific Issues? A Three-Group Experimental Study on Climate Change
citation: Dimitrios Gousopoulos. (2026). Can AI-Assisted Inquiry Enhance Students' Decision-Making Skills in Socio-Scientific Issues? A Three-Group Experimental Study on Climate Change. International Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Studies. https://doi.org/10.62225/2583049X.2026.6.3.6516
title: Design conversational AI partners to question rather than to answer when supporting socio-scientific decision-making
description: The article concludes that generative AI supports decision-making learning best when its role is to probe student reasoning rather than supply conclusions: "AI helps most when it is designed to question rather than to answer." It further notes that "the inquiry it is embedded in carries much of the benefit," so the AI should supplement, not replace, an inquiry structure. Student verification of AI claims against sources is the mechanism the article links to gains.
requirements: Embed the AI within inquiry-based learning
Track whether students check AI claims against sources
constraints: The benefit is attributed partly to the surrounding inquiry, not the AI alone
target_learners: secondary students
target_learning_goals: decision-making on socio-scientific issues
examples: In the experiment, the AI-assisted group outgained inquiry-only and traditional groups, and checking AI claims against sources predicted individual gains

article_title: Artificial Intelligence and Collaborative Learning: Impacts on Creativity, Critical Thinking, and Problem-Solving
citation: Abderrahim Agnaou; Hayat El Asri. (2025). Artificial Intelligence and Collaborative Learning: Impacts on Creativity, Critical Thinking, and Problem-Solving. JERAP Vol. 15 (2025) Iss. 1. https://doi.org/10.5590/JERAP.2025.15.2120
title: Design LLMs that support rather than disrupt human collaboration, aligning AI tools with educational values
description: The article's forward-looking design recommendation is that as AI evolves, tools for collaborative learning should be built to reinforce group processes rather than undermine them. The authors "highlight the importance of designing LLMs that support rather than disrupt human collaboration," and pair this with "the need for alignment between AI tools and educational values." It directs AI developers and educators toward collaboration-preserving tool design.
requirements: AI tools used in collaborative learning must be aligned with educational values
constraints: Recommendation is framed as AI continues to evolve, based on a single study of undergraduate team projects
target_learners: undergraduate students working in teams
target_learning_goals: collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving
examples: The study's findings on LLM use in team-based projects are offered as the basis for emphasizing collaboration-supporting LLM design

article_title: The pitfalls of AI detection in academic writing: bias, false positives, and the need for inclusive assessment
citation: Victor Angelier. (2026). The pitfalls of AI detection in academic writing: bias, false positives, and the need for inclusive assessment. AI and Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-026-01376-w
title: AI-text detectors infer machine authorship from statistical properties of submitted text rather than directly observing provenance
description: The paper's conceptual account holds that passive detectors classify from "statistical or learned properties of submitted text, not provenance itself". Predictability-related properties such as low perplexity, reduced variation in local predictability, and formulaic density make both additional-language writing and highly conventional academic prose vulnerable to machine-authorship classification. Information-theoretic work shows that even an optimal detector "cannot obtain information that is absent from the observed text", so classification error cannot be eliminated when human and machine text distributions overlap. The account explains why vendor percentages should not be read as calibrated posterior probabilities of authorship.
requirements: Detectors require textual properties from which machine authorship can be inferred; the composition of proprietary features is not disclosed, so the mechanism of a proprietary score cannot be established externally
constraints: Classification error cannot be eliminated when underlying distributions are insufficiently separable
Benchmark performance may not transfer to multilingual, collaborative, translated, or heavily revised academic writing
Watermarking supports provenance verification only in controlled systems; absence of a watermark cannot establish human authorship

postgraduate researchers
scholarly authors
target_learning_goals: academic integrity assessment
academic writing evaluation
examples: The paper's Table 1 lists textual features plausibly associated with elevated flag-risk, such as restricted vocabulary range and conventional formulaic phrases, alongside their legitimate human origins

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: Delegate procedural execution to AI but keep prediction, evaluation, and representational coordination as student learning objectives
description: The article proposes a criterion for deciding what may be delegated to AI based on the cognitive level of the operation. It argues that "Procedural execution, running an integration algorithm or generating a standard plot, may legitimately be delegated to AI", by analogy with calculators replacing manual arithmetic. By contrast, predicting what a result should look like, judging whether AI output is physically meaningful, and coordinating representations across modalities are irreducibly human epistemic tasks that cannot be delegated without undermining course learning goals.
requirements: Teachers must judge which operations in a task are procedural versus epistemic before assigning AI support
constraints: The argument is theoretical, grounded in SRL, CTML, MER, and hybrid intelligence research rather than in new empirical data
target_learners: introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: representational competence
physical interpretation of model outputs
epistemic judgment
examples: In the elevator task, numerical integration and curve generation are delegated to AI, while explaining the meaning of slopes and checking physical consistency of the diagrams remain student tasks

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: Theoretical FLOP estimation framework for decoder-only transformer LLMs
description: The article derives theoretical floating-point operation counts for the most common architecture of open source LLMs, the Pre-Layer Normalisation decoder-only transformer, assuming Rotary Position Embeddings, RMS Layer Normalisation, and KV caching. Given the architecture and the numbers of prompt and completion tokens, the total cost of the first token and of subsequent tokens (which are computationally cheaper due to KV-caching) can be calculated from matrix-dimension FLOP rules. A simpler approximation, FLOPs = 2Nn where N is active parameters and n total tokens, was found in previous studies to be accurate within 10%.
requirements: Knowledge of the architecture and the number of prompt and completion tokens; for the full formula, model parameters such as d_model, d_ff, number of heads, layers, and vocabulary size
constraints: Recent DeepSeek versions using Multi-Headed Latent Attention are not considered in the calculations
The authors anticipate the difficulty of finding each required parameter for the full formula could be prohibitive for most users
target_learners: AIED researchers using open source or proprietary LLMs
target_learning_goals: Estimating and reporting the computational cost of LLM-based educational systems
examples: Figure 1 diagrams the decoder-only transformer, with grey arrows indicating matrix dimensions for parameter counts and blue arrows indicating FLOPs required to generate the first token

article_title: AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills
citation: M. Mikhasenko, M. Stahl, I. Segal, D. Parmar, A. Zimmer, and A. Kazatsky. (2026). AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05719
title: Require dedicated unaided practice for foundational knowledge, since assisted performance with AI is not independently retrievable knowledge
description: The article argues that because "assisted performance is not the same as independently retrievable knowledge," AI may act as an effective tutor but students need dedicated unaided practice to obtain foundational knowledge. The prevalent educational criterion should be whether a student can recall and apply knowledge without aid, as in a written examination. The KT1 examination's low, confounded record is offered as a warning supporting this distinction, alongside cited external evidence that unrestricted answer access can decrease long-term learning.
requirements: An assessment format in which students must recall and apply knowledge without aid
Separation of research-shaped exploratory work from foundational-skill assessment
constraints: The KT1 examination record was confounded by incentive structure and format differences, so it serves as a warning rather than a clean measure
target_learners: undergraduate physics students in AI-permitted courses
target_learning_goals: independently retrievable foundational physics knowledge
unaided problem-solving on standard calculations
examples: The revised KT1 plan makes a written examination the focus determining the final grade, with homework counting only toward bonus points and multiple mock examinations offered for unassisted practice

article_title: The Devil is in the Details: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World
citation: Aras Bozkurt, Helen Crompton, & Caroline Fell Kurban. (2026). The Devil is in the Det[ai]ls: AI Agents, Ghost Students, and the Crisis of Verified Presence in an Agentic AI World. Open Praxis, 18(1), 1–12. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.1.1145
title: Design assessment for verified human presence rather than relying on output-based submissions
description: Because agentic surrogates master the product but cannot demonstrate a process, the article recommends moving away from output-based assessments toward presence-required models such as oral examinations and defenses, live presentations with spontaneous questioning, in-person demonstrations, and dialogic assessment and reflective portfolios. These methods remain resistant to automation because they value the process of becoming, not just the product of doing. The article frames this as a structural redesign rather than better detection.
requirements: Faculty understanding of how AI browsers and autonomous agents function, what they can access, and what tasks they can complete
Time, funding, and professional support, since oral defenses and portfolios do not scale with the same frictionless ease as a quiz
constraints: Assessment models relying heavily on oral articulation or sustained reflection can inadvertently disadvantage students with disabilities, language barriers, or neurodivergence, so inclusive presence must be designed
target_learners: higher education students
online and hybrid course learners
target_learning_goals: authentic demonstration of learning
resistance to automated completion
articulation of reasoning in real time
examples: The editorial's audit questions ask educators where student presence is actually required, where learning is inferred rather than verified, and which assessments assume a human behind the keyboard
