article_title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
citation: Fang, L., Zhang, Y., Park, J., Wang, Z., Ma, P., Zhai, X. (2026). Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20264
title: Automated scores should carry explicit confidence so low-confidence responses are deferred to human review
description: Automated scoring systems should output not only a predicted score but also a confidence value that signals when the score can be trusted. The article's selective rule defers uncertain cases for manual evaluation, and states: "By varyingτ, we control the trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk." Varying the confidence threshold lets teachers triage responses and calibrate reliance on automated scores in classroom practice.
requirements: A response-level confidence score derived from test-time predictive distributions and a chosen confidence threshold τ
constraints: Confidence-aware scoring incurs higher inference cost because it aggregates multiple test-time augmented views
target_learners: middle school science students
target_learning_goals: trustworthy automated scoring of student-generated scientific models for formative assessment
examples: The study used the confidence score to decide when automated scores may be used without review and when teacher review is still needed for visually ambiguous drawings.

article_title: The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions
citation: Moiz Imran, Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions. PEAF 2026: Workshop on Pedagogical Evaluation of Automated Feedback. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5878-2143
title: Detect-verify-escalate pipeline with four pedagogically distinct routes
description: The pipeline routes each student submission through an answer-key check and, for correct-answer cases, an LLM graduated assessment producing four routes: Red (wrong answer, automated correction), Green (clear reasoning, no action), Amber-1 (unclear reasoning, automated diagnostic follow-up question), and Amber-2 (misconception detected, verification then teacher escalation). Figure 1 shows approximate volumes per 1,000 submissions: 736 LLM calls and 64 teacher reviews. The design responds to the paper's findings that fine-tuned models cannot assess method validity and that precision is too low for direct teacher escalation.
requirements: Reasoning-capable model, graduated output preserving the routing signal, and intermediate verification before teacher escalation
constraints: All findings come from 15 mathematics questions on one platform, with TM concentrated in 2 items; the diagnostic follow-up proof of concept generated questions for 7 TM instances with no student responses collected
target_learners: school mathematics students and their teachers
target_learning_goals: routing automated feedback according to reasoning validity and diagnostic certainty
examples: Two deployment configurations are proposed: a teacher dashboard mode where the system filters a review queue, and an autonomous tutor mode where each flag triggers a low-cost formative follow-up question

citation: Menggian Wu. (2026). Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming. 2nd International Workshop on AI Literacy Education For All (ALIT4ALL 2026), co-located with AIED 2026, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
title: Design AI-supported learning environments with deliberate instructional support for epistemic engagement, since it does not emerge spontaneously
description: Because robust epistemic engagement rarely emerges without intentional support, AI-supported learning environments should be designed so that task success cannot be achieved through superficial outsourcing. The article warns that 'in unregulated settings, surface-level task success and pseudo-success may become the dominant mode of interaction, as robust epistemic engagement does not reliably emerge without intentional instructional and design support.' This calls for CS curricula prioritizing high-level epistemic engagement over mere task completion.

constraints: Findings come from one undergraduate AI course dataset; the authors note the analyzed dataset's size and scope could be expanded for stronger generalization

target_learning_goals: genuine learning and epistemic engagement rather than pseudo-success
examples: The study used EAIL indicators as signals to identify deficiencies in epistemic engagement within student-AI dialogue

article_title: Artificial intelligence-supported learning and higher-order cognitive outcomes: the mediating role of metacognitive self-regulation
citation: Davor I, Larbi E and Boateng FO (2026). Artificial intelligence-supported learning and higher-order cognitive outcomes: the mediating role of metacognitive self-regulation. Front. Educ. 11:1855869. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1855869
title: Design AI-supported learning so that students actively regulate and scaffold their engagement rather than offload cognition
description: The article concludes that AI should be treated not merely as a learning tool but as a cognitive support system whose value depends on engagement quality: structured AI task scaffolding supports higher-order outcomes, while tendencies to delegate thinking to AI undermine them. It argues "the educational value associated with AI-supported learning depends on how students engage with AI systems," and highlights metacognitive self-regulation as the pathway to cultivate.
requirements: Instruction should promote planning, monitoring, and evaluation of AI-generated information rather than passive acceptance of AI outputs
constraints: Verification practices alone may not automatically strengthen higher-order cognitive outcomes unless learners actively regulate, monitor, and reflect on their cognitive engagement during AI interaction
The cross-sectional design does not permit causal inference, so design recommendations rest on statistical associations

target_learning_goals: critical thinking
technical problem-solving
metacognitive self-regulation
examples: The study measured AI task scaffolding with items such as "AI tools help me break complex academic tasks into smaller steps" and cognitive offloading with items such as "I rely on AI tools to solve problems instead of thinking through them myself"

article_title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
citation: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962
title: Hybrid Personalization Engine: closed-loop personalization coupling static knowledge grounding with dynamic learner memory
description: The Hybrid Personalization Engine is DeepTutor's explanatory architecture for personalized tutoring: it "couples static knowledge grounding with dynamic learner memory", pairing Static Knowledge Grounding (dual-index retrieval over course content) with Dynamic Personal Memory that distills multi-turn interactions into an evolving learner profile D=(Ds,Dw,Dr). The closed loop operationalizes formative assessment: "weaknesses diagnosed during problem tutoring propagate to Dw and directly shape which questions are generated next", while practice outcomes refine future explanations. Each completed interaction appends a trace tree and updates the profile, so every interaction personalizes the next.
requirements: requires a structured memory capturing fine-grained interaction histories rather than scalar skill scores
requires modules that share and continuously update the learner memory
constraints: quantitative evaluation covers only the tutoring core; longitudinal evaluation of the extension layers is left for future work
target_learners: university-level students across humanities, sciences, engineering, business, and frontier research domains
target_learning_goals: diagnosing and remediating individual knowledge gaps
difficulty-calibrated practice
citation-grounded explanation
examples: Tutoring proceeds through investigate, guided solving, and iterative writing stages; question generation separates idea selection from critic-guided question–answer–explanation construction.

article_title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
citation: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962
title: Trace Forest: hierarchical three-level learner memory with programmatic toolkit
description: The Trace Forest is DeepTutor's hierarchical memory in which each tree records one complete tutoring interaction as a multi-resolution, semantically searchable artifact. "Nodes are organized into three levels: Level 1 stores session-level input and a global summary; Level 2 captures intermediate planning units; and Level 3 preserves fine-grained execution records including tool outputs, evidence, and validation outcomes." Every node carries a dense embedding for similarity-based retrieval. A TraceToolkit exposes three operations — SearchTrace, ListTraces, and ReadNodes — letting every agent explore learner history at the resolution it needs.
requirements: every node carries a dense embedding to enable similarity-based retrieval across the forest
target_learners: individual university-level learners in multi-turn tutoring
target_learning_goals: fine-grained learner profiling for gap-aware tutoring and practice generation
examples: Three memory agents actively query the TraceToolkit to compare latest behavior against cross-session patterns before updating the profile.

article_title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
citation: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962
title: TutorBench: student-centric interactive benchmark with source-grounded learner profiles
description: TutorBench is a student-centric benchmark that "couples a detailed learner persona with source-grounded knowledge gaps and an interactive tutoring task". It draws on 30 knowledge bases spanning five broad disciplines, instantiates three learner profiles per knowledge base for 90 profiles, and retains exactly three accepted interactive tasks per profile, yielding 270 tasks. Gaps are typed as misconceptions, incomplete understanding, and missing knowledge, each anchored to specific source pages. Evaluation uses a first-person LLM student simulator and personalized rubrics, with entries checked by human reviewers before release.
requirements: profiles and tasks undergo human review for factual correctness, plausibility, gap–task consistency, and pedagogical naturalness
constraints: relies on LLM-powered student simulators and rubric-based assessors, inheriting a gap between controlled simulation and real learner behavior
target_learners: simulated university-level students at beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels
target_learning_goals: adaptive tutoring behavior across multi-turn dialogue and customized practice generation
examples: Each entry carries three source-grounded knowledge gaps, each anchored to specific pages from the source KB materials.

article_title: Data Annotations as Pedagogical Hints: From Subjective Labels to Critical Thinking
citation: Ralf Raumanns, Theresa Elstner, Louis Ferger-Andrews, Louise M. Carlsen, Martin Potthast, Gerard Schouten, Josien P. W. Pluim, and Veronika Cheplygina. (2026). Data annotations as pedagogical hints: from subjective labels to critical thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20149v2
title: Design annotation-based assignments so disagreement is explicitly framed as a learning opportunity, with sufficient interpretive ambiguity, reduced repetitive workload, and mitigated emotional discomfort
description: The article proposes that manual data annotation tasks serve as pedagogical hints teaching students that human judgement influences model behaviour, but only if designed deliberately. Its four stated takeaways for future iterations are to ensure "sufficient interpretive ambiguity", reduce repetitive workload, mitigate emotional discomfort, and explicitly frame disagreement as a learning opportunity rather than a problem to solve. Without such framing, students tend to treat inconsistency as a defect to eliminate rather than a signal of domain complexity.
requirements: The task must involve genuinely subjective annotation (e.g., hair coverage on a 3-point scale) rather than unambiguous labelling
Appropriate framing of medical-image discomfort and of disagreement as signal
constraints: Emotional discomfort from medical imagery risks overshadowing the learning if not framed appropriately
Repetitive labelling and cumbersome tooling can overshadow the learning potential
target_learners: Bachelor data science and machine learning students in university courses
target_learning_goals: Recognising subjectivity in data annotation
Connecting human judgement to model behaviour and AI bias
examples: At both universities, students annotated skin lesion images for hair coverage on a 3-point scale in groups over two weeks, documented decisions, and compared labels with peers to analyse disagreement

article_title: A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course
citation: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598
title: Deterministic pedagogical orchestration architecture with the LLM as linguistic executor
description: The architecture separates pedagogical orchestration from text generation: instructional decisions (intent recognition, concept selection, chunk typing, prompt structure) are handled by deterministic modules, and the LLM is restricted to controlled disambiguation and surface-form generation. The pipeline proceeds through six stages: intent detection, concept detection, constrained retrieval, didactic resolution, prompt construction, and LLM generation. This separation, in the authors' words, "ensures pedagogical traceability (every decision maps to an explicit rule), enforces correctness through deterministic unit-testable logic, and makes the pipeline model-agnostic". It was designed to operate without commercial LLM budget or GPU infrastructure.
requirements: A formalisation of the instructor's own pedagogical reasoning: intents, a domain ontology, and an instructor-authored structured editorial corpus
Detection lexicons calibrated to the course vocabulary and language
constraints: Adapting to a new course requires the instructor to formalise their own pedagogical practice, not merely configure a tool
Courses centred on theorem derivation, algorithmic processes, or code production may require different taxonomies and retrieval strategies
target_learners: University students in a French-language dimensional modelling course
target_learning_goals: Answering conceptual questions in dimensional modelling in line with the instructor's didactic practice
examples: For the query 'Qu'est-ce qu'une clé naturelle ?', the Definition approach retrieves the definition of the concept and, via the is a relation, its parent concept's definition, while the confused with relation injects a disambiguation note into the prompt

citation: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://luispprieto.com/
title: Design AIED scaffolding to fade: intervene just enough so learners outgrow the support as soon as possible
description: The paper argues against permanent technological presence, proposing instead that AIED systems intervene just enough and only while necessary, using minimum resources, so that learners progressively become autonomous from the scaffolding. It draws an analogy to psychotherapy, where the goal is that learners outgrow and abandon scaffolding as soon as possible, and cites Selwyn's idea of edtech within limits.

constraints: the paper notes fading is seldom studied or implemented in instructional design despite being considered important

self-regulation

citation: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://luispprieto.com/
title: Design to exit the screen: hand learner focus off to the real world rather than optimizing engagement with the system
description: This principle holds that because learning's socialization happens in the real world, technologies optimizing for engagement with the system interfere with such social processes. AIED should point to, foster, and effectively hand off learner focus towards the outside, including collaborative activities with fellow learners and ubiquitous learning activities interacting with the built or natural environment.

target_learners: learners in blended, face-to-face, or ubiquitous learning settings

article_title: The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment
citation: Donya Rooein, Luca Benedetto, Dirk Hovy. (2026). The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16993
title: Require demographic invariance in high-stakes LLM scoring while allowing deliberate demographic adaptation only in instructional feedback
description: The article recommends that automated scoring must be invariant to demographic signals, since essay scores should depend solely on essay quality, whereas instructional contexts may legitimately adapt, for example readability, to student characteristics. Its evidence shows current models cannot be trusted to make this distinction themselves: "current LLMs cannot reliably separate task-relevant information from demographic cues". Deployers therefore need to explicitly control or strip demographic context in evaluative pipelines. The article frames this as essential for fairness, transparency, and avoiding amplification of educational inequities.
requirements: Evaluative tasks must hold demographic context out of scoring prompts, per the finding that implicit cues can inflate scores.
Educational uses should define which demographic adaptations are pedagogically intended versus biased before deployment.
constraints: The article states current LLMs cannot reliably separate task-relevant information from demographic cues, so invariance cannot be assumed from prompting alone.
target_learners: students assessed or given feedback by LLM-based systems, including second-language learners
target_learning_goals: fair and consistent automated assessment
pedagogically appropriate personalized feedback
examples: In the article's AES experiment, most models stayed relatively stable under explicit persona conditioning, but implicit cues produced significant score shifts for several models, motivating invariance requirements for scoring.
key_sources: Donya Rooein, Luca Benedetto, Dirk Hovy. (2026). The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16993

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: Designed-pattern authoring: linking each teaching pattern to its generation rule, check, and reference analysis
description: A designed pattern is "a trend, group difference, interaction, or exception intentionally built into a dataset for students to investigate." The workflow records each pattern in an executable case specification connecting it to its generation rule, comparison groups, measurement, and sample-size requirements, so that the generation rule, numerical check, reference chart, and rubric use the same definition of the intended finding. Verification examines the combined effect of interacting rules on the exported data, and the probability set in the generator is not itself evidence that the pattern appears in the data.
requirements: Each pattern requires one or more checks; the specification defines how overlapping rules interact, since an adjustment made for one pattern may affect another
constraints: The order of generation rules affects what students observe; in WindowDash the ZIP 10011 cuisine adjustment overrides earlier cuisine rules
target_learners: undergraduate business analytics students
target_learning_goals: investigating unfamiliar data with AI
distinguishing counts from shares
justifying conclusions from evidence
examples: The Office Lunch Rush specification records the business question, the office-versus-other comparison over the same weekday lunch interval, the pickup-probability generation rule, and acceptance criteria on the pickup-share difference with minimum sample sizes

article_title: Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education
citation: Tseng, T., Seoror, L.H., Adda, J., Factor, M., Darabi, R., Matschke, K.R., Fu, T., Lin, A., Maram, A., Sinha, A. (2026). Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06721
title: Introduce deliberate friction into AI-generated code assistance to prioritize learning over vibe coding
description: The article argues that code assistants for learning should deliberately slow learners down rather than maximize efficiency. Flowcode instruments friction by "revealing individual explanation steps one at a time and requiring users to directly edit blanks in generated code snippets rather than be given a full solution." The authors see this as distinct from friction arising from LLM misinterpretation, aiming to prioritize deeper learning and direct experimentation.
requirements: An LLM prompted to produce incomplete, fill-in-the-blank code rather than full solutions
An interface that reveals explanations step by step and avoids one-click code transfer
constraints: Friction slows prototyping speed, which the authors present as a trade-off favoring learning
Fill-in-the-blank behavior was not fully reliable even after prompt refinement
target_learners: novice programmers and new creative coders
target_learning_goals: understanding generated and found code
actively writing code rather than pasting AI solutions
examples: Flowcode removed the copy-to-clipboard button, stopped auto-inserting generated code into editors, and required clicking a 'Show Next Step' button to reveal each explanation step

article_title: Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class
citation: Lili Chen, Gavin Buskes, Yuxin Ren and Chin Tong Leong. (2026). Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class. 37th Annual Conference of the Australasian Association for Engineering Education, UNSW, Sydney. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Decouple feedback immediacy from solution verification: keep the human in the loop upstream at answer verification, not at the point of grading
description: This design pattern resolves the tension between feedback immediacy and trustworthy human oversight by relocating human review. As the authors state, "Rather than asking GenAI to grade live submissions, we position human markers as upfront verifiers of answers and use the model only to generate immediate, scaffolded feedback against those human-endorsed solutions." GenAI then generates immediate feedback by reasoning against answers a human has already endorsed, preserving immediacy where it matters pedagogically while retaining oversight where students value it most. The authors argue this is a workable and transferable pattern for trustworthy, scalable formative practice in engineering education.
requirements: An existing, demonstrator-verified solution set for the GenAI to reason against
Staff comfortable with reviewing solutions of AI-generated questions
An institutional environment that permits GenAI for practice
constraints: Positioned as practice rather than assessment; the article does not claim the pattern is validated for graded assessment
target_learners: large undergraduate electrical engineering cohorts
target_learning_goals: formative practice in probability and random models
immediate scaffolded feedback guiding revision
examples: In the pilot, demonstrators verified problem-booklet solutions upfront and the feedback agent generated immediate feedback against those human-endorsed solutions, with prompts designed around the feed-forward principle
key_sources: Lili Chen, Gavin Buskes, Yuxin Ren and Chin Tong Leong. (2026). Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class. 37th Annual Conference of the Australasian Association for Engineering Education, UNSW, Sydney. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Design children's voice interfaces for being misheard, not just heard
description: The article's first lesson is that for young children, ASR errors and disfluencies are the norm, so tolerant multi-layer answer matching is "a first-class requirement in a children's voice interface". Without it, the authors report, correct answers were frequently rejected and the experience felt punitive. Robust matching should therefore be treated as core design, not an optional refinement.
requirements: A tolerant, multi-layer answer-matching pipeline (translation/transliteration, fuzzy matching, normalization)
target_learners: young children whose speech ASR misrecognizes
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair evaluation of spoken answers
examples: In the Kutti AI prototype, removing the tolerant matching layers caused correct answers to be frequently rejected

article_title: Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity
citation: Jonathan A. Karr Jr., Grigorii Khvatskii, Ting Hua, and Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity. Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit (AILS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11256
title: Treat detector output as weak evidence, never standalone misconduct evidence; pair any flag with drafting history and human judgment
description: The article's central policy recommendation is that AI-detector scores are structurally unreliable as sole evidence of misconduct because compliant light editing triggers flags while humanized synthetic text evades detection. It states that "Detector output must be treated as weak evidence, not default misconduct evidence" and that "Any flag must be paired with drafting history and sanctions shall be reserved for cases where human judgment supports a lack of appropriate student effort." Institutions should also expect higher flag rates in non-STEM prose and follow FERPA/GDPR rules before uploading student work to third-party services.
requirements: Any flag must be paired with drafting history and human judgment before sanctions
constraints: Findings are based on published English abstracts, not student essays; detector behavior on classroom genres may differ
Labels are proxy-based at a fixed τ = 0.50; 2023–2025 positives are flag rates, not confirmed false positives
Results used one rewrite generator, two detectors, and one humanizer and may not generalize to other tools
target_learners: higher education students
multilingual and novice writers
target_learning_goals: academic integrity policy and fair assessment of AI-assisted student writing
examples: The study flagged 64–80% of light Gemini edits of human abstracts while more than 96% of humanized AI rewrites evaded Pangram and GPTZero

article_title: LLM-Generated Design Problems for Assessing Higher-Order Thinking in Project-Based Learning
citation: Ahmad D. Suleiman, Daqing Hou, and Maliha Noushin Raida. (2026). LLM-Generated Design Problems for Assessing Higher-Order Thinking in Project-Based Learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.11032. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11032
title: Design problems (DPs): concise scenario-based transfer prompts for assessing higher-order thinking in PjBL
description: Design problems are concise, scenario-based exam prompts that ask students to apply project concepts in a new, realistic situation, targeting analysis, evaluation, and creation in Bloom's taxonomy. The article's prompt template requires that "The problem should begin with a short, realistic scenario" and that "The expected answer length is a few sentences to one paragraph." DPs were generated with LLMs, expert-rated on five criteria, and deployed as 30-minute supervised in-class assessments worth 2% of course grades.
requirements: A target learning objective and project details as prompt inputs; student answers of a few sentences to one paragraph answerable in 30 minutes
constraints: Open-ended grading remains subjective and may require additional support to scale; expert evaluation was conducted by two authors, which may introduce confirmation bias
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in project-based courses
target_learning_goals: transfer-oriented higher-order thinking: analyzing, evaluating, and designing in new contexts
examples: Deployed in three undergraduate courses: Breached! (N=28), Distributed Tic-Tac-Toe (N=40), and Touchalytics (N=10), as 30-minute supervised in-class summative assessments

article_title: How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding
citation: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109
title: Four design goals for automated qualitative coding systems derived from an exploratory literature review
description: From a PRISMA-guided exploratory review that screened 988 articles down to a final corpus of 118 papers, the authors derive four design goals for automated qualitative coding systems. The review holds that "Coding automation should help users make informed decisions by presenting outputs that are transparent in their reasoning and limitations." The goals are: DG1, provide reasons and evidence for how codes are assigned; DG2, illuminate uncertainties and interpretative variability in code assignments; DG3, enable users to calibrate expectations for coding accuracy; and DG4, facilitate users' understanding of how data characteristics affect coding accuracy.
requirements: Automated coding systems must expose coding reasoning, uncertainties, and reliability information so users can calibrate expectations, per the reviewed literature.
constraints: The review is explicitly exploratory rather than a comprehensive systematic review, and screening and codebook assessment were performed by single authors with one expert check.
target_learners: Qualitative researchers using automated coding systems
target_learning_goals: Understanding and interpreting AI-generated qualitative codes and their reliability
examples: The goals directly shaped the pipeline: justifications in prompts (DG1), two independent LLM coders with an 'Undecidable' label (DG2), coder disagreements as an accuracy proxy (DG3), and the dataset-characteristic analysis (DG4).
key_sources: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109

article_title: Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review
citation: Jennifer Lock, Soraya Arteaga, Carol Johnson. (2025). Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review. International Journal on Innovations in Online Education, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1615/IntJInnovOnlineEdu.2026060433
title: Develop AI literacy for both students and instructors as a foundation for intentional AI integration
description: The review concludes that institutions should foster AI literacy, defined by Crabtree (2023) as involving "the skills and competencies required to use AI technologies and applications effectively," including viewing technologies critically and questioning their design and implementation. The review states "an implication for practice is the development of AI literacy for both students and instructors," requiring keen discernment about how AI is used. Reviewed studies link higher AI literacy to academic well-being and success in digital environments.
requirements: Institutional role in helping students and instructors develop AI literacy; educational development provision for instructors
constraints: Reviewed studies note unreliable instructor support often derives from educators' limited AI literacy
target_learners: higher education students
higher education instructors
pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: critical, informed, and ethical use of AI technologies in learning
examples: Bae et al. (2024) found a strong need to focus on AI literacy development with pre-service teachers engaged in critical reflection on practical and ethical factors

article_title: Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?
citation: Luo, J. (Jess), & Eaton, S. (2026). Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(3). https://doi.org/10.53761/887m5346
title: Design teacher AI feedback use to maintain and enhance care, trust, and human connections rather than asking only whether to use AI
description: The article recommends moving "beyond the binary question of whether teachers should use AI or not" toward designing and operating feedback activities and teacher AI use in ways that "maintain and even enhance care, trust, and human connections central to effective feedback processes." The principle directs institutions and teachers to treat AI adoption as a design problem about preserving relational qualities of feedback, not a yes/no adoption decision.
requirements: Feedback activities and teacher AI use must be deliberately designed and operated, not merely adopted or rejected as a binary choice.
constraints: The study focuses on teachers in higher education; the authors note ethical AI use also requires effort from stakeholders beyond teachers.
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: effective, ethically sound feedback on student work
examples: The authors call for exploring how feedback activities and teacher AI use could be designed and operated to sustain care, trust, and human connections.

article_title: Beyond Automation: AI as a Pedagogical Mediator in Collaborative Learning
citation: Niari, M. (2026). Beyond Automation: AI as a Pedagogical Mediator in Collaborative Learning. Umanistica Digitale, 10(24), 121–142. https://doi.org/10.60923/issn.2532-8816/24266
title: Design AI for collaborative learning as a mediator that redistributes agency rather than as an automated tutor
description: This principle holds that AI in collaborative learning should be designed around mediation rather than automation: "Rather than treating AI as a tutor, peer, or automated orchestrator, the framework foregrounds mediation as a pedagogical function through which agency, authority, and responsibility are dynamically redistributed across human and non-human actors." Designers should therefore build AI that participates in orchestrating interaction, sense-making, and regulation while keeping learners and teachers as agents. The paper offers this as a design-relevant implication of its framework.
requirements: AI must participate in orchestration without displacing learner or teacher agency
constraints: The principle derives from a conceptual framework, not from empirical comparison of mediator versus tutor designs
target_learners: learners in collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning
distributed epistemic agency
shared regulation
examples: The paper contrasts mediator-oriented design with tool-centric paradigms and examines implications for collaborative learning design across its three mediating functions.

article_title: A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Shared departmental repository of AI-related teaching resources
description: The series' central product is a shared, evolving departmental repository pairing curated materials with framing for their use. The article reports: "Currently, it holds 5 entries, each pairing curated materials with brief framing for how to use them." Entries cover AI syllabus statements (including four sample policies spanning no use to full use), classroom discussion materials, student surveys with results across courses, homework tasks with AI integration, and assessment structures such as oral exams. Materials were shared with the department at the start of the following semester and continue to be updated.
requirements: Ongoing curation to keep the repository current as tools and practices evolve
constraints: The repository was also intended partly as a response to involving colleagues who did not participate in the series
target_learners: University physics faculty
target_learning_goals: Shaping course AI policies, classroom discussions, homework tasks, and assessment approaches
examples: The AI syllabus statements entry offers four sample policies spanning from no AI use to limited, conditional, and full-use

article_title: Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education
citation: Lawrence Obiuwevwi, Krzysztof J. Rechowicz, Jessica M. Johnson, Erika Frydenlund, Vikas Ashok, Sachin Shetty, & Sampath Jayarathna. (2026). Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214
title: Derive tactile graph parameters from tactile perception research rather than ad hoc choices
description: The pipeline's parameter derivation layer computes feature heights and spacings automatically from plate dimensions using established tactile perception findings, so every generated chart is readable by touch without per-chart manual tuning. Data features are set at 1.5 mm, three times the "0.5 mm height discriminability floor" from Lederman and Klatzky, and scatter-point separation is 3.5 mm, exceeding the 2–3 mm two-point discrimination threshold. Axis rails are taller than data features so a sweeping finger distinguishes structural boundaries from encoded data.
requirements: Plate dimensions in millimeters as input; adherence to BANA guidelines and Library of Congress Braille dot geometry for labels
constraints: Parameters are derived for FDM-printed plates within the clamped [80,250] mm dimension range
target_learners: blind and low-vision students reading tactile graphs by fingertip
target_learning_goals: haptic discrimination of chart structure, data features, and labels
examples: The derivation layer sets baseplate thickness via a clamp formula, reserves an 18 mm margin for dual-format labels, and sets Braille dots at 0.6 mm per Library of Congress standard

article_title: Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields
citation: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158
title: Demystify, use, and reflect: a structured LLM-intervention course design positioning LLMs as tools for supported learning
description: The course design centers on a structured intervention that works by "demystifying LLMs, how they work, their capabilities, and their probabilistic nature and limitations, alongside guided use through prompting strategies and iterative interaction". Rather than mandating or banning LLM use, the course leaves the decision to each student, requires students to understand, explain, and acknowledge AI-generated contributions, and adds a post-assignment reflection survey capturing prompt counts, role conceptualization, and verification strategies. This study extends the intervention by examining how its effects vary at the subfield level rather than only in aggregate.
requirements: Students need access to an LLM tool (institutionally licensed Microsoft Copilot Chat was available, though not restricted to a single tool)
Post-assignment reflection surveys must be administered immediately after task completion to capture interaction
constraints: The course did not explicitly encourage LLM use; the decision of whether and how to use them was left to each student
Findings are tied to the specific assignments and instructional practices of a single course context
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science students in a required post-CS1 problem-solving course
target_learning_goals: Informed and responsible LLM use
Effective prompting and iterative interaction
Assessing the reliability of LLM-generated responses
examples: One representative assignment per subfield: knapsack problem (Algorithms), Git commands practice (Software Engineering), HTTP request methods (Networking), HTML table design (Web Development), usability engineering report (HCI), SQL and Python (Databases), and Naive Bayes training and prediction (Machine Learning)
key_sources: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158

article_title: Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields
citation: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158
title: Design assignments and reflection activities that promote effective and critical LLM interaction rather than restricting LLM use
description: The article concludes that assignment design shapes how students engage with LLMs, and recommends that "Rather than restricting LLM use, educators can design tasks and reflection activities that promote effective and critical interaction with AI tools". This works by pairing structured instruction on how LLMs work with post-assignment reflection, so that student decisions about LLM use become informed rather than ad hoc. The article's evidence shows that under one consistently applied instructional design, adoption, role conceptualization, and verification still varied by assignment, making task design a central lever.
requirements: Structured instruction on LLM capabilities, limitations, and prompting strategies
Post-assignment reflection surveys capturing LLM use
Ethical-use norms requiring students to understand, explain, and acknowledge AI-generated contributions
constraints: The study identifies associations between assignment characteristics and LLM usage patterns but does not establish causality
Results are tied to the specific assignments used and should not be generalized without caution to all tasks in the same subfields
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: Responsible and critical interaction with AI tools
Verification of LLM-generated outputs
examples: The course required students to understand, explain, and acknowledge any AI-generated contributions, and completed a short reflection survey after each of the seven assignments

article_title: Who wrote this? Evaluating the reliability of AI detection tools in higher education
citation: Marijke Van Vlasselaer, Filip Van Droogenbroeck and Bram Spruyt. (2026). Who wrote this? Evaluating the reliability of AI detection tools in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00226-w
title: Use AI detection scores only as initial flags that trigger further review, never as sole evidence in high-stakes academic integrity decisions
description: The article recommends that institutions treat AI detection tool output as one component of a broader evaluation strategy rather than as decisive proof of misconduct. It argues that "tools like Pangram could be considered as an initial flag for further investigation" and that "A flagged result should trigger a more thorough review of the student’s paper content, rather than relying on an AI detection tool to draw a final conclusion." This follows from the study's finding that tools vary strongly in accuracy and can severely underestimate AI content.
requirements: Institutions establish clear and explicit policies outlining when and how the use of generative AI constitutes a breach of academic integrity
constraints: The article notes some tools may use conservative thresholds to avoid falsely labelling human-written text as AI-generated, which may increase the number of false negatives
target_learners: higher education students, particularly master's thesis writers
target_learning_goals: academic integrity in written academic work
examples: The study applied Pangram to 1,163 master's theses and recommends flagged results trigger a more thorough review of the student's paper content rather than a final conclusion

article_title: AI-Mediated Learning and the Restructuring of Interpretive Cognition: A Developmental-Critical Model for Social Sciences and Humanities Education
citation: Voicu, C.-G. (2026). AI-Mediated Learning and the Restructuring of Interpretive Cognition: A Developmental-Critical Model for Social Sciences and Humanities Education. Journal of Digital Pedagogy, 5(1) 37-51. https://doi.org/10.61071/JDP .2665
title: Developmental-Critical Model for AI-Mediated SSH Pedagogy with Six Checkpoints
description: A three-stage pedagogical framework guiding learners from AI-dependent toward AI-critical interpretation, grounded in cognitive-developmental theory, hermeneutics, and critical pedagogy. It is "operationalized through six pedagogical checkpoints that scaffold interpretive autonomy": interpretive grounding prior to AI use, contextual anchoring of AI outputs, critical examination of algorithmic structures, hybrid authorship transparency, reflexive epistemic positioning, and dialogic engagement under human control. Each checkpoint addresses an observed risk including interpretive shortcutting, epistemic outsourcing, and loss of authorial voice, and is derived from the observed interactional patterns.
requirements: Learners engage directly with primary materials before using AI tools (interpretive grounding)
Pedagogical mediation that keeps AI functioning as scaffold rather than substitute for reasoning
constraints: The article states the model is "a flexible framework whose application may vary across disciplines, learner profiles, and levels of AI integration"
Based on qualitative, context-specific observations from a single classroom; does not aim for statistical generalization
target_learners: Lower secondary students (aged 13-15) in SSH education
target_learning_goals: Critical AI literacy
Epistemic responsibility
Interpretive autonomy
examples: The six checkpoints were derived directly from observed interactional patterns in 42 coded episodes and correspond to transitions between the three developmental stages

article_title: Tracing GenAI Literacy: Student-AI Interaction Patterns in Academic Writing
citation: Angxuan Chen, Jiyou Jia. (2026). Tracing GenAI Literacy: Uncovering Student-AI Interaction Patterns in Academic Writing through Epistemic Network Analysis. First International Workshop on Advancing AI Literacy with Learning Analytics (AI-LIT) @ LAK26, April 2026.
title: Custom GenAI writing platform with 30-word prompt limit and copy-paste disabled
description: The learning task used a custom-built platform integrated with the DeepSeek Large Language Model in which students wrote an academic abstract for a research paper. To encourage meaningful interaction, "the platform imposed a 30-word limit per prompt and disabled copy-pasting, forcing students to synthesize AI outputs rather than passively adopting them." article_title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis.
citation: Adesope, O. O., & Nesbit, J. C. (2012). Verbal Redundancy in Multimedia Learning Environments: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026147
title: Add spoken–written redundancy for system-paced, picture-free multimedia aimed at low-knowledge or less fluent readers, using written key terms rather than verbatim text
description: The article's design implication is that verbal redundancy should be applied selectively: adding text to audio narration benefits learning when learners cannot control pacing and materials lack pictorial components, and written text should display key terms extracted from the narration rather than reproduce it verbatim. The article reports that "presentations that use written key terms from spoken narrations are associated with greater learning than are fully redundant spoken–written presentations." Benefits concentrate among low prior knowledge, second-language, and nonfluent readers.
requirements: System-paced presentation without learner control over pacing
Learning materials free of concurrent diagrams, images, or animation
Written text drawn from key terms or abridgements of the narration
constraints: Not beneficial when learners can pause, rewind, or slow materials themselves (learner-paced studies showed no detectable effect)
Not beneficial when images or animation are concurrently presented (g = 0.06)
High prior knowledge learners showed no advantage (g = –0.05)
target_learners: low prior knowledge learners
second-language learners
early or nonfluent readers
target_learning_goals: retention of narrated multimedia content
examples: Mayer and Johnson (2008) studies cited in the article used key phrases of two or three words appearing at appropriate diagram locations as the phrases were spoken

article_title: How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro
citation: Vibeke Normann Andersen and Kasper M. Hansen. (2007). How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro. European Journal of Political Research, Volume 46, Issue 4, pp. 531-556. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6765.2007.00699.x
title: The Deliberative Poll as a quasi-experimental model of deliberative democracy
description: The Deliberative Poll is a deliberative-democracy instrument in which a representative sample of citizens assembles to deliberate on a policy question, and its effects are studied quasi-experimentally. The article states: "As a quasi-experiment, the Deliberative Poll is an example of deliberative democracy." In this Danish application, "a representative sample of 364 Danish citizens assembled to deliberate on Denmark's participation in the single currency," and the resulting opinion change, knowledge gains and improved reasoned opinion formation are treated as evidence about what deliberation does to citizens.
requirements: A representative sample of citizens assembled for deliberation on a defined policy subject
Pre/post measurement of opinions and knowledge to support quasi-experimental analysis
constraints: Findings are tied to a single national Poll on the euro in Denmark; the article treats the Poll as one example of deliberative democracy rather than a general test
target_learners: Adult citizens in a national representative sample
target_learning_goals: Forming reasoned political opinions
Increasing knowledge of the deliberated policy issue
examples: The Danish national Deliberative Poll on the euro, in which 364 citizens deliberated on Denmark's participation in the single currency

article_title: Bayesian knowledge tracing, logistic models, and beyond: an overview of learner modeling techniques
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Bassen, Jonathan Huang, Surya Ganguli, Mehran Sahami, Leonidas Guibas, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein. (2015). Deep Knowledge Tracing. https://github.com/chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing
title: Deep Knowledge Tracing: modeling latent student knowledge with recurrent neural networks
description: Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) applies recurrent neural networks that are deep in time to model a student's latent knowledge state and its temporal dynamics as large vectors of artificial neurons. The latent representation is learned from interaction data rather than hard-coded from expert concept labels. Inputs are one-hot encodings (or random compressed vectors for large feature spaces) of the exercise-answered/correctness tuple, and outputs are predicted probabilities of correctness for each exercise. The article evaluates the LSTM and vanilla RNN variants on simulated, Khan Academy, and Assistments data.
requirements: Requires large amounts of student interaction training data, which the authors say makes RNNs well suited to online education environments
constraints: One disadvantage of RNNs over simple hidden Markov methods is that they require large amounts of training data, making them ill-suited to a small classroom environment, per the article
target_learners: Students interacting with online educational platforms and intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Prediction of student performance on future exercises; modeling knowledge growth over time
examples: The article trains an LSTM with hidden dimensionality of 200 and mini-batch size 100 using stochastic gradient descent with dropout and truncated gradients.
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Bassen, Jonathan Huang, Surya Ganguli, Mehran Sahami, Leonidas Guibas, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein. (2015). Deep Knowledge Tracing. https://github.com/chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing

article_title: Getting a Read on the App Stores: A Market Scan and Analysis of Children's Literacy Apps
citation: Vaala, S., Ly, A., & Levine, M.H. (2015). Getting a read on the app stores: A market scan and analysis of children's literacy apps. New York, NY: The Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop. https://www.joanganzcooneycenter.org
title: Design educational apps for intergenerational joint media engagement with explicit multi-user features
description: The report recommends that developers of children's educational apps build in features that engage multiple users, because "Young children learn best when another caring individual joins in the process." Suggested design moves include designing with the child's interests in mind, adding content or mechanics challenging enough to hold an older co-user's interest, and enabling co-users to create content together. This recommendation responds to the scan's finding that almost no popular literacy apps currently include such features.
requirements: Developers must add explicit design features that engage multiple users, such as collaborative or competitive co-use mechanics
constraints: The scan found only two apps in the sample had explicit co-use functions, so current-market exemplars are scarce
target_learners: children ages 0-8 learning language and literacy
target_learning_goals: language and literacy development through adult-child co-use of digital media
examples: The report suggests "incorporating content or mechanics that are more challenging to maintain an older user's interest, and enabling co-users to create content together"
key_sources: Vaala, S., Ly, A., & Levine, M.H. (2015). Getting a read on the app stores: A market scan and analysis of children's literacy apps. New York, NY: The Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop. https://joanganzcooneycenter.org/publication/getting-a-read-on-the-app-stores-a-market-scan-and-analysis-of-childrens-literacy-apps/

article_title: Digital Games, Design, and Learning
citation: Clark, D. B., Tanner-Smith, E. E., & Killingsworth, S. S. (2016). Digital Games, Design, and Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 86(1). https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065
title: Attend to game design features, not just the medium, when designing games for learning
description: The meta-analysis argues that the learning value of digital games depends on specific design features rather than on the medium as such. It introduced value-added comparisons — "the efficacy of a standard version of a game relative to an enhanced version augmented to test a theoretical design proposition" — precisely to isolate design contributions, and found augmented designs outperformed standard versions. Moderators such as session count, player configuration, visual realism, and story relevance further show design characteristics shape effects.
requirements: Studies or designs must allow comparison of an enhanced game variant against an equivalent standard version of the same game to isolate the design feature's contribution.
constraints: Only one enhancement category (enhanced scaffolding) had substantial representation; other categories' effects were not significantly different from zero, likely due to small numbers of effect sizes.
target_learners: K–16 students, ages 6 to 25
target_learning_goals: Cognitive, intrapersonal, and interpersonal learning outcomes aligned with the NRC Education for Life and Work framework
examples: The review synthesized 40 value-added effect sizes from 20 studies comparing enhanced versus standard game versions, finding g = 0.34 overall and g = 0.41 for enhanced scaffolding designs.
key_sources: Clark, D. B., Tanner-Smith, E. E., & Killingsworth, S. S. (2016). Digital Games, Design, and Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 86(1). https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065

article_title: Effective differentiation Practices:A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education
citation: Deunk, M. I., Jacobse, A. E., de Boer, H., Doolaard, S., & Bosker, R. J. (2018). Effective differentiation Practices: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education. Educational Research Review, 24, 31-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.02.002
title: Systematic review evidence base of 21 primary-education differentiation studies yielding 78 effect sizes
description: The evidence base for this review is a corpus of empirical studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education published since 1995. The authors state they synthesized "the results of empirical studies (n = 21) on this topic since 1995" and that "We extracted 78 effect sizes from the included studies." Outcomes covered are language and math performance in primary education.
requirements: Studies had to be empirical studies of differentiation practices' effects on language or math performance in primary education, published since 1995
target_learners: primary education students
target_learning_goals: language performance
mathematics performance

Educational Research Review, 24, 31-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.02.002

article_title: FREQUENCY EFFECTS IN LANGUAGE PROCESSING
citation: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024
title: Determinants of pattern productivity in construction learning
description: The review identifies a set of learning mechanisms that determine how productive linguistic patterns become. As printed, "Determinants of pattern productivity include the power law of practice, cue competition and constraint satisfaction, connectionist learning, and effects of type and token frequency". This framework explains why some constructions generalize while others remain item-bound, and it connects second language acquisition to general principles of learning drawn from cognitive psychology and connectionism.
requirements: Pattern productivity depends on the interplay of practice history, cue competition, and the type versus token frequency of exemplars.
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: developing productive command of grammatical constructions
key_sources: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024

article_title: Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1)
citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Definitional spectrum of school attendance and its problems from full presence to complete absence
description: The review presents a dimensional approach placing school attendance and its problems on a spectrum "ranging from full presence to complete absence" (Figure 1). The left side includes attendance with little difficulty and early warning signs such as frequent requests to leave the classroom; the middle covers mixed attendance such as tardiness and periodic absences; the right side covers complete absenteeism, stayout, and dropout. The spectrum captures fluid peri-attendance phenomena and treats dropout as a process rather than an event.
requirements: Specific, operational definitions for each panel of the spectrum remain needed
constraints: Lacks current utility in school districts and research studies, provides no etiological or functional information, and is not linked to prevention or intervention protocols
target_learners: children and adolescents in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: rapid, real-time assessment of type of school attendance problem
examples: Pflug and Schneider (2016) found among students with absenteeism in the past 7 days that 35.0% missed a single class or part of a school day, 31.3% missed an entire day, and 33.7% missed 2+ days
key_sources: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Determinant frameworks: descriptive structures specifying classes of determinants influencing implementation outcomes
description: Determinant frameworks form the second category. They "specify types (also known as classes or domains) of determinants and individual determinants, which act as barriers and enablers (independent variables) that influence implementation outcomes (dependent variables)". Their overarching aim is to understand and/or explain influences on implementation outcomes, e.g. predicting or retrospectively interpreting outcomes. Examples include PARIHS, CFIR, the Ecological Framework by Durlak and DuPre, and the Theoretical Domains Framework. They are multilevel and imply a systems approach, but "do not address how change takes place or any causal mechanisms, underscoring that they should not be considered theories".
requirements: Information about what influences implementation outcomes is potentially useful for designing and executing implementation strategies that aim to change relevant determinants
constraints: Most determinant frameworks provide limited how-to support since the determinants usually are too generic to provide sufficient detail for guiding an implementation process; they do not explicitly take a process perspective
target_learners: implementation researchers
health care quality improvement practitioners
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining influences on implementation outcomes
examples: PARIHS emerged from the observation that successful implementation might be premised on three key determinants: characteristics of the evidence, context and facilitation
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy
citation: Su, Y.-L., & Reeve, J. (2011). A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy. Educational Psychology Review, 23, 159–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9142-7
title: Design autonomy-support training programs that train multiple elements of autonomy support in brief, skill-based, multimedia sessions
description: The article's moderator results are presented as design guidance for future programs: relatively more effective programs "trained multiple elements of autonomy support" and were "presented in relatively brief (1–3 h) sessions in a laboratory training setting that focused on skill-based activities and utilized multiple types of media." The authors state the results "identified the conditions under which future programs can be designed to be highly effective."
requirements: Programs must target people who support others' autonomy, such as teachers
constraints: The small number of included studies warrants caution, as the authors state
target_learners: teachers
other professionals who support others' autonomy
target_learning_goals: adopting an autonomy-supportive motivating or teaching style
examples: The meta-analysis compared program subcategories on delivery format, session length, setting, activity type, and media use
