article_title: Picture this! Effects of photographs, diagrams, animations, and sketching on learning and beliefs about learning from a geoscience text
citation: Wiley, J. (2019). Picture this! Effects of photographs, diagrams, animations, and sketching on learning and beliefs about learning from a geoscience text. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 33, 9-19. https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.3495
title: Deception account of seduction effects on comprehension monitoring
description: The deception account holds that the presence of even instructionally-relevant images can deceive readers about their own level of understanding, producing illusions of comprehension. The article states that "the presence of even instructionally-relevant images can impact readers' ability to monitor their understanding", so poor learning may follow from investing too little effort in building a mental model. It extends traditional seduction-effect research beyond irrelevant decorative images to relevant animations and diagrams.
requirements: Readers must make predictive judgments of understanding that can be compared against actual learning outcomes to detect illusions
constraints: The article notes not every image type undermined monitoring; the presence of any type of image was not sufficient to harm monitoring accuracy compared to no-image conditions
target_learners: undergraduate students reading expository science texts
target_learning_goals: accurate comprehension monitoring and causal understanding of scientific processes from expository text
examples: Readers exposed to animated diagrams experienced illusions of understanding, while readers instructed to sketch a model of the earth's climate system did not
key_sources: Wiley, J. (2019). Picture this! Effects of photographs, diagrams, animations, and sketching on learning and beliefs about learning from a geoscience text. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 33, 9-19. https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.3495

article_title: The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing
citation: Marsh, E. J., Roediger, H. L., III, Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2007). The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(2), 194-199. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03192794
title: Design multiple-choice testing to include immediate feedback, a don't-know option with penalties, and varied question formats to reduce the learning of false facts
description: The review offers educators concrete ways to keep the memorial benefits of multiple-choice testing while limiting its negative side effects. Its recommendations are to "give immediate feedback," to follow the SAT II's example of "offering a 'don't know' option, with a penalty for selecting a wrong answer," and to change how concepts are tested across exams. Tools such as the IFAT (Immediate Feedback Test) implement the feedback recommendation by letting students scratch until they reach the starred correct answer.
requirements: Assessment must tolerate a don't-know response option with a penalty for wrong answers, as the SAT II does
constraints: Switching from a definitional multiple-choice question to an application cued recall question reduced but did not eliminate negative testing effects
target_learners: students taking objective tests in educational settings
target_learning_goals: accurate factual knowledge from assessment activities
examples: The IFAT commercial Scantron form gives immediate feedback: a missing star shows the student the selected answer is wrong (Epstein, Epstein, & Brosvic, 2001)
key_sources: Marsh, E. J., Roediger, H. L., III, Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2007). The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(2), 194-199. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03194051

article_title: The effectiveness of collaborative problem solving in promoting students’ critical thinking: A meta-analysis based on empirical literature
citation: Xu, E., Wang, W., & Wang, Q. (2023). The effectiveness of collaborative problem solving in promoting students' critical thinking: A meta-analysis based on empirical literature. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-023-01508-1
title: Design collaborative problem-solving for critical thinking around real problems, mixed courses, small groups, and teacher-supported scaffolds
description: The article distills its meta-analytic findings into instructional recommendations for teaching critical thinking through collaborative problem-solving. Teachers should "put a special emphasis on the two core elements, which are collaboration and problem-solving, to design real problems based on collaborative situations", implement mixed course teaching in parallel with subject teaching, favor small groups of 2–3 members, and provide teacher-supported learning scaffolds, which showed the largest effect (ES = 0.92).
requirements: Teachers must be able to design real problems grounded in collaborative situations and support discussion, negotiation, and argument among group members.
Mixed course implementation requires combining explicit critical thinking method training with the knowledge content of specific disciplines.
constraints: The recommendations rest on the 36 included studies published 2000–2021 in English and Chinese; the authors note the search may have overlooked studies in other languages and that data on teacher training and learner demographics were partially missing.
The independent-course and 1–4-week subgroups had very few effect quantities, so the teaching-type and duration comparisons are limited.
target_learners: K-12 students and college students
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking, including its attitudinal tendency and cognitive skill dimensions
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 79 effect quantities from 36 experimental or quasi-experimental studies to show mixed courses (ES = 1.34) and 2–3-person groups (ES = 0.99) yielded the largest subgroup effects.
key_sources: Xu, E., Wang, W., & Wang, Q. (2023). The effectiveness of collaborative problem solving in promoting students' critical thinking: A meta-analysis based on empirical literature. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-023-01508-1

article_title: How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play
citation: Yuill N, Hinske S, Williams SE and Leith G (2014) How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play. Front. Psychol. 5:418. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00418
title: Design shared play environments to boost successful attention capture, because getting noticed supports getting on
description: The article argues that cooperative interaction depends on "micromoments of successful attention bids": "The more attention bids succeed, the more likely is cooperation." Environments can therefore be designed with shareable, salient attention-getters — such as context-relevant audio that is simultaneously shared and hard to ignore — to raise the success rate of attention bids and thereby sustain cooperative play and shared understanding. The authors frame this as a method of "experimental technology" for testing how psychological mechanisms support interaction.
requirements: Attention-getting cues that are shareable across the group simultaneously, such as audio, rather than cues specific to one individual
constraints: For groups with atypical patterns of attention to other people, as in autism, the authors suggest environmental support may require less novelty and more time for habituation
target_learners: children in early and middle childhood playing or working in small groups
target_learning_goals: cooperative play and collaboration
shared attention and shared understanding
joint narrative production
examples: The AKC produced context-relevant sounds when tagged figures were placed at tagged locations, and children in the AKC condition sometimes captured attention themselves with visual cues or self-made sound effects when no sound was triggered.
key_sources: Yuill N, Hinske S, Williams SE and Leith G (2014) How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play. Front. Psychol. 5:418. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00418

article_title: Instructional technologies in developing countries: A contextual analysis approach
citation: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Challenges of instructional technology initiatives in developing countries span socio-cultural, human capacity and infrastructure categories
description: The article enumerates an illustrative list of challenges that "span the social, cultural, environmental and institutional contexts." Socio-cultural and human capacity factors include an incipient culture of participation, centralized decision-making, resources for learning and support, lack of budget planning and scarcity of qualified personnel. Infrastructure factors include unreliable power and telecommunications grids, hardware/software/maintenance/support needs, and adequate facilities such as cooling, ventilation and dust control.
requirements: Designers must account for these factors during the analysis phase rather than assuming the traditional analysis phase covers them
constraints: The list is presented as illustrative, not exhaustive
target_learners: learners in developing countries at primary, secondary, tertiary and adult training levels
target_learning_goals: implementing sustainable instructional technology initiatives
examples: The article notes users in developing countries may only have internet access through low bandwidth connections, and that hot and humid climates require cooling, ventilation and dust control
key_sources: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528

article_title: Instructional technologies in developing countries: A contextual analysis approach
citation: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Design for available human capacity by planning maintenance or incorporating a simple maintenance structure
description: Because qualified staff to maintain new instructional technology may not be available, the article states that "the design process for developing country contexts needs to consider the amount of human capacity available for maintenance, or ensure that the design incorporates a very simple maintenance structure." Designers should match system complexity to local maintenance capacity.
requirements: Analysis of local human capacity for maintenance during the design phase
constraints: Arises from the scarcity of qualified personnel challenge in developing countries
target_learners: learners and institutions in developing countries
target_learning_goals: sustainable operation of instructional technology systems
examples: The article pairs this with budgeting for import duties and securing maintenance, support and upgrades locally or with the overseas vendor
key_sources: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528

article_title: Instructional technologies in developing countries: A contextual analysis approach
citation: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Deployed instructional technology programs in developing countries (interactive radio instruction, Telesecundaria, Enlaces)
description: The article surveys instructional technologies deployed in developing countries across delivery formats including radio, television, computers, the internet, print, audio cassettes and CD-ROMs. Examples include interactive radio instruction launched in Nicaragua in the 1970s to teach mathematics to isolated rural children, Mexico's Telesecundaria providing televised instruction to seventh through ninth graders in remote areas for over thirty years, and Chile's Enlaces Network launched in 1993 to provide teachers and students with new instructional content, information resources and communications for collaboration.
requirements: Programs were designed explicitly or implicitly using the instructional systems design process, per the article
constraints: Examples are historical deployments described to motivate the need for context-based analysis
target_learners: primary, secondary and tertiary students and teachers in developing countries
target_learning_goals: expanding access to education and improving instructional quality
examples: China reported in 1990 that its television universities had enrolled 1.83 million students

article_title: Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction.
citation: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-6499-1
title: Design a learning companion agent's competency and interaction type according to the desired learning and motivational goals
description: The article concludes that "the competency and interaction type of a PAL should be designed according to the desired learning and motivational goals." High-competency PALs suit goals focused on knowledge and skill acquisition; low-competency PALs suit contexts where learner self-efficacy or confidence in an unfamiliar domain is a major concern; a proactive role is recommended to supply novices with necessary information they would not request. This flexibility is framed as a strength of PAL environments over human peer-mediated and traditional computer-based learning.
requirements: Designers must choose competency level and interaction control deliberately, since each variable affects different outcome measures
constraints: The desirable interaction type may interact strongly with learner characteristics such as prior knowledge, personality, cognitive styles, and age, so permutations are beneficial only when considering the learner and task at hand
target_learners: novice learners in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition; learner self-efficacy and confidence; engagement with agent-provided information
examples: In the experiment, PAL scripts were authored as either novice-like suggestions (8 idea units) or advanced-peer accurate comments (12 idea units), and proactive PALs delivered information on phase entry while responsive PALs spoke only when clicked
key_sources: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-8805-z

article_title: Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally
citation: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x
title: Design for local context rather than implementing one-size-fits-all content or best practices
description: The article argues that implicit in many online instructional design models is the idea that lesson content determines a one-size-fits-all delivery method, which ignores the differential needs of learners in various contexts. Designers should instead determine priorities that "meet local needs/desires," gain support of influential local people, openly discuss concerns with local staff, and leave social norms and traditions untouched where possible.
requirements: Instructional designers need contact with learners and feedback loops; organizations must allow designer involvement in audience analysis
constraints: The article states changing to a more culturally sensitive design paradigm is difficult given IDT's history of overemphasizing content development
target_learners: International and cross-cultural online learners
target_learning_goals: Relevance and usability of online instruction across cultures
examples: Mike recommended not simply implementing best practices and making the hierarchy a group of facilitators; Carrie described Australian designers demoted to technologist roles producing quick-fix courses without ever meeting students.
key_sources: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x

article_title: Critical Ethical Reasoning and Role-Play
citation: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313
title: Descriptive, critical ethics as a two-axis framework for locating ethical theories and as the chosen framework for ethical reasoning education
description: The article defines a two-axis space for locating ethical theories: normative versus descriptive, and dogmatic versus critical. Normative theories judge instances from a priori premised norms, while descriptive ethics derive norms a posteriori from how people actually act; dogmatic approaches assume all good people agree, while critical ethics requires learning another's norms and evaluating behavior on their own criteria. The authors select descriptive critical ethics as the framework for analysis, arguing it is the most appropriate framework for ethical reasoning education in a diverse democratic society.
requirements: Education in ethical reasoning in a democracy must honor principled disagreement as legitimate rather than impose one ethical system dogmatically
constraints: The article locates most historical moral education movements in the descriptive and dogmatic quadrant, with recent work renewing the critical focus
target_learners: students in democratic civic and moral education
target_learning_goals: critical ethical reasoning
empathy and understanding of others' moral contexts
examples: The study applies this framework to analyze how role-players talk about ethical decisions in games, building categories guided by the principles expressed in the descriptive, critical ethics literature
key_sources: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Design mLearning content for the least common denominator of mobile devices
description: The article recommends chunking and packing learning content into multimedia messaging services or SMS so it works on a variety of mobile phones, since simple phones have more limited functions than smart phones. Supporting evidence includes the Shanghai Jiaotong survey showing students prefer short video-based materials. The principle holds that content should be usable across the range of devices learners actually carry.
requirements: Learning content needs to be chunked and packed into multimedia messaging services or SMS
target_learners: learners using simple mobile phones as well as smart phones
target_learning_goals: delivering instructional content usable across varied mobile devices
examples: The article cites the survey of 3000 Online College of Shanghai Jiaotong University participants showing preference for video-based materials under 5 minutes per video
key_sources: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x

article_title: Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period
citation: Clark, C. A. C., Nelson, J. M., Garza, J., Sheffield, T. D., Wiebe, S. A., & Espy, K. A. (2014). Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00107
title: Developmental cascade model: processing speed as a driving mechanism for higher-order cognition including EC
description: The developmental cascade model holds that growth in domain-general processing speed drives gains in higher-order cognition such as working memory and inhibitory control. The article states that "processing speed is conceptualized as a central mental capacity that drives changes in higher-order cognition", with age-related speed gains freeing cognitive resources for executive operations. This study tested the cascade account in early childhood by modeling EC and processing speed as overlapping latents across preschool age points, finding both support (speed contributes substantially to executive performance) and qualitative shifts in their interface over time.
requirements: Latent modeling that simultaneously loads executive tasks on EC and processing speed factors to parse their relative contributions
constraints: The article notes mediation analyses cannot reveal changes in the interplay of processing speed and EC over development, motivating its age-point approach
target_learners: preschool children aged 3 to 5.25 years
target_learning_goals: executive control development supporting mathematics achievement
examples: The study loaded each executive task simultaneously onto EC and processing speed factors at ages 3, 3.75, 4.5, and 5.25, covarying language proficiency
key_sources: Clark, C. A. C., Nelson, J. M., Garza, J., Sheffield, T. D., Wiebe, S. A., & Espy, K. A. (2014). Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00107

article_title: The development of emotion regulation: an fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in children, adolescents and young adults
citation: McRae, K., Gross, J. J., Weber, J., Robertson, E. R., Sokol-Hessner, P., Ray, R. D., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Ochsner, K. N. (2012). The development of emotion regulation: an fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in children, adolescents and young adults. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 7(1), 11–22. https://doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsr093
title: Developmental account of cognitive reappraisal: linearly developing cognitive control with nonlinear adolescent social-cognitive recruitment
description: This framework explains reappraisal development as comprising two dissociable components: cognitive control supported by prefrontal regions that develop linearly, and social-cognitive/mental-state-attribution processes showing nonlinear adolescent patterns. The study used "a task that distinguishes negative emotional reactivity from reappraisal ability" across three age groups to test linear versus nonlinear predictions of socio-emotional development.
requirements: Neuroimaging or behavioral measures that separate emotional reactivity from reappraisal ability
Age-span samples covering childhood through young adulthood
constraints: Findings based on cross-sectional comparison of three age groups (10–13, 14–17, 18–22) on one reappraisal task
target_learners: children (10–13)
adolescents (14–17)
young adults (18–22)
target_learning_goals: emotion regulation via cognitive reappraisal
examples: Comparing older children, adolescents, and young adults on a reappraisal task during fMRI scanning
key_sources: McRae et al. (2012). The development of emotion regulation: an fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in children, adolescents and young adults. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 7(1), 11–22. https://doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsr093

article_title: Aging and cortical mechanisms of speech perception in noise
citation: Wong Patrick C. M., Jin James Xumin, Gunasekera Geshri M., Abel Rebekah, Lee Edward R., Dhar Sumitrajit. (2009). Aging and Cortical Mechanisms of Speech Perception in Noise. Neuropsychologia 47(3), 693-703. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2008.11.032
title: Decline-compensation hypothesis applied to the auditory domain
description: The decline-compensation hypothesis holds that cognitive aging involves "a combination of decline in sensory processing (and cortical activation) that is accompanied by an increase in the recruitment of more general cognitive areas (e.g., prefrontal cortex) as a means of compensation." In this study, the hypothesis was tested against the common cause hypothesis (general decline across sensory and cognitive regions) by examining spoken word perception in noise in younger and older adults with fMRI. The findings — reduced auditory cortex activation with increased prefrontal and precuneus activation that correlated positively with behavior — supported generalizing the hypothesis to the auditory domain.
requirements: Compensation is only claimed when increased activation in attention/working-memory areas is linked to behavioral performance, as the article states: "this hypothesis is only true if indeed increased activation in areas that are associated with attention and working memory is associated with performance."
constraints: The article tested adults with normal peripheral hearing and normal-range cognitive screening; generalization to hearing-impaired or cognitively impaired older adults is not established here.
target_learners: older adult listeners
target_learning_goals: spoken word identification in noisy environments
examples: In the fMRI experiment, older subjects showed reduced right superior temporal activation but increased prefrontal and precuneus activation, and frontal/parietal activation correlated positively with accuracy across all listening conditions.
key_sources: Wong Patrick C. M., Jin James Xumin, Gunasekera Geshri M., Abel Rebekah, Lee Edward R., Dhar Sumitrajit. (2009). Aging and Cortical Mechanisms of Speech Perception in Noise. Neuropsychologia 47(3), 693-703. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2008.11.032

article_title: Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence
citation: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/
title: Developmental mismatch account of adolescent emotion regulation
description: The review describes the developmental mismatch or imbalance model, in which prefrontal regulatory systems mature more slowly than limbic systems during adolescence. According to the review, "during adolescence the development of prefrontal regions lags behind that of limbic structures such as the amygdala, ventral striatum (VS) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC)", so adolescents are less effective at regulating emotions during the functional maturity lag. The review also presents the Triadic Systems Model as a refinement adding approach and avoidance systems.
requirements: Posits asynchronous maturation between prefrontal and limbic systems as the basis for adolescent regulatory difficulty
constraints: The review notes the model has been criticised because several studies have not consistently found heightened amygdala responses in adolescence, and heightened VS responses are sometimes associated with adaptive functioning
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding why emotion regulation is harder in adolescence
explaining adolescent emotional reactivity and risk-taking
examples: The review cites Hare et al. (2008) finding exaggerated amygdala activity in adolescents relative to children and adults as consistent with mismatch accounts
key_sources: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/

article_title: A Longitudinal Investigation of the Role of Quantity and Quality of Child-Directed Speech in Vocabulary Development
citation: Rowe Meredith L. (2012). A longitudinal investigation of the role of quantity and quality of child-directed speech in vocabulary development. Child development. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3440540/
title: Developmental scenario: different aspects of input quality matter at different child ages
description: The article proposes a developmental scenario in which the most beneficial type of caregiver input shifts with child age. As the authors state, "the results are consistent with a developmental scenario in which quantity of input is most important during the second year of life, the diversity or sophistication of the vocabulary in the input is most important during the third year of life, and the use of decontextualized language such as narrative and explanations in the input is most beneficial during the fourth year of life." This framework organizes the study's regression findings by age period and implies that scaffolding should match the child's current language ability.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement of multiple input dimensions at successive child ages
Control of SES, prior vocabulary skill, and input quantity when testing each input dimension
constraints: Based on 50 dyads from the greater Chicago area where SES is confounded with race
Not all features of input quality were examined
target_learners: children aged 18 to 54 months
target_learning_goals: receptive vocabulary development
examples: Regression models at each age showed the age-specific input measure adding explained variance beyond controls
key_sources: Rowe Meredith L. (2012). A longitudinal investigation of the role of quantity and quality of child-directed speech in vocabulary development. Child development. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3440540/

article_title: Understanding deficient emotional self-regulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a controlled study
citation: Surman Craig B. H., Biederman Joseph, Spencer Thomas, Miller Carolyn A., McDermott Katie M., Faraone Stephen V. (2013). Understanding deficient emotional self-regulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a controlled study. Attention deficit and hyperactivity disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4009378/
title: DESR as an emotional expression of ADHD-related self-regulation difficulty, partially independent of comorbidity
description: The article frames deficient emotional self-regulation as the affective arm of ADHD's self-regulation deficit, following Barkley's proposal that DESR traits be considered a core feature rather than associated symptoms. It operationalizes DESR with eight self-report items covering temper, frustration, and emotional overreaction, and interprets its findings as consistent with "the idea that DESR is an emotional expression of the ADHD patient’s difficulties with self-regulation." The framework holds that DESR is overrepresented in ADHD, partially independent of comorbid disorders, and functionally consequential.
requirements: DESR is measured here via eight self-report Barkley Current Behavior Scale items rated over the prior 6 months
constraints: The article states it cannot identify from its data whether DESR should be considered as co-occurring with ADHD or a result of ADHD
the sample was primarily Caucasian and may not generalize to other ethnic groups
target_learners: adults with ADHD
target_learning_goals: understanding emotional self-regulation difficulties associated with adult ADHD
examples: The study operationalized emotional impulsivity using items from the Barkley Current Behavior Scale and tested the framework in a controlled community sample
key_sources: Surman Craig B. H., Biederman Joseph, Spencer Thomas, Miller Carolyn A., McDermott Katie M., Faraone Stephen V. (2013). Understanding deficient emotional self-regulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a controlled study. Attention deficit and hyperactivity disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4009378/

article_title: Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy
citation: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://www.upenn.edu
title: Deprivation and threat as distinct dimensions of early adversity with partly different neural mechanisms
description: The article adopts the distinction, attributed to Sheridan and McLaughlin, that different life adversities affect brain development through at least partly different mechanisms. "Sheridan and McLaughlin have distinguished between the impacts of deprivation and threat, which presumably operate in different proportions in poverty and maltreatment, on different neural correlates." Socioeconomic disadvantage is multifactorial and distinct from abuse and neglect, so findings from broader adversity literatures do not automatically transfer to poverty. This framework bounds the scope of SES-neuroscience findings.
requirements: Researchers must treat poverty as a distinct risk category rather than assuming generalization from cumulative-stress or adverse-childhood-experiences literatures
constraints: The article states that findings on adverse childhood experiences or cumulative stress "should not be assumed to generalize to poverty or low SES"
target_learners: children from low socioeconomic status backgrounds
target_learning_goals: understanding how socioeconomic adversity relates to brain development and cognitive development
examples: The article cites a study finding childhood SES and childhood maltreatment have distinct associations with brain structure
key_sources: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41583-018-0023-2

article_title: Rational snacking: Young children’s decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability
citation: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004
title: Establish demonstrated reliability before asking young children to delay gratification or wait for a better reward
description: Before asking children to forgo an immediate lesser reward for a later greater one, give them direct evidence that promises in this setting are kept. The article demonstrated that "children's sustained decisions to wait for a greater reward rather than quickly taking a lesser reward are strongly influenced by the reliability of the environment (in this case, the reliability of the researcher's verbal assurances)". In the experiment this was done via a two-part art task in which the experimenter either delivered or failed to deliver promised supplies.
requirements: Learners must actually observe the promised better outcome being delivered (or withheld) at least once before the delay decision
constraints: The evidence comes from a single small randomized study (N = 28) with preschool-aged children; the authors note further work is required to test the relative contributions of different factors
target_learners: young children in instructional or experimental settings
target_learning_goals: waiting for larger delayed rewards
self-regulation in the face of immediate temptation
examples: In the reliable condition the researcher returned from both art-task delays with the promised new art supplies and better stickers before the marshmallow task began
key_sources: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004

article_title: Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension Among At-Risk Readers
citation: Miller Amanda C., Fuchs Douglas, Fuchs Lynn S., Compton Donald L., Kearns Devin, Zhang Wenjuan, Yen Loulee, Patton Samuel, Kirchner Danielle. (2014). Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension among At-Risk Readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 7(3), 232-249. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2014.906691
title: Decoding/Fluency tutoring program: 20-week adaptive one-on-one intervention with six scripted lesson components
description: A one-on-one decoding and fluency treatment delivered over 20 weeks using 10 books ordered by reading difficulty, with placement and lesson repetition/skipping adaptive to student performance. "Each Decoding/Fluency lesson consisted of six scripted components: (1) Sight Words, (2) Sounds, (3) Decodable Words, (4) Spelling, (5) Text Reading and Fluency, and (6) Sight Word Challenge." A Decoding/Fluency Placement Test of 125 items in five bands determined students' starting book. Year 2 added a seventh component, Sentence Read.
requirements: Tutors deliver scripted components; a Decoding/Fluency Placement Test determines initial book placement
constraints: The study excluded the comprehension-training group and no-treatment control group, so the program was studied combined with classroom instruction, not as a standalone comparison
target_learners: first-grade students at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: decoding
word reading
fluency
examples: Students progressed through increasingly difficult material; lesson performance determined whether they repeated, proceeded, or skipped the next lesson
key_sources: Miller Amanda C., Fuchs Douglas, Fuchs Lynn S., Compton Donald L., Kearns Devin, Zhang Wenjuan, Yen Loulee, Patton Samuel, Kirchner Danielle. (2014). Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension among At-Risk Readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 7(3), 232-249. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2014.906691

article_title: Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development
citation: Pauker, K., Ambady, N., & Apfelbaum, E. P. (2010). Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development. Child Development, 81(6), 1799–1813. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01511.x
title: Developmental intergroup theory: psychological salience, categorization, and essentialism as core processes in stereotype formation
description: The article draws on Bigler and Liben's (2007) developmental intergroup theory, which proposes that "three core processes contribute to the formation of social stereotypes and prejudice: (a) establishing the psychological salience of different person attributes, (b) categorizing individuals by salient dimensions, and (c) developing sets of traits, behaviors, and emotions that are associated with particular salient social groups." The theory holds that once a dimension becomes salient, essentialism, in-group bias, and explicit and implicit attributions mold the development of stereotyping about that dimension, with perceptual discriminability, proportional group size, and explicit and implicit use shaping salience. The present study tested two components the theory suggests should affect racial stereotyping: race salience and essentialist thinking.
requirements: Race must become a psychologically salient dimension before categorization and stereotype development proceed along it
constraints: The article tested only the race salience and essentialist thinking components of the theory, not the full model
target_learners: children ages 3–10
target_learning_goals: understanding the development of racial stereotypes and prejudice in childhood
examples: The study measured children's spontaneous sorting by race, racial justification, and racial constancy for self and others as operationalizations of the theory's salience and essentialism components
key_sources: Pauker, K., Ambady, N., & Apfelbaum, E. P. (2010). Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development. Child Development, 81(6), 1799–1813. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01511.x

article_title: Using design thinking to improve psychological interventions: The case of the growth mindset during the transition to high school.
citation: Yeager, David S., Romero, Carissa, Paunesku, Dave, Hulleman, Christopher S., Schneider, Barbara, Hinojosa, Cintia, Lee, Hae Yeon, O'Brien, Joseph, Flint, Kate, Roberts, Alice, Trott, Jill, Greene, Daniel, Walton, Gregory M., & Dweck, Carol S. (2016). Using Design Thinking to Improve Psychological Interventions: The Case of the Growth Mindset During the Transition to High School. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000098
title: Design-thinking methodology for improving and scaling psychological interventions: user-centered qualitative inquiry plus rapid randomized A/B testing
description: The article formalizes a methodology for preparing psychological interventions to be scaled, combining two design traditions. User-centered design privileges the user's subjective perspective via qualitative methods and prototypes, because "users may be excellent reporters on what they dislike or are confused by." A/B testing supplies "low-cost, short-term, large-sample, random-assignment experiments to test revisions to intervention content." The methodology was applied to redesign a growth mindset intervention for students transitioning to high school, then evaluated in two experimental studies.
requirements: Access to members of the target population for qualitative feedback on prototypes
A platform or sample enabling rapid, adequately powered randomized A/B experiments on minor content variations
An existing theoretical process model to guide which proxy measures and revisions matter
constraints: The authors state the re-designed intervention was not viewed as final or ready for universal scaling
A/B experiment conclusions were tempered by qualitative feedback because adult Mechanical Turk participants are not the target adolescent population
target_learners: 9th grade students transitioning to public high schools in the United States
target_learning_goals: Growth mindset of intelligence beliefs, challenge-seeking, persistence, and core-course academic achievement
examples: One-on-one meetings, group sessions of 2–10 students, and pilots with 20–25 9th graders reviewing minimally viable intervention drafts; two A/B studies with 7 fully crossed factors across N=3,004 participants
key_sources: Yeager, David S., Romero, Carissa, Paunesku, Dave, Hulleman, Christopher S., Schneider, Barbara, Hinojosa, Cintia, Lee, Hae Yeon, O'Brien, Joseph, Flint, Kate, Roberts, Alice, Trott, Jill, Greene, Daniel, Walton, Gregory M., & Dweck, Carol S. (2016). Using Design Thinking to Improve Psychological Interventions: The Case of the Growth Mindset During the Transition to High School. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000098

article_title: Defensive and Expansive Cycles of Learning: A Study of Home Care Encounters
citation: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970
title: Defensive learning cycle: learning to protect routines and avert adoption of novel actions
description: Defensive learning occurs when actors facing a demanding new practice learn to protect their existing routines and avert or forestall adoption of novel actions. The article states that "In such defensive learning, actors learn to protect their routines and to avert and forestall the adoption of novel actions." When combined and repeated, defensive actions may form complex defensive routines. The authors construct a substance-specific model of defensive learning for home care, projecting the vicious circle of fear-of-falling onto both client and worker, and code defensive actions with minus signs across the seven cycle positions.
requirements: Introduction of a demanding new practice that challenges existing routines
Actors must have invested in or identified with the existing practice script
constraints: Defensive learning has received scant attention within the learning sciences until quite recently
Defensive actions may be manifested as passivity and indifference rather than active rejection
target_learners: Home care workers defending standard scripts
Elderly clients preferring passivity and service reception
target_learning_goals: Protecting existing routines from disruption
Averting adoption of novel actions perceived as threatening workload or safety
examples: In Case A, the worker diverted the client's exercise hints toward substitute topics (armchair color, a flower), extinguishing the client's initiative to use the armchair as an exercise device
key_sources: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970

article_title: An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom
citation: Cuendet, S., Dehler Zufferey, J., Ortoleva, G., & Dillenbourg, P. (2015). An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(2), 183–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9213-3
title: Design CSCL environments for classroom constraints from the start
description: The article argues that computers remain scarcely used in classrooms partly because designers neglect classroom constraints, and proposes designing CSCL environments for classroom usage from the start. It states that "the constraints of the classroom environment are neglected by designers" and presents TapaCarp as "a CSCL environment designed for a classroom usage from the start."
requirements: Attend to the constraints of the classroom environment during design
Ground the activity design in the specific educational context, such as dual apprenticeships
constraints: Integration into the classroom does not by itself guarantee a meaningful learning activity
target_learners: classroom learners, here vocational apprentices
target_learning_goals: learning activities that fit and function within real classroom conditions
examples: TapaCarp was designed for classroom usage from the start and deployed in a multi-step activity across 3 apprentice classes
key_sources: Cuendet, S., Dehler Zufferey, J., Ortoleva, G., & Dillenbourg, P. (2015). An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(2), 183–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9213-3

article_title: Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom
citation: Wen, Y., Looi, C.-K., & Chen, W. (2015). Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(1), 77–108. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9208-0
title: Design collaborative L2 learning in networked classrooms so that representational tools supplement face-to-face communication
description: The article draws "implications for the design of collaborative L2 learning in networked classrooms" based on its finding that a representational tool's beneficial affordances supplement face-to-face communication for second-language learning. Designers should therefore treat the tool as a complement to, not a replacement for, face-to-face interaction, leveraging the intertwined media of the networked classroom.
requirements: A networked classroom where face-to-face and online interactions are intertwined
Collaborative L2 activity structures such as small-group writing
constraints: Grounded in a single contextual case study of second-language learning
target_learners: second-language learners in networked classrooms
target_learning_goals: collaborative second-language writing
examples: The study explored the tool's affordances in collaborative L2 writing activities and drew design implications from that exploration
key_sources: Wen, Y., Looi, C.-K., & Chen, W. (2015). Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(1), 77–108. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9208-0

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Design collaboration technologies to support mediation across all planes of learning
description: Because computer technologies play a central role in mediating multi-level learning processes, the article recommends that "innovative technologies should be designed to support this mediation". Design must consider how to prepare groups, individuals and communities to take advantage of designed functionality and promote learning on all planes. This follows directly from the three-planes framework.
requirements: Design processes must consider preparing groups, individuals and communities to take advantage of the designed functionality
target_learners: individuals, small groups, and classroom communities in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: problem-solving, content acquisition and knowledge building across planes
examples: The article cites provision of resources for teacher professional development, scripted collaboration activities and student curriculum as design provisions
key_sources: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7

article_title: Exploring the impact of chat-based collaborative activities and SRL-focused interventions on students’ self-regulation profiles, participation in collaborative activities, retention, and learning in MOOCs
citation: Psathas, G., Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S. N., & Tsiatsos, T. (2023). Exploring the impact of chat-based collaborative activities and SRL-focused interventions on students’ self-regulation profiles, participation in collaborative activities, retention, and learning in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 18:329–351. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09394-0
title: Deliver even low-effort, general weekly SRL interventions in MOOCs to scaffold participation, retention, and learning
description: The article supports sending weekly email interventions that make the learning analytics dashboard visible and prompt students to interpret visualizations against their goals. Both a generic intervention and a personalized version increased participation, retention, and quiz scores relative to control. The authors conclude that "even the generalized SRL intervention mode, which requires less setup effort on behalf of the teaching staff, can be effective in improving learning outcomes and reducing dropout rates."
requirements: Weekly email interventions sent at the start of each week that direct students to learning analytics visualizations linked to skills needed for the chat activities
constraints: Effects were demonstrated in a 5-week, single-country, Greece-based programming MOOC; the personalized mode significantly outperformed control on SRL scores while the general mode did not; interventions bundled several SRL prompts whose separate effects were not isolated.
target_learners: MOOC learners with heterogeneous self-regulated learning skills
target_learning_goals: Improved participation in collaborative chat activities, course retention, and learning outcomes in an introduction-to-programming MOOC
examples: Three weekly email interventions prompted the general group to consider which learning analytics graphs offered valuable information; the personalized group received named, compliance-tracking messages referencing specific skills and graphs.
key_sources: Psathas, G., Tegos, S., Demetriadis, S. N., & Tsiatsos, T. (2023). Exploring the impact of chat-based collaborative activities and SRL-focused interventions on students’ self-regulation profiles, participation in collaborative activities, retention, and learning in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 18:329–351. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09394-0

article_title: CSCL has come of age
citation: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2
title: Adopt a design science stance so that artefacts and design theories both count as knowledge in CSCL research
description: The editors propose importing Design Science Research from Information Systems into CSCL. DSR holds, quoting the editorial, that "knowledge is possible and valuable not only in abstract form but also in the form of artefacts," with design theories as mid-range theories accounting for why an artefact works, under which circumstances and for whom. Artefacts worth building must be motivated by deep problem understanding and rigorous analysis of existing solutions, and designed iteratively with prototyping and formative evaluation. The editorial invites designs, including via a new Short Paper format.
requirements: Good designs need to be motivated by a deep understanding of the problem, stakeholder needs, and rigorous analysis of existing solutions; designers should follow an established design method and document all steps
constraints: DBR has faced methodological critique as a weak experimental method (Kelly, 2004), raising the question of how such a method can serve as the foundation for advancing learning theories
target_learners: CSCL researchers, learning scientists, and designers of collaborative learning technologies
target_learning_goals: Producing design theories and useful computational and instructional artefacts for collaborative learning
examples: The editorial lists arteacts already developed in CSCL: design documents and models such as wireframes, collaboration scripts, teacher manuals, worksheets, and protocols for reproducible data analysis
key_sources: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Design IVR-supported collaborative learning activities so learners can ask 'What?', 'How?', and 'Why?' about recorded actions
description: Because ABC-VR orients to the activity level, designs should span the hierarchy of operations, actions and activities rather than only training procedure. The article argues traditional IVR designs afford moving from identifying what actions are performed to how, while ABC-VR "also implies asking why actions are performed", and that it is important to design links between the two ends of the activity hierarchy. Shared reflection can be designed through reflection prompts or by including learners with multiple perspectives.
requirements: Design must link procedural knowledge to its situated context and reflections about the broader setting to the operations that drive actions
constraints: Activity-level orientation introduces open-endedness and increases the complexity of designing supportive HCI systems (Kuutti, 1995)
target_learners: medical students
newly qualified teachers
interdisciplinary professional groups
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
classroom interaction analysis
professional communication reflection
examples: Medical students learned both how to decide which knee tests to perform and the steps for performing them; mentoring case participants alternated between identifying actions and reasoning about the overall teaching practice
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Design virtually mediated environments that are situated in practice, engaging stakeholders to select relevant recorded activities
description: ABC-VR environments should use situated 360-degree recordings of real-world activities rather than computer-generated reproductions, selected collaboratively with learners and practitioners. The article states it is important "to engage with learners/educators/professionals to identify tensions and possibilities in current practices" learners wish to examine, e.g. professors selecting knee-exam sequences or teachers choosing clips to analyse with mentors. Design must also shift from affording social interactivity to social interaction.
requirements: Settings with a tradition for using video (e.g., teacher training) and access to 360-degree capture with appropriate ethical approval
constraints: Recordings are never neutral; they capture a version of a situation as it unfolds
Real knee exams can be difficult to record owing to GDPR concerns
target_learners: students and professionals analysing recorded practices
target_learning_goals: establishing joint attention
perspective taking
collaborative imagining
examples: In the medical case relevant sequences were selected with a professor; in the mentoring case teachers identified relevant clips themselves
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

article_title: From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL
citation: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7
title: Design CSCL environments that explicitly support timely re-annotation so annotations become dynamic resources rather than static artifacts
description: The article argues that social annotation tools and instructional strategies should actively foster re-annotation practices so that peer annotations are revisited rather than left static. In CEASAR, synchronized visual highlights across devices allowed peers to "align their attention and jointly interpret celestial data during discussion". The authors state that these insights "emphasize the importance of designing CSCL environments that explicitly support re-annotation as a tool for attention coordination and collaborative meaning-making".
requirements: Annotations must be visible synchronously across group members' devices so a peer's highlight can serve as a shared visual reference.
constraints: Evidence comes from one 16-group analysis in an immersive astronomy simulation; the authors note that peer engagement and social dynamics cannot be taken for granted even in synchronous settings.
target_learners: undergraduate non-majors in introductory astronomy
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
attention coordination and mutual awareness
examples: Students in the Lost at Sea task annotated constellations such as Ursa Major and Crux as reference points, and peers re-annotated the same objects within 120 s to signal shared attention.
key_sources: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7

article_title: Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl
citation: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2
title: Design instruction in any learning environment so students will engage in active sense-making and knowledge construction
description: The authors endorse Renkl's claim that one cannot deduce from constructivist assumptions that so-called constructivist environments are superior to traditional arrangements. Rather, 'instruction should be designed in such a way that there is a high probability students will engage in active sense-making and knowledge construction'. They extend this to recommending research on how to best induce sense-making irrespective of whether the environment is traditional or constructivist.
requirements: Instruction must be deliberately designed to make active sense-making and knowledge construction probable; the claim does not follow from constructivist assumptions alone
constraints: Traditional or constructivist labels alone do not guarantee better outcomes; the article explicitly denies that superiority can be deduced from the basic constructivist assumptions
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning
active sense-making
knowledge construction
examples: The special issue encouraged research looking at a wide range of effects in a wide range of learning environments, including traditional ones designed to induce meaningful learning activities
key_sources: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2

article_title: Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought
citation: de Jong, T. (2010). Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9110-0
title: Cognitive load theory: limited working memory and three types of load contribution
description: Cognitive load theory asserts that learning is hampered when working memory capacity is exceeded, and distinguishes three contributions to total load. As the article states, "Cognitive load theory distinguishes three different types of contributions to total cognitive load": intrinsic load from the content's inherent characteristics, extraneous load from the instructional material, and germane load from learning processes. The theory has had great impact on educational researchers and designers.
requirements: Working memory capacity is limited, so instructional systems must optimize its use and avoid cognitive overload
constraints: The article argues the three-type distinction itself is conceptually and empirically problematic
target_learners: learners in educational research settings generally
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation as the main goal of learning
key_sources: de Jong, T. (2010). Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9110-0

article_title: Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation
citation: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5
title: DCog model of debriefing as a coordination device for conversational remembering and distributed metacognition
description: The article reconceptualises the three-phase simulation debriefing through distributed cognition, arguing that the debriefing conversation itself is the major coordination device. Its model holds that "debriefing conversations function as coordination devices for two key processes: conversational remembering and distributed metacognition", coordinating a cascade of representations from private memory to public speech. A coordination device is a structure or practice that constrains participants' actions to control how representations propagate within a distributed cognitive system. The model emerged abductively from cognitive-ethnographic analysis of one exemplary debriefing case.
requirements: A facilitator-led debriefing structured through consecutive phases, in which talk-in-interaction can manage the transformation of representations between media
constraints: The model was developed from a single exemplary case of a nursing simulation debriefing, chosen for analytical richness rather than statistical typicality
target_learners: second-year nursing students
healthcare simulation participants
target_learning_goals: reflexive analysis of simulated clinical performance
professional knowledge and judgment in acute care
examples: The authors analyse a 55-minute debriefing after a hypoglycemia management simulation, showing description-phase remembering followed by analysis and application phases of distributed metacognition
key_sources: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5

article_title: Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments
citation: Sarah Shi Hui Wong. (2026). Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09819-x
title: Derring effect and deliberate erring as a guided-error learning approach within the Prevention–Permission–Promotion (3P) framework
description: The derring effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon in which "deliberate erring has been found to enhance learning", implemented by having students intentionally generate a plausible conceptual error, then strike it out and correct it. The article situates it in Wong and Lim's (2019b) 3P framework, under which "errors in learning can be observed, allowed, induced, or guided when not avoided": learning from others' invalid designs involves observing errors, whereas deliberate erring guides students into making and correcting their own errors in low-stakes contexts after correct instruction. Candidate mechanisms include failure-driven learning, development of negative knowledge, suppression of incorrect pathways, attention to correction, and structural alignment between incorrect and correct responses.
requirements: Deliberate errors must be generated after instruction on the correct principles and in low-stakes practice contexts, as in the study's open-book practice with a principles handout
constraints: The article states the benefits are specific to guiding students to commit and correct their own errors, since observing and correcting others' errors does not yield the same extent of gains
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: experimental design principles
scientific reasoning
transfer of domain-general principles
examples: Students in the derr-explain-fix condition designed a non-optimal study to test a coffee-drinking hypothesis, explained their deliberate errors, then corrected them within a 15-minute equated practice session
key_sources: Sarah Shi Hui Wong. (2026). Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09819-x

article_title: What matters for students’ learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment!
citation: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x
title: Design laboratory instrumentation and tasks for the discernment of critical features, and specify the technology when drawing conclusions about lab learning
description: Because experience in labs is mediated through technologies, the possibilities for discernment and variation depend on the technology used. The article argues that "the role of experimental technologies in students' learning in labs should not be neglected" and that "crucial aspects of the technology used are not its simplicity or complexity, but the opportunities (and constraints) for discernment and (hence) learning it affords". Teachers should use these possibilities constructively by carefully designing tasks that help students discern the critical aspects of the object of learning.
requirements: Task designs based on variation theory, since probeware use alone does not necessarily lead to good learning results
Teachers who deliberately choose and exploit the affordances of the instrumentation
constraints: The use of computers and high-tech equipment is not a requirement for student learning; simple materials can work
General conclusions about learning in labs should be drawn cautiously, specifying the conditions and technology used
Belief in technological determinism is fallacious
target_learners: students in physics, science and engineering laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: discerning critical aspects of the object of learning, such as the relation between velocity and acceleration
examples: In the studied cases, photogates afforded only unsigned speed, the tape timer only downward motion, while probeware afforded study of up, down and turning-point motion; probeware tasks built on variation theory led students to discern critical aspects without prior knowledge
key_sources: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x

article_title: Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions
citation: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8
title: Use post-game debriefing to unpack what the wargame experience does not transparently communicate about tactics
description: The article's central design implication is that knowledge of tactics requires reflective unpacking in debriefing rather than being transparently communicated through game participation. As the authors put it, "Knowledge of tactics is found to not be transparently communicated through participation in the wargame, but to require unpacking in reflective discussions". Post-simulation discussion connects concrete game experiences to generalized, conceptual understanding of the discipline, making debriefing an arena where functional concepts are put to use and anchored to shared experience.
requirements: Debriefing sessions after each game or exercise day, led by a military teacher or self-led, in which the concept of tactics is explicitly invoked
target_learners: officer students in simulation-based professional military education
target_learning_goals: connecting simulated concrete experience to conceptual disciplinary understanding
examples: Debriefings after each game in the recorded wargaming-based tactics courses, lasting from around 20 minutes to over 1.5 hours after multi-week games
key_sources: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8

article_title: Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams
citation: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5
title: Design principles as 'ideal type' boundary objects crossing between research and educational design practice
description: The article frames a set of design principles as a boundary object of the 'ideal type' Star and Griesemer describe: "entities that are to be used and adapted flexibly in several different contexts". Because an ideal type is an abstraction without local contingencies, utilization proceeds by first decontextualizing the principles (viewing them as abstract concepts independent of their original context) and then recontextualizing them (creatively designing new features in another educational context). Brokers and reified artifacts such as a guidebook support this crossing.
requirements: The boundary object must be perceived as valuable across different contexts or perspectives
Additional information about the original context and examples of features should accompany the principles
The principles, context description and examples must be reified or materialized as a usable product
constraints: The authors note a boundary object's main function is often described as facilitating collaboration among social worlds, and a principle set traveling from research to practice facilitates potential rather than immediate ongoing collaboration
target_learners: interprofessional design teams of teachers, managers, consultants and clients designing hybrid learning configurations
target_learning_goals: utilizing research-based design principles as rationale ('know-why') for designing or redesigning educational interventions
examples: The set of seven HLC design principles was reified in a guidebook and introduced by a researcher-broker via workshops with four design teams
key_sources: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5

article_title: Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9
title: Demonstration-based training (DBT) grounded in Bandura's four-process theory of observational learning
description: DBT is a design approach for teaching procedures by observation: "DBT is a design approach in which a dynamic example of performance is complemented with instructional features." Its basis is Bandura's theory, which "posits that observational or model-based learning hinges on the four interrelated processes of attention, retention, production, and motivation." The article couples specific design measures to each process: signaling and pre-training for attention, segmentation and pauses for retention, practice for production, and simple-to-complex sequencing plus domain anchoring for motivation.
requirements: A dynamic example of performance (task demonstration) that is complemented with instructional features targeted at the four observational learning processes
constraints: During a demonstration the designer has no influence over top-down attentional processes because these depend on the user's prior knowledge; instructional measures concern bottom-up attentional processes
target_learners: novice software users, including primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge of software task completion
examples: The tutorial in the study was developed in accordance with DBT, adding cues, segmentation, pauses, practice, reviews, simple-to-complex ordering and domain-anchored tasks to task demonstrations
key_sources: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9

article_title: Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks
citation: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1
title: Favor tasks that are cognitively demanding from the outset and include desirable difficulties such as interleaved practice
description: Based on their findings, the authors recommend that educators "incorporate tasks with consistently high complexity or desirable difficulties" to foster cognitive engagement and metacognitive strategy use. Practically, this means "favoring tasks that are cognitively demanding from the outset rather than those that progressively increase in complexity", with interleaved practice as an additional desirable difficulty, while considering learners' existing knowledge.
requirements: Educators should carefully consider learners' existing knowledge, since successful engagement with challenging tasks depends on sufficient prior knowledge
constraints: The motivational measures showed no effects, and the learning content's low personal relevance may have shaped results
target_learners: university students
learners in school contexts acquiring complex skills
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer of complex problem-solving skills
metacognitive strategy use
