examples: In the experiment, high-complexity conditions required assigning suffixes for all six grammatical persons in each exercise, while interleaved conditions practiced all six tenses within each round in randomized order
key_sources: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1

article_title: Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1
title: Debate-tool (Graphical and Textual versions) in the VCRI CSCL environment
description: The Debate-tool is an argumentation tool embedded in the VCRI groupware environment, used by student groups to co-construct a representation of the Martyrs-versus-Propaganda historical debate before co-authoring an essay. The article states: "Compared to the TD-tool, the GD-tool uses several visualization techniques to make information salient and to help students complete the representation more effectively and efﬁciently." The GD-tool distinguishes arguments, supports, and refutations, visualizes how well positions are supported, shows progress through the problem, and allows rating element importance; the TD-tool adds information in a listwise manner without these distinctions.
requirements: Students work in groups of two to four, each on a separate computer, with historical sources provided and a subsequent co-authored argumentative essay task.
constraints: The article notes the GD-tool's increased complexity might make it "less suited to support the linearization process that occurs when writers have to transfer the content of the ER to an essay."
target_learners: eleventh-grade secondary history students
target_learning_goals: analyzing and reconstructing a historical debate
formulating arguments, supports, and refutations
co-authoring an argumentative essay
examples: Groups used the tool during three 50-minute lessons within the VCRI environment, which also provided Chat, Sources, Cowriter, Diagrammer, Planner, and Participation tools.
key_sources: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1

article_title: The effect of time pressure on metacognitive control: developmental changes in self-regulation and efficiency during learning
citation: Gönül, G., Tsalas, N., Paulus, M. (2021). The effect of time pressure on metacognitive control: developmental changes in self-regulation and efficiency during learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09262-y
title: Deterioration versus enhancement hypotheses of time pressure on metacognitive control
description: The article derives two competing hypotheses about how time pressure affects metacognitive control during learning. The deterioration hypothesis holds that awareness of time constraints distracts learners and reduces cognitive capacities such as working memory resources, harming self-regulation especially in children whose monitoring and control are loosely coupled. The enhancement hypothesis holds that slight time pressure improves performance because learners avoid failing courses of action and act in a more strategic and situation sensitive manner. The study frames its self-regulation and efficiency predictions around these two accounts.
requirements: A learning situation in which time constraints are made salient (e.g., a countdown) so that time pressure can influence metacognitive decisions
constraints: The article notes there were limited prior studies on study time allocation under time pressure, making developmental effects hard to predict from existing literature
target_learners: children (10-year-olds)
adolescents (14-year-olds)
adults
target_learning_goals: metacognitive self-regulation of study time
efficient allocation of study effort
examples: The study tested both hypotheses by comparing gamma-based self-regulation and efficiency rates across timed and untimed study blocks in three age groups
key_sources: Gönül, G., Tsalas, N., Paulus, M. (2021). The effect of time pressure on metacognitive control: developmental changes in self-regulation and efficiency during learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09262-y

article_title: Commentary: Is disfluency desirable?
citation: Bjork, R. A., & Yue, C. L. (2016). Commentary: Is disfluency desirable? Metacognition Learning, 11, 133–137. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9156-8
title: Desirable difficulties framework: difficulties enhance learning only when they trigger encoding and retrieval processes the learner can engage
description: The commentary situates disfluency within the desirable-difficulties framework (Bjork 1994), arguing that the word desirable is critical: difficulties such as generation, variation, spacing, contextual interference, and testing can trigger "the very encoding and retrieval processes that support learning, comprehension, and remembering," but whether that happens depends on the learner and the materials. Difficulties become undesirable when learners lack the background knowledge or skills to respond successfully. The special issue's contribution is establishing conditions separating desirable difficulties from simply difficulties.
requirements: The learner must have the background knowledge or skills to respond to the difficulty successfully
constraints: Even proven desirable difficulties (generation, spacing, testing) can be undesirable in specific instances
Whether a difficulty is desirable depends on learner characteristics and on the to-be-learned materials
target_learners: All learners encountering intentionally introduced difficulties during instruction
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and transfer of learned material
examples: The commentary cites McDaniel and Einstein's material-appropriate processing framework: sentence re-arrangement helps with expository text but not familiar fairy-tale organization, while letter deletion shows the opposite pattern
key_sources: Bjork, R. A., & Yue, C. L. (2016). Commentary: Is disfluency desirable? Metacognition Learning, 11, 133–137. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9156-8

article_title: Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses
citation: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x
title: Deliver metacognition interventions for young children through teachers or task materials rather than researchers
description: This principle recommends that metacognition interventions for young children be delivered predominantly by teachers, task materials (computer programs or workbooks), or a combination, rather than by researchers. It rests on the meta-analytic moderator finding that "interventions that were delivered by teachers or task materials were more effective than interventions that were delivered by researchers for two outcomes related to self-regulated learning". The authors attribute this to recent improvements in how teachers and researchers collaborate to develop intervention programs.
requirements: Teachers or task materials must actually implement the metacognitive components (planning, monitoring, control, reflection) as designed
constraints: The finding applies to two outcomes related to self-regulated learning; the article does not claim delivery-mode superiority for all outcomes
target_learners: typically developing pre- and elementary school children up to 12 years of age
target_learning_goals: metacognitive skills and self-regulated learning outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis coded mode of delivery as teacher, researcher, task materials (computer program or workbooks), or a combination of teacher and task materials across 67 studies
key_sources: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x

article_title: The Value of Using Tests in Education as Tools for Learning—Not Just for Assessment
citation: Dillon H. Murphy, Jeri L. Little, Elizabeth L. Bjork. (2023). The Value of Using Tests in Education as Tools for Learning—Not Just for Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09808-3
title: Desirable difficulties framework: challenges that slow apparent performance gains can produce long-lasting, transferable learning
description: The commentary organizes its argument around the desirable difficulties framework (Bjork & Bjork), under which learning strategies that "create challenges for learners" and initially slow apparent performance can ultimately produce "learning that is both long-lasting and transferable." It names four examples: spaced practice, contextual variation, interleaving, and testing/retrieval practice. Crucially, difficulty alone is not sufficient—what matters is whether the challenge induces the cognitive processes that enhance retention and understanding. The framework explains why learners and instructors are often tricked into preferring easier methods whose gains are superficial.
requirements: The difficulty must induce the type of cognitive processing that enhances learning, not merely make the task harder
constraints: Desirable difficulties can slow apparent performance gains and be misinterpreted as impairing learning
Students with prior academic success without desirable difficulties may resist changing their study approach
target_learners: students in high school and college courses
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer of course content
examples: The commentary lists spaced practice, contextual variation, interleaving, and testing/retrieval practice as examples of desirable difficulties
key_sources: Dillon H. Murphy, Jeri L. Little, Elizabeth L. Bjork. (2023). The Value of Using Tests in Education as Tools for Learning—Not Just for Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09808-3

article_title: A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity
citation: Ouhao Chen · Fred Paas · John Sweller. (2023). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09782-w
title: Instructional design must account for element interactivity because cognitive load effects shrink or reverse as it decreases
description: The article recommends that instructional procedures be chosen according to the element interactivity of the material and the learners' expertise: "As element interactivity decreases, the size of effects decreases and may reverse." Because "most cognitive load theory effects disappear or even reverse when students study low element interactivity information", the same information may suit one knowledge level and be unsuitable for another. Element interactivity or a similar architecture-aware complexity measure is described as "an essential ingredient of a viable instructional design science."
requirements: Instructors must estimate learners' prior knowledge and the element interactivity of materials and procedures
constraints: Element interactivity estimates are not precise; effects of small differences in interactivity are unlikely to be visible in experiments, whereas very large differences are readily demonstrated
target_learners: Learners at differing expertise levels studying biologically secondary information
target_learning_goals: Selecting instructional procedures appropriate to task complexity and learner expertise
examples: The review notes experiments typically study only very large differences in element interactivity, such as memorising periodic table symbols versus balancing chemical equations
key_sources: Ouhao Chen · Fred Paas · John Sweller. (2023). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09782-w

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Provide repeated, deliberately practiced opportunities to make connections over sustained time, with continually varying contexts
description: The third principle extends deliberate practice from skill acquisition to conceptual understanding: instructional materials must maintain a high level of challenge as abilities develop, raising the difficulty of the connections practiced along a learning trajectory. The authors state that "Deliberate practice requires that instructional materials maintain a constant (and high) level of challenge as abilities develop." Varying contexts, such as introducing new data sets nearly every class session, forces learners to adapt their conceptual understanding and stretches the range of situations a concept covers. The authors stress deliberate practice must be combined with the first two principles, since skill progression alone can occur without attention to conceptual connections.
requirements: Practice opportunities must recur over long periods as knowledge deepens
Task difficulty must be raised to match growing capability, targeting specific weaknesses
constraints: Repetitive practice aimed at automaticity produces a feeling of fluency that signals plateau, not deepening understanding; deliberate practice alone risks skill learning without conceptual connection
target_learners: Students developing expertise in a complex academic domain over a semester or longer
target_learning_goals: Strengthening and robustness of connections across contexts, concepts, and representations
Applying domain knowledge flexibly across varied contexts
examples: Although the online book uses a limited number of data sets, the authors introduce new data at almost every class session so students connect data analysis to the contexts they care about.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305
title: Deliver dementia education with a total duration of at least 8 hours and individual sessions of 90 minutes or more
description: This principle holds that workforce education on dementia should be long enough to allow depth and consolidation: the review's synthesis found more efficacious programs "have a total duration of at least 8 hours with individual sessions of 90 minutes or more." It applies to designing training schedules for health and social care staff learning dementia knowledge and skills.
requirements: Programs must be planned so total contact time reaches at least 8 hours and individual sessions run 90 minutes or more, as the synthesis identified as a feature of more efficacious programs.
constraints: The duration thresholds come from a critical interpretive synthesis of papers of variable quality; the review itself calls for further robust research to develop the evidence base.
target_learners: Health and social care workforce staff receiving dementia education and training
target_learning_goals: Dementia knowledge, skills, and care practice for the health and social care workforce
examples: The synthesis of 152 papers identified the 8-hour total and 90-minute-plus session thresholds as common features of more efficacious educational programs.
key_sources: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305

article_title: Democratic Education: A Theoretical Review (2006–2017)
citation: Edda Sant. (2019). Democratic Education: A Theoretical Review (2006–2017). Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654319862493
title: Democratic education as a floating signifier constructed by eight competing political discourses
description: The review theorizes democratic education as a nodal point or floating signifier in education scholarship: a contested term that rival political discourses struggle to invest with their own meaning. Discourse analysis of 377 articles yielded eight versions: two against (elitist, neoliberal) and six pro (liberal, deliberative, multiculturalist, participatory, critical, agonistic). Each version is distinguished by ontological and epistemological assumptions, normative approaches to democracy, and conceptions of the education–politics relationship. The review states that "Democratic education functions as a privileged nodal point of different political discourses."
requirements: Articles must explicitly discuss the term democratic education and aim to invest it with meaning, since the term is treated as a floating signifier
constraints: Findings are limited to theory and research published in English language peer-reviewed journal articles between 2006 and 2017; dissertations, books, and other languages were excluded
target_learners: students in formal education, particularly primary and secondary institutions
target_learning_goals: education for democratic citizenship and participation in democratic life
examples: The review maps each version's key principles, educational implications for policy and practice, and the debates and critiques raised against it
key_sources: Edda Sant. (2019). Democratic Education: A Theoretical Review (2006–2017). Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654319862493

article_title: School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies
citation: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511
title: Four-component conceptualization of democratic competences: knowledge, attitude, skill, and behavior
description: The review conceptualizes democratic competences along four components. The article states it analyzed "for which democratic competences (i.e., knowledge, attitude, skill, behavior) they were effective." This four-part framework serves as the outcome axis of the review, paired against the five teaching-method types, allowing the authors to report which methods were effective for which competence components across the included interventions.
requirements: Studies must measure democratic competences in terms of knowledge, attitude, skill, and/or behavior
constraints: The review reports that there is still much to be gained in the conceptualization of democratic competences, indicating the framework's limits in the existing literature
target_learners: School students in democratic education interventions
target_learning_goals: Democratic knowledge, democratic attitudes, democratic skills, democratic behavior
examples: The review mapped each included intervention's outcomes onto the four competence components
key_sources: Teegelbeckers, J.Y., Nieuwelink, H., & Oostdam, R.J. (2023). School-based teaching for democracy: A systematic review of teaching methods in quantitative intervention studies. Educational Research Review, 39, 100511. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100511

article_title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
citation: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6
title: Design tasks and tools so that constitutive work stays with the learner: withhold answers, demand justification, and reward unaided capability
description: The article identifies task and assessment design as the system-side lever on the cognitive partition: whether tasks demand justification and exhibition of process, whether assessment rewards a finished product or evidence of unaided capability, and whether the tool surrenders answers or offers only hints all determine what it is rational to offload. Design can compensate for weak regulation, as hint-based tutors protected students who would not have regulated their own offloading with a permissive tool. Design and regulation function as partial substitutes and complements toward keeping offloading peripheral to the target.
requirements: Tasks and assessments that demand justification and evidence of unaided capability
Tool configurations that sequence assistance after an unaided attempt or require verification
constraints: Protection engineered into the environment prevented erosion without, by itself, producing augmentation
target_learners: STEM learners, including novices doubly exposed because they least equipped to vet AI output
target_learning_goals: Preserving goal-constitutive processing such as model selection, justification, and proof construction
examples: Bastani et al.'s GPT Tutor provided teacher-crafted hints rather than solutions and eliminated the learning penalty of the answer-giving interface; Kestin et al.'s tutor guided, questioned, and paced rather than surrendering solutions
key_sources: Daiki Nakamura. (2026). Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10224-6

article_title: One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education
citation: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7
title: DeFT framework's three normative functions of multiple external representations
description: The article describes Ainsworth's Design-Functions-Tasks (DeFT) framework as the guiding framework for research on multiple external representations, covering design parameters, normative functions, and cognitive tasks. It states that "The DeFT framework lays out three major functions for MERs": complementary roles, constraining interpretation, and allowing construction of deeper understanding. Complementary roles mean different representations convey different pieces of information; constraining interpretation works by familiarity or inherent properties; deeper understanding arises, for example, when analogies support abstract, transferable mental representations. The framework also captures how cognitive tasks influence construction of and changes to internal representations.
requirements: The framework prescribes what external representations are supposed to do (normative functions)
constraints: The article notes the framework's description of learning is rather unspecific and requires precise description of triggered learning processes
target_learners: learners in STEM education settings
target_learning_goals: learning with multiple external representations
key_sources: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7

article_title: Children’s Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education
citation: Bjorklund, D.F. (2022). Children's Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2243-2273. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09688-z
title: Follow developmentally appropriate practices, which are also evolutionarily appropriate practices
description: The article recommends that educators follow developmentally appropriate practices, arguing these are "also evolutionarily appropriate practices" because they align instruction with children's evolved learning mechanisms. It presents this as the first of four ways educators can "minimize the effects of evolutionary mismatches" between ancient learning mechanisms and modern schooling.
requirements: Educators must match instructional practices to children's developmental level and evolved learning tendencies
constraints: Presented as a recommendation for minimizing mismatch effects, not as a directly tested intervention in this article
target_learners: children in early childhood and elementary education
target_learning_goals: aligning instruction with children's evolved learning abilities to improve enjoyment and success
key_sources: Bjorklund, D.F. (2022). Children's Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2243-2273. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09688-z

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Design digital tools by starting from content-specific knowledge components and learning activities, not by picking a tool first
description: The article recommends that research on digitally enriched learning start with analyses of the to-be-learned content, the necessary knowledge elements, and the required learning activities, rather than selecting a digital tool first. Knowledge about content-specific learner models should be used to design instructional features well-suited to stimulate the relevant generative cognitive processes. The authors state they "consider it necessary for researchers to engage in the development (or selection) of digital prototype tools that are explicitly designed to align with the learning mechanisms assumed."
requirements: Detailed specification of the content-specific knowledge components students need to acquire, and of the learning activities leading to their acquisition
constraints: The article notes this design endeavor may be demanding as it can vary between domains, content, and learning goals
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings across domains
target_learning_goals: acquisition of specified content-specific knowledge components
examples: For a fraction-arithmetic online math tutor, adaptive feedback and adaptive increase in task difficulty were suggested; for physics, a simulation enabling the control of variables strategy
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation
citation: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8
title: Design misinformation education to enhance discrepancy detection
description: Based on its synthesis, the review recommends that interventions to reduce misinformation susceptibility be designed to enhance learners' noticing of discrepancies between original information and subsequent misinformation. The authors state that "our review suggests that specific pre-warnings and explicit types of attention-focusing interventions might be better suited to enhance discrepancy detection and reduce susceptibility to misinformation." Retrieval practice alone did not seem suited to this goal, though detail-focused and criterion testing were exceptions. The review also recommends testing combinations of intervention types.
requirements: Interventions must direct learners' attention to discrepancies, e.g., via explicit discrepancy-indication instructions, veracity judgments, or specific warnings
constraints: General pre-warnings and mindfulness approaches mostly failed; retrieval practice often increased susceptibility except under verbatim or criterion testing
target_learners: adults and children learning to resist misinformation
target_learning_goals: detecting discrepancies between original and post-event information
reducing misinformation endorsement
examples: The review found explicit instructions to press a button when noticing discrepancies and veracity-judgment instructions were effective across studies
key_sources: Rau, M. A., & Premo, A. E. (2025). Systematic Review of Educational Approaches to Misinformation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10012-8

article_title: Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age?
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09571-9
title: Developmental prerequisites framework: knowledge, cognitive capacities, and metacognitive abilities explain age-related differences in generative learning strategy effectiveness
description: The review proposes that age-related differences in the effectiveness of generative learning strategies stem from three developmental processes: "Increases in knowledge", "Increases in cognitive capacities", and "Increases in metacognitive abilities". World knowledge provides a richer semantic network and frees cognitive capacity; working memory and inhibition — "collectively termed executive functions" — underlie reasoning and mental-model revision; and monitoring and control skills follow a late-maturing trajectory. Differences between strategies' developmental trajectories are attributed to their differing specific prerequisites, such as reasoning for explaining and metacognitive monitoring for questioning.
requirements: Strategies capitalizing on prior-knowledge activation require learners to have sufficient world knowledge, executive functions, and metacognitive monitoring for the strategy's specific mechanisms
constraints: The review restricts this account to individually performed generative strategies targeting declarative knowledge enrichment, excluding collaborative generation, procedural knowledge, and children below school age
target_learners: school-age students from elementary school through university
target_learning_goals: acquisition of declarative knowledge through generative learning strategies
examples: The review links lower elementary students' failure to profit from the forward testing effect to difficulties combating interference related to executive-function development
key_sources: Garvin Brod. (2021). Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09571-9

article_title: Examining Black and Latine Students’ Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review
citation: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0
title: DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's five purposes for considering race in educational psychology research
description: The review adopts DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's (2014) classification as a common language for analyzing each article's approach to race. The five purposes are "descriptive or demographic (i.e., to describe the sample or another level of demographics; explanatory (i.e., to use race or ethnicity to explain variance); comparative (i.e., to compare racial and/or ethnic groups to each other); race-focused (i.e., to center race in the analysis and build upon race-based or cultural theories); and race-reimaged (i.e., to build upon race-based or cultural theories or lenses as a means to add nuance to traditional constructs) purposes." The authors turned these categories into a decision tree (Fig. 1) to classify each study's treatment of participants' race/ethnic identity and to center studies going beyond treating race as a "diverse sample."
requirements: Researchers code each study's approach to race/ethnicity using the decision tree rather than treating racial identity as merely a demographic descriptor
constraints: The classification descriptions are taken from DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's 2014 paper, not developed anew by this review
target_learners: Black and Latine adolescent mathematics students in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: Guiding belonging research that centers students' race and ethnicity without causing harm
examples: The review used the categories to classify its 20 included studies, e.g., labeling Barbieri and Miller-Cotto (2021) as comparative and Matthews et al. (2021) as race-focused
key_sources: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Developmental levels of self-regulation: adaptive scaffolding from observation to self-regulation
description: The article describes models in which teachers' support changes over time in accordance with students' developmental level. Collins et al.'s cognitive apprenticeship distinguishes modeling, scaffolding, fading, and coaching; Zimmerman describes four levels—observation, emulation, self-control, and self-regulation. At the highest level, "the students monitor their behavior, and are able to adjust their learning systematically to changing requirements and conditions", and the teacher offers an environment allowing performance without supervision. Both approaches share that teacher control is reduced as students move to the next self-regulatory level.
requirements: Learners first need to learn regulation strategies before they can regulate their learning effectively; teachers gradually fade scaffolding as students practice under supervision
constraints: Modeling of strategy use can take place implicitly, but may become explicit once the teacher addresses metacognitive aspects of strategy use
target_learners: primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: development of self-regulated learning
gradual assumption of responsibility for learning
examples: At the emulation level, students attempt to follow behavior modeled by their teacher or peer, and the teacher supports, encourages, and provides feedback
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0

article_title: Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation
citation: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y
title: Time parental scaffolding shifts to match adolescents' demonstrated competence
description: The article argues parental mediation should be developmentally contingent: authority and autonomy are adjusted in tandem with demonstrated competence. It states that "optimal timing involves gradually increasing adolescents' decision-making authority in tandem with their demonstrated competence, ensuring that autonomy is experienced as supported rather than abandoned." Introducing autonomy-supportive strategies too late after strict control may undermine trust, while withdrawing scaffolds too early may increase risk exposure and regulatory failure.
requirements: Parental strategies must be responsive to adolescents' developmental signals such as growing self-awareness, expressed values, or responsible behavior
constraints: The article warns that introducing autonomy-supportive strategies too late after prolonged strict control may be experienced as abrupt or inconsistent, and withdrawing scaffolds too early may increase risk exposure and regulatory failure
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: internalization of digital self-regulation
autonomy-supportive parent-adolescent regulation
examples: The article describes parents shifting from restrictive mediation and closer monitoring early in adolescence toward non-intrusive inspection, active mediation, and collaborative rule-setting as adolescents demonstrate competence
key_sources: Wang, M.-T. (2026). Developing Digital Self-Regulation in Adolescence: A Developmental Self-Determination Model of Digital Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10183-y

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: The DeFT framework: design parameters, functions, and tasks of multirepresentational learning
description: The Design, Functions, and Tasks (DeFT) framework (Ainsworth, 2006) is an overarching framework for describing external representation compositions of any kind and making assumptions about their usage. Its design parameters are "the number of representations, the distribution of information among the representations, the form of the representations, the sequence of their presentation, and the provision of support to translate between representations." Its functions component holds that MERs can complement each other, constrain each other's interpretation, and help learners construct deeper understanding; its tasks component relates to the cognitive activities learners engage in when using representations. The review uses DeFT to organize its moderator analysis.
requirements: Learners need to understand how information is encoded within each provided representation and how to relate the individual representations to each other.
target_learners: Students in STEM education at primary, secondary, and postsecondary levels
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge and problem-solving with multiple external representations
examples: The review coded the presence of support, mode of presentation, and informational redundancy of MERs as moderators following the DeFT framework.
key_sources: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y

article_title: Learning scientific concepts through material and social activities: Conversational analysis meets conceptual change
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572
title: Design and study of learning environments should follow from a sociocultural perspective on conceptual change
description: The article outlines key implications of its sociocultural, conversation-analytic perspective for the design and study of learning environments. Because "meaning negotiation and appropriation are identified as mechanisms for achieving such conceptual change," environments for learning scientific concepts should be designed and studied so that learners can negotiate meanings in material and social activity and appropriate them. The abstract states that "Key implications of this perspective for the design and study of learning environments are outlined."
requirements: Learning environments should be designed and studied in terms of the sociocultural mechanisms of meaning negotiation and appropriation.
constraints: The perspective is developed for conceptual change in scientific thinking as the central case.
target_learners: learners developing scientific concepts
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in scientific thinking
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Learning Scientific Concepts Through Material and Social Activities: Conversational Analysis Meets Conceptual Change. Educational Psychologist, 28(3), pp.265-277. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190572

article_title: Beyond Amplification: Using the computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536
title: Because cognitive technologies redefine what learners do, defining educational values must be a foreground issue in educational computing
description: The principle holds that choosing and designing cognitive technologies for education is a values-laden act, since these tools "shap[e] who we are by changing, not just amplifying, what we do." Therefore educators must explicitly define educational values when adopting computing tools, rather than treating technology adoption as value-neutral amplification of existing practice.
requirements: Educators must explicitly articulate educational values before selecting or designing cognitive technologies for learning.
constraints: Grounded in the article's conceptual argument rather than in empirical testing.
target_learners: all learners affected by educational computing
target_learning_goals: alignment of educational goals with the reorganizing effects of cognitive technologies
examples: The article's software analyses are offered as illustrations of how the reorganizer view changes the perceived cognitive benefits of computing.
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536

article_title: Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction
citation: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363
title: Developmental situativity theory: situated learning from a Vygotskian perspective
description: The article presents a situated cognition framework, the developmental situativity theory, in which "situated learning is viewed from a Vygotskian perspective". It assumes learning is "basically a non-symbolic inductive process that is greatly enhanced by formal systems which act as tools", so formal systems function as culturally provided instruments for an otherwise inductive learning process. The theory is used to derive an instructional balance between situated activity and formal tools, and was tested through logic instruction with Tarski's World.
requirements: Instruction must provide an environment containing elements for situated activity together with appropriate formal tools for the theory to be enacted.
target_learners: Students learning formal logic and conditional reasoning
target_learning_goals: Conditional reasoning in formal logic
examples: The authors present the theory and test it empirically by comparing instruction based on only-situated tasks, only-formal tasks, and a combination.
key_sources: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363

article_title: Taking a closer look at how higher education students process and use (discrepant) peer feedback
citation: Van Meenen, F., Masson, N., Catrysse, L., & Coertjens, L. (2023). Taking a closer look at how higher education students process and use (discrepant) peer feedback. Learning and Instruction, 84, 101711. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101711
title: Design feedback-uptake training informed by how students actually process and use (discrepant) peer feedback
description: The article argues that its eye-tracking insights into how students process and use peer feedback should inform instruction: "These insights can be used when designing training to foster students' uptake of (discrepant) PF." Training should therefore target both the processing subphase (noticing discrepancies) and the use subphase (time on the essay, higher order comments, incremental correction, final proofreading).
requirements: Training should address both PF processing and PF use subphase behaviours identified in the study
constraints: Grounded in one eye-tracking study of 59 higher education students revising a fictional essay
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: improving essay revision quality through uptake of (discrepant) peer feedback
examples: 59 participants read feedback of two peers on a fictional essay and revised it while gaze behaviour was recorded
key_sources: Van Meenen, F., Masson, N., Catrysse, L., & Coertjens, L. (2023). Taking a closer look at how higher education students process and use (discrepant) peer feedback. Learning and Instruction, 84, 101711. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101711

article_title: The college laggard.
citation: J. B. Miner. (1910). The College Laggard. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+College+Laggard%22+Miner+Journal+of+Educational+Psychology
title: Remediation for scholastic laggards should target habits of application and resistance to distraction rather than instruction in content
description: The article proposes that the supplementary teacher or college advisor faces a problem bigger than teaching the laggard the lesson: developing habits of application and resistance to distracting temptations, framed as the general problem of interest and control. This follows from the finding that moral factors dominated over intellectual ones in the author's case tabulations.
requirements: Requires identifying laggards early, since the article reports personal characteristics affecting scholarship are largely established by high school graduation
constraints: The article presents this as a suggestion based on a small, local, tentative study rather than a tested intervention
target_learners: college freshmen on academic probation
secondary school students at risk of retardation
target_learning_goals: study habits and self-control
resistance to social and fraternity distractions
examples: The author suggests the supplementary teacher in elementary and secondary schools or the college advisor take up developing habits of application and resistance to temptation
key_sources: J. B. Miner. (1910). The College Laggard. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+College+Laggard%22+Miner+Journal+of+Educational+Psychology

article_title: The contribution of psychology to education.
citation: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074512
title: Teaching methods may be deduced outright from the laws of human nature, as when habit interference explains pupils' difficulty dividing by a fraction.
description: The article's first way psychology contributes to teaching method is deduction from psychological laws. Its example: pupils' difficulty in dividing by a fraction is attributed largely to the entrenched habit from thousands of previous divisions that the result is smaller than the number divided. A method should then be devised or selected that reduces this interference from old habits without weakening them in their proper functioning.
requirements: knowledge of the laws of human nature and of the prior habits that interfere with the new learning
target_learners: elementary and secondary pupils learning arithmetic
target_learning_goals: division by fractions
examples: The fraction-division analysis: the interference is traced to the habit of division-decrease, and method design aims to reduce it to a minimum.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L. (1910). The contribution of psychology to education. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070113

article_title: Achievement goals, reasons for goal pursuit, and achievement goal complexes as predictors of beneficial outcomes: Is the influence of goals reducible to reasons?
citation: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240
title: Design dynamic learning systems for competence-asymmetric interactions with learners' performance goals in mind
description: Because interventions promoting interaction with more-knowledgeable peers expose learners to self-evaluation threat, designers should anticipate that performance-approach goals push learners toward dominant, self-confirming responses and performance-avoidance goals toward submissive compliance. The article argues that "understanding the motivational determinants of its regulation may be of utmost importance to design facilitating interventions" for confrontations with more-competent others, a situation it calls common in educational settings such as unequal-status classroom interactions.
requirements: Knowledge of learners' performance-goal orientation or a way to reduce the self-evaluation threat posed by a more-competent partner
constraints: The evidence concerns disagreement (socio-cognitive conflict) with a more-competent or equally competent partner, not all collaborative learning
target_learners: learners in unequal-status classroom interactions
students in peer tutoring and collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: constructive engagement with a more-competent disagreeing partner
coordinated rather than dominant or compliant conflict regulation
examples: The four studies manipulated or measured partner competence via academic status, bogus test scores, or dyadic score asymmetry while assessing competitive and protective regulation
key_sources: Sommet, N., Darnon, C., & Butera, F. (2015). To Confirm or to Conform? Performance Goals as a Regulator of Conflict With More-Competent Others. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(2), 580–598. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037240

article_title: Long-term positive effects of repeating a year in school: Six-year longitudinal study of self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, school grades, and test scores.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Lichtenfeld, S. (2017). Long-term positive effects of repeating a year in school: six-year longitudinal study of self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, school grades, and test scores. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109 (3). pp. 425-438. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000144
title: Developmental equilibrium perspective on retention effects
description: The article introduces an apparently new developmental equilibrium perspective in retention research, evaluating whether retention effects are consistent across the potentially volatile early-to-middle adolescent period. It defines equilibrium as when "a system achieves a state of balance between the potentially counter-balancing effects of opposing forces". Applied here, the hypothesis is that retention effects are the same for students retained in Years 5-8; support indicates the self-system has achieved developmental balance in relation to retention effects over this period.
requirements: Longitudinal data with multiple retention groups spanning the age range of interest, so lagged effects can be constrained equal across groups and tested for invariance
constraints: The article notes this is an apparently new strategy in retention research and that future research should test the generalizability of the retention effects to students of other ages
target_learners: German secondary school students in Years 5-8 (early-to-middle adolescents)
target_learning_goals: Academic self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, and math achievement following grade retention
examples: The study tested a developmental invariance model constraining lagged retention effects equal across four retention groups (Years 5-8), imposing 60 invariance constraints
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Lichtenfeld, S. (2017). Long-term positive effects of repeating a year in school: six-year longitudinal study of self-beliefs, anxiety, social relations, school grades, and test scores. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109 (3). pp. 425-438. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000144

article_title: How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards were Obtained.
citation: Walter F. Dearborn and Edward A. Lincoln. (1922). How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards Were Obtained. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Dearborn separate-community age-standards method
description: A test-standardization method in which scores from each community are treated separately rather than lumped, distributed by months so both median score and median age can be found, then plotted so standards can be chosen at each half year. The aim is that "the median child of each age should have an intelligence quotient within the normal group (0.90 to 1.10) no matter which community he was in." The article presents this as an alternative to the customary large-N norming that produced classes placed too high or too low and inconsistent rankings across tests.
requirements: Examinations administered in every grade from the second through the senior high school class
Scores distributed by months within each community so median ages as well as median scores can be computed
constraints: Series I lacked enough upper-grade children, so standards from the twelfth year on had to be estimated from the continuation of the plotted lines
The towns were near Boston with agriculture and manufacturing and a sprinkling of children of foreign parents, so generalization to other town types is not directly established
target_learners: school pupils from grade two through senior high school
target_learning_goals: age- and grade-based intelligence-test norms
fair classification of pupils relative to standards
examples: Series II examinations were given in three towns and each community's results were treated separately and plotted on a diagram from which half-year standards were read
key_sources: Walter F. Dearborn and Edward A. Lincoln. (1922). How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards Were Obtained. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075378

article_title: How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards were Obtained.
citation: Walter F. Dearborn and Edward A. Lincoln. (1922). How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards Were Obtained. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Dearborn Intelligence Examination Series I and Series II
description: The Dearborn tests are group intelligence examinations standardized by the separate-community method described in this article. Series II was administered in three towns in every grade from the second through the senior class of high school, while Series I was standardized the same way but "it was not practicable to get results from so many upper grade children," so its upper standards were estimated. The resulting standards take the form of plotted points at each half year of age.
requirements: Administration across grades so median score and median age can be plotted for each community
constraints: Series I upper-grade standards (twelfth year onward) were estimated from the continuation of the lines rather than directly measured
target_learners: pupils from grade two through senior high school
target_learning_goals: measuring pupil intelligence relative to age norms
examples: Series II scores were distributed by months in each of three towns and plotted, with standards chosen at each half year
key_sources: Walter F. Dearborn and Edward A. Lincoln. (1922). How the Dearborn Intelligence Examination Standards Were Obtained. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075378

article_title: Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence.
citation: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507.
title: De Sanctis six-test series for measuring and grading mental deficiency
description: A six-test series proposed by De Sanctis in 1906 (tests of 1905) and printed here in operational detail: handing a named colored ball, recognizing the ball just given, selecting cubes from mixed shapes, matching a cube to a form chart, counting and comparing graduated cubes, and weight and optical-illusion questions. Scoring rules grade deficiency: failing the second test indicates high-grade deficiency, and completing the sixth test without mistake indicates no mental deficiency. The author states the tests were designed to measure the degree of mental defect, not primarily the level of intelligence.
requirements: A table, a screen, five glass balls of different colors, twelve graduated wooden cubes, three cones, two parallelopipeds, a form chart of triangles, rectangles and squares, and a stop-watch measuring fifths of a second
constraints: The tests divide institutionalized defectives into three grades (idiots and imbeciles versus morons) and are intended for medico-pedagogical placement rather than fine-grained intelligence measurement
target_learners: mental defectives in institutions
abnormal children in special schools
target_learning_goals: classification of degree of mental deficiency for educational placement
examples: The author reports the tests are in general use in certain American, Russian, and Italian institutions and quickly distinguish idiots and imbeciles from morons
key_sources: De Sanctis, S. (1911). Mental development and the measurement of the level of intelligence. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 498-507. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069835

article_title: Psychology Coming into Its Own in the Making of Children's Books.
citation: A. I. G.; H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 186-187. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Teachers need an up-to-date, described bibliography of the biological, psychological and sociological evidence about the child as an essential curriculum-making tool
description: The reviewer argues that in making a curriculum, teachers constantly need evidence on mooted points about children, and that "one of the essential tools of the progressive and experimentalist in school practice is an up-to-date, complete and described bibliography" of what biology, psychology and sociology say about the child and the educative process. Hartman's The Child and His School is offered as a book that does this well, adding liberal quotations from leaders and definite suggestions about usable books and materials.
requirements: The bibliography must be up to date, complete, and described, and ideally supplies liberal quotations from leaders of prestige plus suggestions of materials usable with children.
target_learners: teachers making curricula for school children
target_learning_goals: evidence-informed curriculum decisions about children's needs, learning and interests
examples: The reviewer recommends Hartman's book as supplying a classified 850-item bibliography plus an interpreted summary of the scientific basis of education.
key_sources: A. I. G.; H. O. R. (1922). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 186-187. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: A brief scale of intelligence for use in school surveys.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Design brief group tests for convenience, brevity, and teacher-interpretable scores
description: The article argues that group intelligence tests for schools should be built around "convenience, brevity, cost and ready interpretation of results in terms of school practice". The Cross-out scale realizes this: one 9" by 12" sheet, twenty-five minutes of testing, scoring at "90 an hour" by student help or one minute per blank by a teacher, and cheap blanks, so a survey is possible "at a minimum of expense and labor".
requirements: Directions occupy one side of a typewritten sheet, are read verbatim, and scoring requires only counting correctly crossed-out words, one per line
constraints: Insufficient attention to such practical considerations is criticized in other group scales; individual-diagnosis accuracy is limited by brevity
target_learners: school children in grades 4-8 surveyed at class, school, or system level
target_learning_goals: efficient measurement of general ability for survey comparisons and preliminary diagnosis
examples: All cases in one city survey were examined by the writer in one school day, and total scoring-blank cost with student help was $5.00
key_sources: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Differential codevelopment of vocabulary knowledge and reading comprehension for students with and without learning disabilities.
citation: Quinn, Jamie M.; Wagner, Richard K.; Petscher, Yaacov; Roberts, Greg; Menzel, Andrew J.; Schatschneider, Christopher. (2020). Differential Co-Development of Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Comprehension for Students with and without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000382
title: Developmental lag versus developmental deficit accounts of reading growth differences for students with learning disabilities
description: Two competing developmental theories the article tests against its longitudinal data. The "developmental lag model posits that children with an LD start out lower in reading than their peers without an LD, but grow much faster in their reading to catch up over time," whereas "the developmental deficit model posits that children with an LD... are poor readers because of a deficit in a skill that does not properly develop." The study's multiple-group LCS results are used to adjudicate between them: the persistent reading comprehension gap favoring a deficit interpretation, while vocabulary trajectories remained similar across groups.
requirements: Longitudinal multi-year measurement of the target skills to distinguish starting-level differences from growth-rate differences
constraints: The authors caution their model may have covered too narrow a developmental period for a catch-up effect to manifest, leaving the lag account not fully ruled out
Results come from a Title 1 Florida sample under Reading First-era instruction, with no information on curriculum or instructional practices
target_learners: Students in kindergarten through fourth grade
Students with school-identified learning disabilities
Typically developing students in Title 1 schools
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary knowledge (receptive vocabulary breadth)
Reading comprehension growth
examples: The study compared fitted LCS growth trajectories for 627 students with a school-identified LD against 14,146 typically developing peers from kindergarten through fourth grade
key_sources: Quinn, Jamie M.; Wagner, Richard K.; Petscher, Yaacov; Roberts, Greg; Menzel, Andrew J.; Schatschneider, Christopher. (2020). Differential Co-Development of Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Comprehension for Students with and without Learning Disabilities. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000382

article_title: The effects of declarative learning on early and late motor skill learning
citation: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2025). The Effects of Declarative Learning on Early and Late Motor Skill Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00386-3
title: Three-hypothesis framework for declarative interference with motor learning: consolidation disruption, breakdown of inhibition, and resource competition
description: The article organizes competing mechanistic accounts of why an interleaved declarative task might impair motor performance into three named hypotheses. The consolidation-disruption hypothesis holds that "a declarative task commandeers hippocampal–neocortical micro-consolidation during any break period"; the breakdown-of-inhibition hypothesis ties impairment to failed dissipation of reactive inhibition via somatosensory surround inhibition; and the resource-competition hypothesis posits a shared limited cognitive resource with declarative-linked fast learning, predicting impairment only early in training. The experiments adjudicate among them.
requirements: Distinguishing the hypotheses requires varying when the intervening declarative task occurs during training (late versus early) and the amount of reactive inhibition accrued
constraints: The article limits its conclusions to the finger-tapping task, noting the FTT is simple and learned quickly
target_learners: adult undergraduate students learning motor sequences
target_learning_goals: motor sequence skill acquisition and its interaction with declarative memory
examples: Experiment 1 and 2 placed the 4- and 14-minute intervening tasks after substantial training; Experiment 3 placed it after the first three trials to target the fast declarative-linked process
key_sources: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2025). The Effects of Declarative Learning on Early and Late Motor Skill Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00386-3

article_title: Unveiling the impact of goal types: enhancing self-efficacy in rehabilitation robotics
citation: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4
title: Decompose rehabilitation goals into achievable components and continually adjust them to sustain self-efficacy
description: The article argues that rehabilitation professionals should break overarching goals into manageable parts and update them as patients progress, because goal proximity and attainable standards sustain self-efficacy and motivation. It states that "physicians and other rehabilitation professionals must decompose overarching goals into achievable components and continually adjust them based on patients' progress in order to sustain self-efficacy, maintain motivation, and ultimately promote performance gains." This follows from the study's finding that high self-efficacy did not by itself produce performance gains, implying goals must remain proximal and attainable over time.
requirements: Accurate assessment of patients' current abilities so decomposed goals stay closely connected to current attainment
constraints: The article's own findings come from healthy novices in a single session; the recommendation is argued for rehabilitation contexts rather than tested clinically in this study
target_learners: stroke rehabilitation patients
adults in robot-assisted motor rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: sustaining self-efficacy across rehabilitation
motor performance improvement through attainable goal progression
examples: The authors recommend SMART goals and structured team meetings with standardized measurements and ongoing progress monitoring as implementation practices
key_sources: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4

article_title: Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan
citation: Raffington, L. (2024). Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00239-5
title: Theories of development and biological aging differ in whether aging and development are coupled or distinct processes
description: The article organizes competing biological and psychological theories of how development relates to aging (Table 1), including antagonistic pleiotropy, DOHaD, disposable soma, life history theory, the Ground Zero Model, lifespan psychology, and the pseudo-programmatic theory, under which "the ticking of epigenetic clocks reﬂects the continuation of developmental processes". These theories yield contrasting predictions for whether methylation profile scores of child development should correlate with adult biological aging. The article uses them to frame testable competing hypotheses about fast versus slow early development forecasting midlife aging.
requirements: Testing the theories empirically requires molecular quantifications of child development and longitudinal cohorts spanning childhood into adulthood
constraints: The article notes the theories have historically resided in philosophy due to lack of empirical investigation
target_learners: children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding how childhood development and experience relate to later-life biological aging and plasticity
examples: The article contrasts evolutionary life history theory (children who develop faster age faster) with DOHaD (children who develop slower age faster), predicting a non-linear relation if both are true
key_sources: Raffington, L. (2024). Utilizing epigenetics to study the shared nature of development and biological aging across the lifespan. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00239-5

article_title: A better alignment between chronotype and school timing is associated with lower grade retention in adolescents
citation: Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, Andrea P. Goldin, Mariano Sigman and María Juliana Leone. (2023). A better alignment between chronotype and school timing is associated with lower grade retention in adolescents. npj Science of Learning 8:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00171-0
title: Delay school start times to mitigate the disadvantage of later chronotypes on adolescent academic success
description: The article proposes delaying school start times as a policy response to the synchrony effect: because later chronotypes show lower grades and higher grade retention mainly in morning timings, the authors argue that "delaying start times could be a possible policy to mitigate this disadvantage". They ground this in their randomised three-timing design and note the benefit is likely largest for students with later chronotypes at the start of secondary school and for older students in math.
requirements: Schools must be able to offer more than one school timing, or policy makers must change fixed early start times, for the recommendation to be implementable
constraints: The article calls for translational studies and more local evidence before designing educational public policies; the results are correlational, with random assignment supporting comparability but not causal claims
target_learners: Adolescents in secondary school, especially those with later chronotypes
target_learning_goals: Academic performance (grades) and timely completion of secondary school (grade retention)
examples: In the studied school, students were randomly assigned by lottery to morning (07:45–12:05), afternoon (12:40–17:00) or evening (17:20–21:40) timings and kept their timing throughout secondary school
key_sources: Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, Andrea P. Goldin, Mariano Sigman and María Juliana Leone. (2023). A better alignment between chronotype and school timing is associated with lower grade retention in adolescents. npj Science of Learning 8:21. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00171-0

article_title: Insights from 200+ years of personalized learning
citation: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x
title: Design learning environments proactively around anticipated learner variability, not exceptions to a group lesson
description: A personalization-based pedagogy, the article argues, starts from the assumption that each student differs across multiple dimensions, not just domain knowledge and skill. Rather than constructing lessons for the group and differentiating for outliers, "learning environments and related tasks, often supported by technology, can be constructed to remove expected barriers and bolster supports to address anticipated needs, including affective and behavioral ones, and both proactively and reactively." Design and materials should focus on the variability within the target population that matters most for learning and demonstrating competence.
requirements: Instructional design and materials informed by data and learning science about the target population's anticipated variability
constraints: Teaching and learning in this system "won't be uniform," so it conflicts with infrastructure built on same-content-same-pace assumptions
target_learners: all K-12 learners, including those with affective, behavioral, and executive-function needs
target_learning_goals: academic competence alongside motivation, mindset, and self-regulated learning
examples: The article argues research should identify under what conditions each intervention works with different learner characteristics, matching an instructional action with the right learner at the right time
key_sources: David Dockterman. (2018). Insights from 200 + years of personalized learning. npj Science of Learning 3:15. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0033-x

article_title: Mapping the Montessori mathematics curriculum to Dehaene’s four pillars of learning
citation: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4
title: Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning: attention, active engagement, error feedback, and consolidation
description: The article's organizing framework, drawn from Dehaene's 2020 book 'How we learn': four evidence-based pillars that must be in place for learning to succeed. Attention is "the mechanism by which the brain selects, amplifies, and channels information for processing and encoding as memory"; active engagement requires effortful involvement so experience enables building mental models; error feedback arises when predicted expectations are violated; consolidation is a shift from slow, conscious, effortful processing to fast, automatic expertise.
requirements: All four pillars must be in place for the learning process to be successful, per Dehaene as the article summarizes
constraints: The framework concerns learning rather than pedagogy; the article extends it to pedagogy by mapping a curriculum onto it
target_learners: 3- to 6-year-old children learning mathematics, as applied in this article
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of abstract mathematical knowledge
examples: The article maps each Group 1 Montessori material onto a pillar: single-quality isolation for attention, fetch-and-match activities for active engagement, the Spindle Box for error feedback, and cumulative sequences for consolidation.
key_sources: Marshall, C., Livingston, L., & Van Herwegen, J. (2026). Mapping the Montessori Mathematics Curriculum to Dehaene's Four Pillars of Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00436-4

article_title: Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment
citation: Antonie Knigge, Ineke Maas, Kim Stienstra, Eveline L. de Zeeuw and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2022). Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 7:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00122-1
title: Defer definite track placement until partway through secondary school, or reassess track level during secondary school, to reduce inequality of opportunity
description: The article proposes that educational systems with early tracking avoid fixing track level at the end of primary school. If the observed associations reflect a causal effect of delayed tracking, the authors advise that systems seeking to combat inequality of opportunity "delay deﬁnite tracking to a later age", and suggest it may be more logical to "assess, or at least reassess, the track level of a child at some point in secondary school" so talents and track level do not mismatch early.
requirements: A school system in which secondary schools offer both immediate single-track placement and combined heterogeneous classes, so that definitive tracking can be postponed while students are observed.
