constraints: The authors state the design is not experimental: whether children delay tracking is not exogenously controlled, other confounders cannot be ruled out, and the advice is conditional on the findings reflecting a causal effect.
target_learners: Students transitioning from primary to secondary education in tracked systems
target_learning_goals: Realizing students' genetic potential and reducing dependence of track placement on family background
examples: In Dutch secondary schools, some students are placed in a class combining two or more levels for 1–3 years before teachers decide the definitive track, and the study compared these delayed-tracking twins with immediately tracked twins.
key_sources: Antonie Knigge, Ineke Maas, Kim Stienstra, Eveline L. de Zeeuw and Dorret I. Boomsma. (2022). Delayed tracking and inequality of opportunity: Gene-environment interactions in educational attainment. npj Science of Learning 7:6. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00122-1

article_title: Neural mechanisms underpinning the association between visual arts education and creativity
citation: Jing Teng, Xinuo Qiao, Kelong Lu, Tuo Liu, Xinyue Wang, Zhenni Gao, Tingting Yu & Ning Hao (2025). Neural mechanisms underpinning the association between visual arts education and creativity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00388-1
title: Incorporate design-related visual arts practices such as sketching, visual imagination, and visual-spatial problem solving into general curricula as elective or supplementary courses
description: This principle holds that elements of design-related visual arts education — practices such as sketching, visual imagination, and visual-spatial problem solving — can be incorporated into general curricula as elective or supplementary courses. The article argues these practices "directly engage cognitive processes such as flexibility, imagination, and problem-solving, which are essential for success in various fields". It is grounded in the study's findings that design majors showed higher creative performance and more efficient, flexible neural processing, though the authors note further research is needed before policy conclusions.
requirements: The recommended practices are design-related ones the study links to creative engagement: sketching, visual imagination, and visual-spatial problem solving, offered as elective or supplementary courses.
constraints: The article states the findings are quasi-experimental, may reflect pre-existing differences, and should not be generalized beyond the design-major context; further research is needed.
target_learners: university students
students in general (non-design) curricula
target_learning_goals: domain-general creativity
divergent thinking
flexibility, imagination, and problem-solving
examples: The study compared design majors with propensity-score-matched non-design majors and found the design group performed better across creative tasks and showed more efficient, flexible brain network engagement.
key_sources: Jing Teng, Xinuo Qiao, Kelong Lu, Tuo Liu, Xinyue Wang, Zhenni Gao, Tingting Yu & Ning Hao (2025). Neural mechanisms underpinning the association between visual arts education and creativity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00388-1

article_title:
Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple 
memory systems
citation: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2
title: Three shared oscillations (delta, theta, gamma) span hippocampal, cortical, and striatal memory circuits
description: The review defines three rhythms it treats as common across memory systems: "delta (0.5 – 2 Hz), theta (6– 9 Hz), and gamma (35– 100 Hz)" recordable from or influencing the cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. It explains their generation mechanisms: cortical intrinsic circuitry for delta, medial septum pacing for hippocampal theta, and pyramidal-interneuron recursion for gamma, with gamma nested under and modulated by the slower rhythms. This shared substrate is presented as a general-purpose coordination mechanism largely blind to information content.
requirements: Afferent excitatory drive and reciprocal pyramidal-interneuron connectivity for gamma; MS-DBB and entorhinal inputs for theta; intrinsic cortical circuitry for delta
constraints: Nested phenomena such as spindling (7–14 Hz) and faster delta (2–4 Hz) are explicitly excluded from the review's scope
target_learners: adults and animals across declarative and procedural memory tasks
target_learning_goals: neural coordination of memory encoding, consolidation, and retrieval
examples: The review's Fig. 1–3 depict delta propagation, MS-DBB theta pacing, and PING gamma generation across the three regions
key_sources: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2

article_title: To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators
citation: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4
title: Design AI education tools around educators' existing workflows, with clear value propositions for their time investment
description: Because implementing AI in education is a sociotechnical challenge, technology designers need to understand the status quo of educators' environment, workflow, schedule, and resources to find entry points with a clear value proposition for educators' return on time investment. Tools that fit seamlessly into ubiquitous systems like learning management systems and help with effortful tasks such as grading or summarizing student responses are more likely to be adopted; cost and reliability of hardware and software also matter, reliability being especially salient for educators who have encountered issues during class time.
requirements: Designers must understand educators' existing environment, workflow, schedule, and resources before introducing a new tool.
constraints: Educators have limited time and flexibility to engage in new activities.
target_learners: Educators in schools and higher education
target_learning_goals: Effective integration and adoption of AI tools in teaching practice
examples: The article notes educators' familiarity with gradual AI feature introductions in tools like Google Docs (e.g., rephrasing suggestions) as easy-to-integrate models.
key_sources: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4

article_title: Identification of Patterns to Prevent the Failure of Engineering Students
citation: Fabian Santiago-Muñoz, Mikel Larrañaga, Jon A. Elorriaga, Ana Arruarte. (2025). Identification of Patterns to Prevent the Failure of Engineering Students. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:3356–3405. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00502-9
title: DEMRE pre-admission dataset of 2,292 engineering students with 68 attributes reduced to 12 features
description: The dataset comes from DEMRE, the organisation managing Chile's university selection process, covering students admitted to Engineering at the University of Tarapacá between 2018 and 2022 (2,292 students). "Data consists of 68 individual characteristics per student grouped into: personal information, academic background, geographical origin, economic income, grants and marks from the university entrance exam." Preprocessing (cleansing, redundancy removal, correlation filtering at a 0.4 threshold, normalization) reduced the 68 variables to 12 key features including GPA, entrance-exam scores, gender, per-capita income, and geographic origin.
requirements: Privacy and data protection compliance required removal of contact details, addresses, and scholarship details
Correlation-based filtering at a 0.4 threshold to remove redundant attributes
constraints: Natural class distribution was preserved without balancing techniques, reflecting the imbalanced real population
target_learners: First-year engineering university students in Chile
target_learning_goals: Characterising pre-admission profiles associated with dropout, failure, or passing
examples: GPA was retained while ranking (r = 0.978 with GPA) and NEM (r = 0.999 with GPA) were discarded
key_sources: Fabian Santiago-Muñoz, Mikel Larrañaga, Jon A. Elorriaga, Ana Arruarte. (2025). Identification of Patterns to Prevent the Failure of Engineering Students. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:3356–3405. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00502-9

article_title: Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited
citation: B. Barros & M. F. Verdejo (2015). Computer-Based Interaction Analysis with DEGREE Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ (2016) 26:113–123. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0063-y
title: DEGREE collaborative learning tool with semi-structured communication, experiment configuration, interaction analysis, and interventions
description: DEGREE is a collaborative learning tool that "uses semi-structured communication (with sentence openers, tagged dialogs)" and offers tools to configure a collaborative experiment, provide an analysis of the collaboration process, and offer interventions to improve the interaction. The authors report that its sentence-opener model of facilitating collaborative interaction was re-implemented in a collaborative version of the SIETTE system for collaborative small-group assessment and interaction analysis. The community also cited DEGREE as an integrated approach to designing, conducting, and analysing a collaborative experiment.
requirements: Teachers' criteria for indicator values must be modelled when the learning activity is designed; the technological setup of activities and monitoring was deliberately undertaken to avoid increasing teachers' workload
constraints: The authors decided not to address automated tagging of discourse units because NLP technology at the time would not have yielded a result sufficiently reliable for use in the system
target_learners: distance-education students at UNED working in small groups of two to three students
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning and group interaction analysis
examples: DEGREE was cited by the community as "a framework for configuration, execution, and interaction analysis" and as a CSCL system

article_title: Investigating the Impact of Backward Strategy Learning in a Logic Tutor: Aiding Subgoal Learning Towards Improved Problem Solving
citation: Preya Shabrina, Behrooz Mostafavi, Mark Abdelshiheed, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2024). Investigating the Impact of Backward Strategy Learning in a Logic Tutor: Aiding Subgoal Learning Towards Improved Problem Solving. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:825–861. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00338-1
title: Deep Thought logic tutor with backward worked examples and backward problem solving proof types
description: Deep Thought (DT) is an intelligent logic-proof tutor organized into 7 levels in which students apply logic rules to premises to reach a conclusion. For this study two new proof types were added: Backward Worked Examples, where “the tutor constructs an entire proof by using BW derivation only as students click on the > button,” and Backward Problem Solving, where “forward derivations are disabled” and students refine the conclusion into unjustified subgoal nodes until all connect to premises. Problem scores combine accuracy, time function and solution size equally.
requirements: Requires the tutor interface with forward/backward derivation modes, rule list, and on-demand forward hints during training PS problems
constraints: There are no backward hints in DT, and BPS problems are restrictive by design, requiring proofs entirely in the backward direction
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science majors in a discrete mathematics course
target_learning_goals: Logic proof construction
Subgoaling and problem-solving strategy learning
examples: The training session contained 20 problems across levels 2-6, with BPSs distributed only in the first half so T2 could independently master backward strategy later; students spent around 6 hours on training on average
key_sources: Preya Shabrina, Behrooz Mostafavi, Mark Abdelshiheed, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2024). Investigating the Impact of Backward Strategy Learning in a Logic Tutor: Aiding Subgoal Learning Towards Improved Problem Solving. article_title: Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach
citation: R. Charles Murray, Kurt Vanlehn, Jack Mostow. (2004). Looking Ahead to Select Tutorial Actions: A Decision-Theoretic Approach. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197308
title: Decision-theoretic framework for selecting tutorial actions by looking ahead to their anticipated effects
description: The article proposes a framework in which an intelligent tutoring system selects tutorial actions by anticipating their consequences for the student and the tutorial state before acting. It is stated to "use a dynamic decision network to consider the tutor's uncertain beliefs and objectives in adapting to and managing the changing tutorial state". The framework treats action selection as decision making under uncertainty rather than fixed rule following.
requirements: A model of the tutorial state including student attributes and task and discourse state, as instantiated in the article's prototype engines
constraints: The abstract does not report results from a complete integrated intelligent tutoring system
target_learners: students in calculus tutoring
elementary reading students
target_learning_goals: domain skill acquisition in calculus and elementary reading
examples: Prototype action selection engines for calculus and elementary reading illustrate the approach

description: The authors proposed a novel deep learning approach for automatic detection of hand-over-face gestures in images, achieving "a classification accuracy of 86.87%". This model enables automated, non-intrusive monitoring of learner nonverbal behavior using a low-cost webcam, supporting integration with intelligent tutoring systems.

article_title: The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor
citation: Christa Cody, Mehak Maniktala, Nicholas Lytle, Min Chi, Tiffany Barnes. (2021). The Impact of Looking Further Ahead: A Comparison of Two Data-driven Unsolicited Hint Types on Performance in an Intelligent Data-driven Logic Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05741
title: Deep Thought logic proof tutor with unsolicited Assertions hint delivery
description: Deep Thought is a propositional logic tutoring system used in a discrete mathematics course, with four phases: introduction, pretest, training (18 problems), and posttest (four harder, non-isomorphic problems). It provides immediate error feedback on justifications and derived statements, automated proof-completion detection, and node coloring based on necessity and frequency in historical correct solutions. Unsolicited hints are delivered as Assertions — "unsolicited, tutor-initiated steps inserted into the student workspace" — which prior work showed resulted in better performance than text-based messages.
requirements: Historical student solution data for hint generation and node coloring
constraints: No bottom-out hints: only level 1 pointing hints were used, with hint levels 2-4 disabled; hints are not necessarily provided when most needed
target_learners: undergraduate students in a discrete mathematics for computer scientists course
target_learning_goals: efficient logic proof solving in time, steps, and accuracy
examples: Students solved 18 training problems with data-driven hints and took a four-problem posttest without any assistance

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Decision Tree model: a non-incremental apprentice learner model within the Apprentice Learner Architecture
description: The Decision Tree model is one of two apprentice learner models built within the Apprentice Learner Architecture. It uses a non-incremental decision tree learner for when-learning, meaning it reprocesses all experienced training examples each time it updates its learned classifier. Like the Trestle model, it draws on the same small set of prior knowledge (six operators and three types of relational knowledge) to support expert model authoring. The model was used to author a novel experimental design tutor and evaluated across seven additional tutoring domains.
requirements: Needs access to a relational representation of each step in the tutor interface, which CTAT can automatically generate from drag-and-drop authored interfaces
constraints: Non-incremental approaches are less efficient to train because they reprocess all examples after each new example
target_learners: non-programmer tutor authors
target_learning_goals: learning expert models for tutoring systems from demonstrations and feedback
examples: Used to author an experimental design tutor via interactive training on 20 problems
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action
citation: Teresa Swist, Simon Buckingham Shum, Kalervo N. Gulson. (2024). Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:670–705. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00380-z
title: Deliberative Democracy and the Deliberative Mini-Public framework
description: Deliberative Democracy emerged around 1990 as a "deliberative turn" in democratic theory, responding to a crisis of confidence in how typical democratic systems engage citizens. It operates by convening a Deliberative Mini-Public (DMP) with three core features: "Influence", "Inclusion", and "Deliberation", the latter providing "open dialogue, access to information, respect, space to understand and reframe issues, and movement to toward consensus". Random or stratified selection delivers the mini-public aspect; neutral facilitation, balanced expert witnesses, and senior-leadership sanction are further key features. The article applies DD as an organisational consultation on AI ethics in higher education.
requirements: Sanction by senior leadership with commitment that the DMP's recommendations matter, so the process is not tokenistic
Neutral facilitation by a person or team with no stake in the outcome
Random or stratified sampling to deliver the mini-public aspect and mitigate bias
constraints: The use of DD for an organisational rather than citizen consultation, and for AI ethics, is novel, so established practice evidence is limited
Who sets the DMP's purpose/agenda may be contentious; arm's-length conduct is advised if framing bias is feared
target_learners: higher education students
educators and tutors
institutional leaders
target_learning_goals: understanding ethical issues of analytics/AI educational technology
deliberative decision-making and consensus skills
examples: The UTS consultation convened a DMP of 20 recruited from 131 applicants via stratified sampling, running five Zoom sessions over seven weeks with external DD facilitation
key_sources: Teresa Swist, Simon Buckingham Shum, Kalervo N. Gulson. (2024). Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:670–705. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00380-z

article_title: Online learning under COVID-19: re-examining the prominence of video-based and text-based feedback
citation: Istenič, A. (2021). Online learning under COVID-19: re-examining the prominence of video-based and text-based feedback. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 117–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09955-w
title: Design online learning environments that address the multidimensional nature of feedback rather than favoring one medium
description: The article argues that learning design should select technology affordances according to learning principles rather than comparing media. It states that "the specific context of learning design requires the selection of learning technology affordances according to the principles of learning (e.g., the authenticity of learning and learners' characteristics and needs)". Following Mayer (2001), the focus should be a learner-centered approach on "how to integrate media to enhance human learning".

Consideration of learners' characteristics and needs
constraints: Comparing textual-based and video-based feedback is inconclusive
target_learners: higher education students in online and blended courses
target_learning_goals: personalized learning
authentic learning
examples: Learning analytics informs the provision of written and/or video-based feedback
Video-based feedback and instructional video provide ground for contextualized, situated learning

article_title: The role of mobile technologies in shifting to digital
citation: Hale Ilgaz. (2021). The role of mobile technologies in shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 189–190. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09945-y
title: Define the unique functions and affordances of mobile learning environments and tools before designing for them
description: For a successful learning process, the editorial holds that researchers and practitioners should first define what mobile learning environments and tools uniquely do. It cites Grant (2019) on difficulties in defining mobile learning, analysis, design characteristics and implications. The principle treats mobile learning as distinct from other digital learning rather than a smaller version of it, so design should start from the tool's own affordances.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners must analyze the specific mobile learning environment or tool rather than assuming generic features
target_learners: online university students
mobile learners
target_learning_goals: effective design of mobile learning environments
examples: The editorial cites Grant (2019), 'Difficulties in defining mobile learning: Analysis, design characteristics, and implications,' as the basis for defining affordances before design

article_title: The role of mobile technologies in shifting to digital
citation: Hale Ilgaz. (2021). The role of mobile technologies in shifting to digital. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 189–190. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09945-y
title: Consider design issues alongside accessibility, ease of use, and speed when shifting education to mobile and digital technologies
description: The editorial argues that in today's world speed, accessibility and mobility are important themes, and that mobile devices and mobile-compatible applications play an important role in the educational digital shift. However, it states that "In addition to the accessibility, ease of use, and speed features, design issues should also be considered." Design quality is therefore a co-equal requirement with access when building mobile learning.
requirements: Design issues must be addressed in addition to accessibility, ease of use, and speed features
target_learners: online and mobile learners
learners in emergent remote teaching contexts
target_learning_goals: successful learning processes in mobile and digital learning environments
examples: The special issue pairs an international perspective on device portability and availability with an inclusion perspective presenting design and practical solutions for income, country-status and digital-skill barriers

article_title: Influencing the design outcome
citation: Camille Dickson-Deane. (2021). Influencing the design outcome. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09943-0
title: Design is not a panacea, but more planning and design capacity benefits all stakeholders
description: The editorial anchors both response themes in Goodyear's (2015) statement that "design is not a panacea", while asserting that "with more planning and capacity to design there will be benefits for all of the stakeholders". The principle cautions against treating instructional design as a cure-all while still recommending investment in teachers' planning and design capacity, particularly for digital transitions.
requirements: Investment in planning time and design capacity for teachers
constraints: Design alone does not guarantee outcomes; it is not a panacea
target_learners: teachers
instructional designers

examples: The editorial uses this framing to organize the eight response essays into two themes: who designs for learning, and the practice of designing for learning.

citation: Meier, E. B. (2021). Designing and using digital platforms for 21st century learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09880-4
title: Design online platforms that give learners equitable access and support interest-driven ownership of learning
description: The article endorses the aim, drawn from Nacu et al., of designing network platforms that give learners "equitable access to systems that inspire young people 'to pursue their interests and take ownership of their learning'." It argues such design became especially important when platforms assumed a central role during the Covid-19 pandemic. The principle is presented as a design orientation rather than an empirically tested recommendation.

citation: Dexter, S. (2023). Developing faculty EdTech instructional decision-making competence with principles for the integration of EdTech. Education Tech Research Dev, 71, 163–179. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10198-0
title: Competence as a linking middle view between competencies and competence
description: The article proposes that the dichotomy between competencies (knowledge, skills, affect and motivation) and competence (demonstrated behaviors) is better treated as a continuum with a fruitful middle point. This middle view 'emphasizes the processes faculty use to recognize what the situation demands and make decisions about what to do and operationalize competencies into competence.' It serves as the conceptual basis for the article's principles for EdTech integration.
requirements: Faculty professional learning should target the linking middle view rather than only component competencies or only observed performance
constraints: Framed for higher education faculty integrating EdTech into courses

target_learning_goals: EdTech integration decision making
Online teaching competence

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Deep learning as back-propagation through weighted multi-layer neural networks
description: The article characterizes machine deep learning via LeCun et al.'s account, in which "Deep learning discovers intricate structure in large data sets by using the back-propagation algorithm". Back-propagation occurs during training: predictions are compared with known target values and the weights of links between adjacent layers are adjusted backwards to minimize error, making the systems non-deterministic and adaptive through experience. Because of the complexity and probabilistic nature of these multi-layered networks, deep learning typically operates as a black box, which grounds the article's later explainability arguments.
requirements: Depends on weighted neural networks trained with datasets, learning rate parameters and a training regime chosen by system engineers
constraints: Typically trained on static datasets, and incorporating new data requires retraining which can result in catastrophic forgetting of existing knowledge
target_learners: students learning about machine learning
educators and system developers
target_learning_goals: understanding how machine learning systems work and their limits

This design activity raised students' interest and motivation as they became designers rather than formula appliers, addressing the problem that students 'may merely recall formulas and apply them'. The article proposes a set of design principles for integrating CT into mathematics curriculum from this approach.

Teacher experience with mobile app development activities

computational thinking
problem-solving skills

article_title: Utilising learning analytics to support study success in higher education: a systematic review
citation: Dirk Ifenthaler, Jane Yin-Kim Yau. (2020). Utilising learning analytics to support study success in higher education: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09788-z
title: Three-method taxonomy of learning analytics: descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics
description: The review organises learning analytics methodologies into three types. "Descriptive analytics use data obtained from sources such as course assessments, surveys, student information systems, learning management system activities and forum interactions mainly for reporting purposes." Predictive analytics use similar data to measure onward learning success or failure, while prescriptive analytics deploy algorithms mainly to predict study success and course completion and to recommend immediate interventions. The review uses this taxonomy to characterise the diversification of early trace-data approaches into broader educational applications.
requirements: Data from sources such as course assessments, surveys, student information systems, learning management system activities and forum interactions
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: study success, course completion, and dropout prevention
examples: The review's Table 1 classifies the 46 key publications' data analytics methods, including binary logistic regression, decision tree analysis, and support vector machines, with main predictions on course completion, grades, and dropout rates.
key_sources: Dirk Ifenthaler, Jane Yin-Kim Yau. (2020). Utilising learning analytics to support study success in higher education: a systematic review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09788-z

article_title: Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool
citation: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2
title: Detached digital self-explication SRL tool with five prompt categories, refined prompt cards, and strategy cards
description: A web-application offering detached, domain-general or domain-specific metacognitive support in parallel to ongoing learning. It prompts learners to make implicit metacognition concrete via five main prompt categories (ideas about learning, goals, plans, checks, improvements to learning), each with 6–9 refined prompt cards and one metacognitive strategy card providing direct instruction. Learners "could freely navigate through the different categories as available and add, review, or update their responses as desired", with responses saved automatically. Materials were reviewed in a student focus group and by two educational experts.
requirements: Support must be made progressively available so as not to overwhelm learners or preclude self-initiated metacognitive processing
constraints: The domain-specific configuration requires designers to have some knowledge of the subject matter, limiting when and where the tool can be used
target_learners: 1st-year higher-education students in a multimedia design program
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness across all phases of self-regulated learning
examples: In the evaluation, the most frequently requested feature was an option to receive reminders to check up on learning within the tool
key_sources: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2

article_title: Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks
citation: Ludo W. van Meeuwen, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Paul A. Kirschner, Jeano J. P. R. de Bock, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2018). Fostering self-regulation in training complex cognitive tasks. Education Tech Research Dev 66, 53–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9539-9

Regulation prompts at the right moments, prior to and after learning tasks

Domain-specific ATC competences
Self-efficacy for learning

article_title: Activity-Centred Analysis and Design (ACAD): Core purposes, distinctive qualities and current developments
citation: Peter Goodyear. (2015). Teaching as design. HERDSA Review of Higher Education. https://www.herdsa.org.au/herdsa-review-higher-education-vol-2/27-50
title: Science of design partition: epistemology, phenomenology and praxiology as three areas for studying teachers' design work

educational designers

article_title: Shifting to digital with 21st century skills
citation: Hale Ilgaz. (2021). Shifting to digital with 21st century skills. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09946-x
title: Design online learning environments to support educators as well as learners
description: The editorial's closing recommendation is that online learning design attend to educators, not only learners: "Online learning designers should pay attention to not only the experiences of learners but also to how educators are enabled to support their learning." Environments used to train individuals with 21st-century skills "should also support the educators in this regard," and defining educator roles and tasks is presented as important for an effective learning process.

constraints: Stated in the context of environments aiming to cultivate 21st-century skills

educators in online learning environments

effective educator support of learning

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: Detect-diagnose-act framework for adaptive learning technologies
description: The article explains the functioning of adaptive learning technologies through the detect-diagnose-act framework (Molenaar, 2022). As printed: "Detect represents the input data, such as answers to questions to measure students' current knowledge". Diagnosis assesses current knowledge and predicts future progress, and diagnoses are translated into pedagogical-didactical actions that either inform the teacher or are taken adaptively by the ALT. The framework contextualizes where teacher dashboards sit within ALTs.
requirements: Input data on student responses must be collected before diagnosis and action can occur
constraints: Current ALT dashboards mostly present cognitive progress indicators rather than metacognitive ones
target_learners: primary school students
target_learning_goals: monitoring student progress
adaptive instruction
examples: Dutch primary education context where 60% of students use an ALT daily (Kennisnet, 2019)

citation: Xi Xiang & Michael E. Meadows. (2025). Being proactive about anthropogenic environmental changes: augmenting students' decision making with artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10523-9
title: Decision making about the future learning outcome framework with twelve components
description: The article develops a 'decision making about the future' learning outcome framework informed by decision-making science, AI methodologies, and educational and psychological perspectives. It has twelve components and treats sustainability as dynamic: "AI technology enables sustainability to be treated as a dynamic and evolving concept of sustainability, and learners are able to study the nature and rate of anthropogenic environmental change, identify likely future challenges and opportunities, and make decisions". It serves as a methodological guide for designing AI-supported activities.
requirements: A data-intensive learning environment in which learners study environmental change and make decisions
constraints: Designed for the formal school geography curriculum context
target_learners: high school geography students (Grade 12)
target_learning_goals: decision-making competency for sustainable development
understanding anthropogenic environmental change
examples: Used to guide the design of two learning activities: managing the future of coasts and combating future forest fires

title: Decision quality framework with six elements for assessing decisions about the future
description: Adapted from a decision quality framework based on decision analysis concepts and tools, the article represents decision quality regarding the future in six elements: "setting an appropriate frame, considering creative and practical alternatives, gathering meaningful and reliable information, identifying synergies and trade-offs to evaluate the consequences of alternatives, using logical reasoning to weigh decisions, and implementing action". Geography teachers can develop assessments to gauge decision quality at any point of the decision-making process.

constraints: Intended for uncertain and dynamic environments such as future-oriented sustainability decisions

article_title: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners
citation: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w
title: Delayed-uptake: learners' delayed reflective responses to asynchronous online feedback as an indicator of the learning developmental process
description: Delayed-uptake is the authors' term for students' delayed or 'soon after responses' of reflective thoughts following asynchronous online feedback, gathered after students had time to form thoughts. Whereas uptake research examines immediate learner responses after feedback, this concept captures perceptions expressed later, here as metaphors. The authors argue that "online feed -back creates a more profound delaye d-uptake" and that this delayed-uptake "is deemed an indicator of the learning developmental process". It extends uptake analysis to technology-mediated written feedback contexts.
requirements: Asynchronous online feedback must give learners time to reflect before responses are collected
constraints: The article states it is far from sufficient to claim the 'effectiveness' of online tools in contributing to conclusive outcomes for language learning
target_learners: introverted Chinese-educated undergraduate language learners
target_learning_goals: second-language writing improvement and reflective awareness of feedback
examples: Students who received GradeMark feedback completed an open-ended questionnaire days later and expressed perceptions as metaphors such as footprints on the beach, showing reflection after the feedback event.
key_sources: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w

article_title: From evaluation to learning: Some aspects of designing a cyber-university
citation: Anna Helga Jonsdottir, Gunnar Stefansson. (2014). From evaluation to learning: Some aspects of designing a cyber-university. https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.5552
title: Design drill systems for learning rather than evaluation, since classical statistical models for mere evaluation do not apply
description: The article argues that because students improve their knowledge while using the system, "the usual IRT models do not apply to the present setup, nor do any conceptual models or frameworks designed only for testing purposes". Item selection methods from computerized adaptive testing were developed to measure abilities and do not account for learning in a dynamic environment.
requirements: Item allocation and grading methods that account for learning in a dynamic environment
constraints: Applies to on-line learning environments where knowledge changes during use, not to static testing settings
target_learners: on-line learners in dynamic learning environments
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition through drill practice
examples: The tutor-web permits students to continue requesting drill items until the system reports a grade satisfactory to the student

article_title: Computer-supported collaborative learning: An analysis of the relationship between interaction, emotional support and online collaborative tools
citation: Hernández-Sellés, N., Muñoz-Carril, P.-C., & González-Sanmamed, M. (2019). Computer-supported collaborative learning: An analysis of the relationship between interaction, emotional support and online collaborative tools. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.04.012
title: Design online collaborative learning to intentionally build intra-group emotional support, not just cognitive interaction.
description: Because intra-group emotional support is the strongest predictor of collaborative learning, instructors should deliberately design activities and structures that build emotional bonds within work groups, including personal links, mutual encouragement, and a sense of belonging. The article emphasizes that social interaction does not happen spontaneously and must be actively scaffolded by the teacher, especially in the early phases of collaboration.
requirements: Teacher presence in early phases to scaffold group formation and socio-emotional bonding.
constraints: Social interaction should not be assumed to occur naturally; it requires deliberate design.
target_learners: Higher education students working in online groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning
Social presence
examples: The study's subjects used a structured eight-phase collaboration script including group agreements, teacher feedback, and self- and peer-assessment.

article_title: Design fictions for learning: A method for supporting students in reflecting on technology in Human-Computer Interaction courses
citation: Rapp A. (2020). Design fictions for learning: A method for supporting students in reflecting on technology in Human-Computer Interaction courses. COMPUTERS & EDUCATION, 145, 1-18. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103725
title: Design fiction as a reflective learning framework in HCI education
description: The article frames design fiction as an approach that leverages speculative scenarios to provoke reflection on technology's social and ethical dimensions. It positions this within HCI education as a way to move beyond technical skills toward critical engagement. The framework connects fiction-making with learning through imagination and critique.

understanding social implications of computing

article_title: Formative e-assessment: Practitioner cases
citation: Norbert Pachler, Caroline Daly, Yishay Mor, Harvey Mellar. (2009). Formative e-assessment: practitioner cases. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00592754
title: Design pattern methodology for developing cases of formative e-assessment with practitioners
description: The article documents a design pattern methodology in which cases of formative e-assessment were developed iteratively with the UK education practitioner community. Practitioners from a range of post-16 education contexts collaboratively developed cases of practice, from which patterns were extracted to inform future software design. The methodology aimed to scope the 'domain' of formative e-assessment by developing cases and identifying key formative processes within them that are affected by the use of technologies.

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement
citation: Lynch, K., Gonzalez, K., Hill, H., & Merritt, R. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251335302
title: Desimone/Garet framework of effective professional development elements
description: An influential 2000s framework positing that effective teacher PD should contain several common elements. As the article states, it held that "effective teacher PD should contain several common elements: con- tent focus, active learning, coherence, sufficient duration, and collective participation (Desimone, 2009; Garet et al., 2001)." The framework was generative for the field and structures the moderators this meta-analysis codes, but federally commissioned large-scale tests of PD containing these elements had disappointing results, prompting refinement efforts.
requirements: PD programs must be designed and evaluated against the five common elements for the framework's predictions to apply
constraints: Several federally commissioned large-scale studies aiming to test PD containing these elements had disappointing results, raising questions about potential refinements

classroom instruction
examples: The framework informs the moderator codes for PD duration, curriculum materials inclusion, and programmatic foci used in this meta-analysis

article_title: Endless justification: A scoping review of team-based learning research in medical education.
citation: Cleland JA, Pienkowska A, Kitto SC. (2026). Endless justification: A scoping review of team‐based learning research in medical education. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70041
title: Cook, Bordage and Schmidt's description–justification–clarification typology as a lens for tracking the maturity of an educational research field
description: The review adopts Cook, Bordage and Schmidt's threefold classification of research purposes: "description (what was carried out), justification (does it work), and finally, clarification (how does it work)". Description covers perceptions and implementation accounts, justification covers comparative effectiveness studies, and clarification covers theory- or framework-driven studies of how TBL works. The review uses this typology to classify 288 studies and to diagnose the field's lack of progression, inspired by wave analyses of PBL and programmatic assessment research.
requirements: Clarification research is characterised by the presence of a conceptual framework or theory, which the reviewers used collective judgement to categorise when implicit
constraints: The reviewers report lively debates about categorising individual studies and struggled most with implicit versus explicit frameworks
target_learners: medical students
health professions educators and researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding the state and progression of educational research on team-based learning
examples: The review classified 288 studies into the three categories and tracked their proportions from 2005 to 2024 and from 2015 to 2024
key_sources: Cleland JA, Pienkowska A, Kitto SC. (2026). Endless justification: A scoping review of team‐based learning research in medical education. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70041

article_title: Angoff methods in standard setting in health professional education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Kannan, S., & Gowri, S. (2025). Angoff methods in standard setting in health professional education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education, 25, 1727. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08300-6
title: Select the Angoff variant deliberately, aligned with assessment purpose and context
description: Because Angoff variants differ substantially in stringency and reliability, educators should select a specific variant as "a conscious decision aligned with the assessment's purpose and context." The Modified Angoff with a reality check is recommended as the preferred variant for psychometrically defensible and reliable processes, while the Angoff (Yes/No) method should be employed with caution and only alongside extensive judge training.
requirements: Requires awareness of the learner level, academic discipline, and assessment format when selecting a variant.
constraints: The choice of variant allows for deliberate setting of more lenient or stringent standards; an uninformed choice can lead to unintended pass rates.
target_learners: Undergraduate and postgraduate learners in medicine and other health professions
target_learning_goals: Setting defensible and context-appropriate passing standards in health professional education

article_title: Impact of station number and duration time per station on the reliability of Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) scores: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Peng Qiyun, Luo Jiani, Wang Chunyan, Chen Lei, Tan Shenglan. (2025). Impact of station number and duration time per station on the reliability of Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) scores: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06691-0
title: Design OSCEs with 5-10 stations, each lasting less than 10 minutes, to achieve good internal consistency
description: The article recommends that OSCE designers set the station number between 5 and 10 with each station lasting under 10 minutes, because this configuration yielded the highest pooled reliability (alpha = 0.88) in the meta-analysis. The authors state this balance helps 'design an optimal OSCE for medical students' while minimizing costs. This principle directly translates the review's headline finding into assessment design practice.
requirements: Station number set between 5 and 10
Duration time per station under 10 minutes
constraints: Applicable to medical student assessment contexts included in the review
Fewer stations may not cover all needed skills and knowledge
target_learners: medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical competence assessment
clinical skills reliability
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 23 studies and found the 5-10 station, under-10-minute configuration achieved alpha = 0.88

article_title: Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors.
citation: Rakesh, D., Lee, P. A., Gaikwad, A., & McLaughlin, K. A. (2025). Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 66(4), 417–439. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.14082
title: Deprivation, rather than threat, is associated with cognitive outcomes like EF and language ability
description: The review discusses the distinction between deprivation and threat as forms of adversity, noting that the finding that cognitive stimulation mediates SES links with cognitive and language outcomes is consistent with the notion that deprivation, which is the absence of enriching cognitive and social inputs, rather than other types of adversities such as threat, is associated with cognitive outcomes like EF and language ability. This distinction is supported using network analyses.
requirements: This framework distinguishes deprivation (absence of enriching inputs) from threat as distinct forms of adversity with different cognitive outcomes.

target_learning_goals: Executive function
Language ability

article_title: The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery - a systematic review.
citation: Wickramasinghe D, Vincent J. (2025). The use of deliberate practice in simulation-based surgical training for laparoscopic surgery – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07613-w
title: Deliberate Practice framework as an instructional design model for simulation-based surgical training
description: The review applies Ericsson's Deliberate Practice (DP) framework as an evaluative and design lens for simulation-based surgical training (SBST) in minimally invasive surgery. DP's "core components include clear goal definition, focused effort during learning, repeated practice until reaching desired proficiency, individual coaching, and immediate feedback". The review uses these components to assess adherence across ten studies, contrasting DP's aim of expert performance for all learners with discriminant, remedial-oriented models.
requirements: Requires clear goal definition, focused effort, repeated practice, individual coaching, and immediate feedback as stated core components
constraints: DP assumes minimal transfer of skills between apparently similar domains
Surgery lacks an explicit definition of expert performance, complicating DP application compared to sports and music
target_learners: surgical trainees
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic psychomotor skills

article_title: The development and implementation of a 12-month simulation-based learning curriculum for pediatric emergency medicine fellows utilizing debriefing with good judgment and rapid cycle deliberate practice.
citation: Jeffers, J. M., & Poling, S. (2019). The development and implementation of a 12-month simulation-based learning curriculum for pediatric emergency medicine fellows utilizing debriefing with good judgment and rapid cycle deliberate practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1417-6
title: Debriefing with good judgment: a reflective-practice debriefing method using performance gaps to explore learner frames
description: Debriefing with good judgment is a well-established debriefing method in which the debriefer uses observations of performance gaps to explore learner frames and thought processes. It "uses a 3-phase (reaction, analysis, and summary) conversational approach based in reflective practice". In this curriculum it was used in one of each session's two scenarios to focus on mental models, teamwork, and thought processing to fill in performance gaps, and was chosen for its established track record and associated assessment tool.
requirements: A debriefer who observes performance gaps and can explore learner frames and thought processes
An associated assessment tool (DASH-SV) for instructor feedback
constraints: The article states there is currently no definitive literature describing which debriefing method is better or best for a given situation or learner objective

target_learning_goals: mental models and thought processing
teamwork and crisis resource management
medical management of pediatric emergencies
examples: One scenario in each two-hour session utilized debriefing with good judgment to focus on mental models, teamwork, and thought processing to fill in performance gaps

article_title: Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math.
citation: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117
title: Deliberate-practice course design with four facets: focused effort, scaffolded exercises, immediate feedback, and repetition
description: The article enumerates the deliberate-practice elements it considers required for courses that reduce or eliminate achievement gaps: "1) extensive and highly focused efforts geared toward improving performance... 2) scaffolded exercises designed to address specific deficits in understanding or skills, 3) immediate feedback, and 4) repetition". It presents these as facets of evidence-based best practice in active learning, and pairs them with a culture of inclusion as the two key design elements.
requirements: Students work hard on relevant tasks; exercises are scaffolded to specific deficits; feedback is immediate; practice is repeated
constraints: The article presents this as a hypothesis component; rigorous testing of the combined design has yet to be done
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: improved performance on course assessments
narrowed achievement gaps
examples: High-intensity active-learning classrooms, where students spend a large reported proportion of class time on in-class activities, are consistent with the deliberate-practice element per the article

article_title: Experiential Learning Interventions and Healthy Eating Outcomes in Children: A Systematic Literature Review.
citation: Varman Sumantla D., Cliff Dylan P., Jones Rachel A., Hammersley Megan L., Zhang Zhiguang, Charlton Karen, Kelly Bridget. (2021). Experiential Learning Interventions and Healthy Eating Outcomes in Children: A Systematic Literature Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182010824
title: Design experiential learning interventions with multiple combined strategies, parent involvement, engaging hands-on activities, theory grounding, and targeted food behaviours
description: The review distils design implications for experiential learning interventions targeting children's healthy eating. It recommends that interventions "include multiple or a combination of experiential learning strategies", involve parents in activities such as cooking and gardening models, make strategies fun and engaging, ground them in behaviour change theory such as social cognitive theory, and target specific food behaviours such as "choose vegetables as snacks". These recommendations derive from patterns across the 25 included RCTs and CRCTs.
requirements: Interventions should include multiple or a combination of experiential learning strategies and be grounded on an effective behaviour change theory
constraints: The review notes the impact of individual experiential learning approaches could not be established because most studies used combinations
Evidence is limited by high risk of bias in most included studies
target_learners: children aged 0–12 years in preschool, primary school, and community settings
target_learning_goals: nutrition-related knowledge, attitudes, and dietary behaviours towards healthy eating
examples: The most effective primary school studies combined games, role-playing, food preparation/cooking, school gardens, and taste-testing; two high-effect studies involved parents directly in intervention activities

Experiential Learning Interventions and Healthy Eating Outcomes in Children: A Systematic Literature Review. article_title: A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on Graphing Numerical Data in K-12 STEM Education
citation: Verena Rufai, Dominik Thüsbj, Sarah Malonecj, Stefan Küchemanndi, Sebastian Becker-Genschowe, Markus Vogelf, Roland Brünkengj, Jochen Kuhnhi. (2024). A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on Graphing Numerical Data in K-12 STEM Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Ainsworth's design, function, and task (DeFT) framework applied to self-generated graphs
description: The review describes Ainsworth's DeFT framework, which proposes that aspects of design, functions, and tasks should influence the creation of learning material with multiple representations. It considers five design parameters: "the number of representations, how the information is distributed across representations, the types of representations, the order of representations, and the amount of support needed to translate between representations." The review applies this framework to argue that self-generated graphs can serve all of Ainsworth's functions and that graphing includes the framework's cognitive tasks, since learners must choose and correctly generate a representation.
requirements: Learners need the ability to describe and use multiple representations appropriately, including choosing a representation based on context, task demands, personal ability, and goals.
constraints: The review restricts its scope to transformations within one register (treatments), such as creating a graph based on a table, and excludes transformations between registers (conversions).
target_learners: K-12 students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: Constructing and selecting appropriate graphical representations of numerical data
Translating between representations such as tables and graphs
