article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: Design LLM scoring systems for robustness to child text by testing sensitivity to misspellings, invented words, and nonstandard morphology, and avoiding extremes of vocabulary size
description: The article states that "Tokenization and vocabulary design are not incidental implementation details; they are part of the reliability mechanism" for scoring child-written responses. Practitioners should "explicitly test sensitivity to misspellings, invented words, and nonstandard morphology, and avoid extremes of vocabulary size". This principle follows from the meta-analytic finding that extremely small vocabularies over-fragment idiosyncratic spellings while extremely large vocabularies include rare or under-trained tokens that behave unpredictably on out-of-distribution orthography, both reducing scoring reliability.
requirements: Explicit sensitivity testing during model selection or training for child-written responses; vocabulary design treated as part of the reliability mechanism
constraints: The article notes vocabulary size and tokenizer family are partially confounded with model families in the ecosystem
target_learners: K-12 students, especially younger children whose writing employs phonetic spelling and imperfect word approximations
target_learning_goals: Accurate and fair automated scoring of child-written short answers
examples: The article's observation that children learning to write often employ phonetic spelling and imperfect word approximations that are out-of-vocabulary for GPT models but easily decipherable for humans
key_sources: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820

article_title: How are "teaching the teachers" courses in evidence based medicine evaluated? A systematic review.
citation: Walczak Jacek, Kaleta Anna, Gabryś Elżbieta, Kloc Krzysztof, Thangaratinam Shakila, Barnfield Gemma, Weinbrenner Susanne, Meyerrose Berit, Arvanitis Theodoros N, Horvath Andrea R, Zanrei Gianni, Kunz Regina, Suter Katja, Burnand Bernard, Arditi Chantal, Oude Rengerink Katrien, Harry Gee, Mol Ben WJ, Khan Khalid S. (2010). How are "teaching the teachers" courses in evidence based medicine evaluated? A systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-10-64
title: Develop educationally sound assessment tools for EBM teaching-the-teachers courses, designed as part of an ongoing evaluation cycle
description: The review concludes that because no well-developed assessment tools exist for EBM teacher courses, the effect of tutors' teaching skills is currently not measurable, and calls for developing educationally sound assessment tools to encourage clinically integrated EBM teaching. It states that "assessment tools need to be designed as a part of an ongoing evaluation cycle" to maintain course relevance and achieve intended objectives. Without such tools, it argues, it would be impossible to ascertain whether TTT courses have the desired effect.
requirements: Assessment tools should be educationally sound and designed as part of an ongoing evaluation cycle
constraints: The review notes existing assessment methods are very few and of poor quality, and identified tools were intended for traditionally conducted courses rather than clinically integrated courses
target_learners: Health care professionals with teaching responsibilities attending EBM teaching-the-teachers courses
target_learning_goals: Effective teaching of evidence-based medicine in clinical settings
examples: The review identified the components of Scherrer et al's twenty-three-question telephone-interview questionnaire as material that might be useful in initiating development of such an assessment tool
key_sources: Walczak Jacek, Kaleta Anna, Gabryś Elżbieta, Kloc Krzysztof, Thangaratinam Shakila, Barnfield Gemma, Weinbrenner Susanne, Meyerrose Berit, Arvanitis Theodoros N, Horvath Andrea R, Zanrei Gianni, Kunz Regina, Suter Katja, Burnand Bernard, Arditi Chantal, Oude Rengerink Katrien, Harry Gee, Mol Ben WJ, Khan Khalid S. (2010). How are "teaching the teachers" courses in evidence based medicine evaluated? A systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-10-64

article_title: Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. NCEE 2017-4026
citation: Kautz, T., Schochet, P., & Tilley, C. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation (NCEE 2017–4026). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.rct-yes.com
title: Design-based theory of impact estimation grounded in the potential outcomes framework
description: A framework in which impact estimators are derived from the known features of the experiment rather than from an assumed data-generating model. The report explains that "Design-based estimators are derived from the known features of experiments and are based on the Neyman-Holland-Rubin causal inference model," using the random assignment process to build the estimation model so that potential outcomes are treated as fixed. Compared with model-based methods, these methods "tend to make fewer assumptions about the nature of the data" and explicitly account for known design information.
requirements: Requires knowledge of the experimental or sampling design, since the random assignment process is used to build the impact estimation model
constraints: The report notes model-based approaches specify an ad hoc model structure whose assumptions cannot be fully verified, while design-based error terms are random only because assignment is random
target_learners: education researchers conducting or supporting impact evaluations
target_learning_goals: understanding how estimation method choice affects impact estimates and their precision in education RCTs
examples: The report applies the framework by re-estimating impacts from nine past education RCTs using RCT-YES, covering non-clustered, clustered, non-blocked, and blocked randomization designs
key_sources: Kautz, T., Schochet, P., & Tilley, C. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation (NCEE 2017–4026). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED575021

article_title: Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill
citation: Iman, J. N. (2017). Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 87-108. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1046a
title: Dewey's 5-phase critical thinking model mapped onto the debate process
description: The article adopts Dewey's 5-phase critical thinking model — suggestions, problem definition, hypothesis generation, reasoning, and hypothesis testing — and maps each phase onto debate activity. In debate, students brainstorm suggestions for the motion, "define the problem of the debate motion word by word", generate evidence-based solutions, critique and reason with examples and data, and finally evaluate and present arguments. The article uses this mapping to explain why debate should cultivate critical thinking.
requirements: Students must actively and persistently participate in their own thinking process through reflections, giving reasons and interpreting conclusions
target_learners: senior high school and university students in debate activities
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills and dispositions
examples: The article pairs the model with Bloom's six levels, describing what students should learn at each level during the debate process, from researching facts to defending and opposing arguments
key_sources: Iman, J. N. (2017). Debate Instruction in EFL Classroom: Impacts on the Critical Thinking and Speaking Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 10(4), 87-108. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2017.1046a

article_title: Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School
citation: Apdoludin, Abdul Rahim Saidek, Raisul Islami. (2016). Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.23. https://www.iiste.org
title: Debate learning model for yellow book study combining independent guidance, classroom activities, and dormitory activity
description: The article proposes a debate model for yellow book learning structured in three linked components: guidance independent, activities in the classroom, and activity in dormitory, culminating in outputs of new knowledge, professional attitude, and readiness to teach or preach. The classroom strand runs from information communication of learning readiness through developing strategies, implementation, monitoring, formative and summative evaluation, and revision. The authors state the model's purpose is "to train the model debate learners in order to seek a strong argument in solving a problem is controversial". It is grounded in behaviorist, cognitivist, and constructivist learning theory.
requirements: A debate theme determined and published before the debate is staged
A moderator who masters the material and is neutral in upholding order and time discipline
Participants divided into opposing supporter and denier parties
Time allocation designed and elaborated before the debate starts
constraints: Developed and tested in the context of Islamic boarding school yellow book learning in Jambi, Indonesia
target_learners: Islamic boarding school students (santri) studying yellow book texts
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and in-depth analysis of learning material
Constructing strong arguments on controversial problems
Discovering implicit and explicit knowledge in yellow book study
examples: The model was implemented in classes XI at Islamic Boarding School Al-Hidayah Jambi, with experimental classes applying the debate model and control classes applying conventional learning
key_sources: Apdoludin, Abdul Rahim Saidek, Raisul Islami. (2016). Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.23. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112798

article_title: Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School
citation: Apdoludin, Abdul Rahim Saidek, Raisul Islami. (2016). Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.23. https://www.iiste.org
title: Four-role structure of a classroom debate: theme, moderator, participants, and listeners
description: The article enumerates the aspects of a debate as a reusable lesson-level design: a theme chosen for interest and published beforehand; a moderator who leads, mediates, and referees while remaining neutral; participants divided into opposing supporter and denier parties; and listeners who observe actively and may vote or give opinions at the end. The article states "Participants were divided into two or more opposing parties, namely the party supporters and deniers", and that organizers must design time allocation before the debate begins.
requirements: The theme should be an interesting, actual problem able to attract attention
The moderator must master the debated material and uphold order, decorum, and time discipline
Listeners are asked at the end to submit opinions or vote on the debate results
target_learners: Boarding school students participating in or observing classroom debates
target_learning_goals: Respect for differences of opinion
Democratic attitude
Active listening and evaluation of arguments
examples: The article specifies that the theme of the debate should be determined and published before the debate itself was staged
key_sources: Apdoludin, Abdul Rahim Saidek, Raisul Islami. (2016). Model Debate for the Yellow Book Learning in Islamic Boarding School. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.23. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112798

article_title: The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes
citation: Mutrofin, Degeng, I.N.S., Ardhana, I.W., & Setyosari, P. (2017). The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143985
title: Descriptive theory of instruction linking instructional methods and learner conditions to learning outcomes
description: The article frames its hypotheses within the descriptive theory of learning and instruction proposed by Reigeluth (1983) and Reigeluth & Merrill (1978, 1979), in which "the effectiveness of learning outcomes as a instruction al variable can be predicted or estimated based on effect of the interaction of instructional methods and conditions". The theory requires scrutiny of a method's scope, generality, precision, power, and consistency; this study focused on power of a method (a continuum from low to high). Teaching methods must be linked with a component of instructional condition, i.e. the characteristics of students, as a foothold for prescribing optimal learning methods to achieve specific learning outcomes.
requirements: Instructional methods must be linked with components of the instructional condition, i.e. the characteristics of students, before choosing teaching methods
constraints: The study focused only on power of a method (a continuum from low to high) among the theory's scrutinized properties
target_learners: teacher trainees in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding of learning theory and instruction content (facts, concepts, principles, procedures)
examples: The study operationalized the theory by crossing instructional method (lecture-discussion vs group discussion) with teaching talent (strong vs weak) in a factorialized 2 x 2 quasi-experiment
key_sources: Mutrofin, Degeng, I.N.S., Ardhana, I.W., & Setyosari, P. (2017). The Effect of Instructional Methods (Lecture-Discussion versus Group Discussion) and Teaching Talent on Teacher Trainees Student Learning Outcomes. Journal of Education and Practice, 8(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1138824

article_title: Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course
citation: Korsun, I. (2017). Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 229-244. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_15.pdf
title: Two types of biographic material study: detailed biographies and fragmentary biographical information
description: The article proposes that study of biographic materials can take two forms: "first, the detailed biographies of individual scientists and, secondly, the fragmentary biographical information". Detailed biographies suit extracurricular activities such as learners' conferences and seminars, while fragmentary information fits limited lesson time. A biography is treated not as a chronological set of dates but as a "biography" of thoughts, words and actions against the scientist's socio-political context.
requirements: Selection of material according to criteria such as organic connectedness with the curriculum and availability for understanding
constraints: Little time at lessons limits what can be presented during regular instruction
target_learners: secondary school physics learners
target_learning_goals: interest in physics
moral and humanistic development
examples: Biographical material was reported at the lessons and during extracurricular activities such as learners' conferences, and learners prepared reports about scientists
key_sources: Korsun, I. (2017). Expediency of Study of the Scientists' Biographies in Physics Course. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 229-244. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_15.pdf

article_title: Depicting and Outlining as Pre-Writing Strategies: Experimental Results and Learners' Opinions
citation: Hung, B. P., & Van, L. T. (2018). Depicting and Outlining as Pre-writing Strategies: Experimental Results and Learners' Opinions. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 451-464. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11231a
title: Depicting pre-writing strategy: sketch-based idea presentation for descriptive writing
description: Depicting is defined by the article as "a pre-writing strategy in which ideas are presented through sketching, depicting or drawing with or without verbal words." Basic lines and basic shapes are the tools students use, and the final depictive presentation serves as a container of ideas whose comprehensiveness to outsiders is not required. In the study, 20 EFL novices were trained to depict before writing descriptive paragraphs across 10 weekly two-and-a-half-hour meetings.
requirements: Students must be capable of using basic lines to present ideas, verified in a pretest
Meticulous care on the appearance of the presentation should not be given, but the participants' ideas instead
constraints: Depicting appeared challenging because it was unfamiliar and some ideas were hard to depict
It could confuse the organization of ideas for some writers
target_learners: EFL novice adult learners aged 18 to 27
target_learning_goals: brainstorming topic-related ideas
preparing for descriptive writing tasks
examples: Participants were reminded of the role of the depictive presentation as the container of ideas and given topic-related samples before writing
key_sources: Hung, B. P., & Van, L. T. (2018). Depicting and Outlining as Pre-writing Strategies: Experimental Results and Learners' Opinions. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 451-464. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11231a

article_title: Bridging Gender Gap in the Physics Classroom: The Instructional Method Perspective
citation: Obafemi, D. T. A. (2015). Bridging Gender Gap in the Physics Classroom: The Instructional Method Perspective. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.20. http://www.iiste.org
title: Use Demonstration method to help close the gender gap in learning difficult physics concepts
description: The article concludes that Demonstration method (teacher-student demonstration) is the instructional method in which female students gained most across all three levels of Light waves, and recommends it for bridging the gender gap. It states that "Demonstration method therefore stands out as an effective method in bridging gender gap in the learning of Light waves." Female students' mean gain percentages in Demonstration method (117.6%, 76.5%, 130.0%) exceeded males' gains at the three levels.
requirements: Teachers must use the appropriate instructional method; the article states female students will not compete favourably "if the appropriate ins tructional method is not used"
constraints: Finding is specific to Light waves and difficult physics concepts in Nigerian SS2 classrooms with 55 students
target_learners: Senior Secondary 2 physics students, male and female
target_learning_goals: Understanding, application and analysis of Light waves in physics
examples: In the quasi-experiment, female students' highest mean gain percentages at understanding (117.6%), application (76.5%) and analysis (130.0%) all occurred in Demonstration method
key_sources: Obafemi, D. T. A. (2015). Bridging Gender Gap in the Physics Classroom: The Instructional Method Perspective. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.20. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079043

article_title: A Mixed-Method Study of the Effect of the Demonstration Method on Students' Achievement in Financial Accounting
citation: Inuwa, U., Abdullah, Z., & Hassan, H. (2018). A Mixed-Method Study of the Effect of the Demonstration Method on Students' Achievement in Financial Accounting. International Journal of Instruction, 11(4), 577-592. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Model for Demonstration Method Effect: a three-sub-theme thematic model of why the demonstration method works
description: The article generates a thematic model (Figure 1) linking the main theme, demonstration method effect, to three sub-themes drawn from student interviews: Enjoy DM, Achievement in FA, and Likeness in DM, each with dimensions. The article states these "refers to the participants' perceptions and views on whether they enjoy learning financial accounting using demonstration method, what makes them to achieve better in financial accounting when taught using demonstration method and what they like in demonstration method". It serves as the qualitative explanation of the quantitative achievement advantage.
requirements: Qualitative data collected through face-to-face interviews and thematically analysed following Clarke and Braun's (2013) thematic analysis procedures
constraints: Generated from interviews with only four students in level two financial accounting classes in Gombe state, Nigeria
target_learners: senior secondary school level two (SSII) financial accounting students
target_learning_goals: financial accounting achievement and understanding of accounting practices and principles
examples: Figure 1 of the article presents the main theme and its three sub-themes with their dimensions as generated from participants' responses
key_sources: Inuwa, U., Abdullah, Z., & Hassan, H. (2018). A Mixed-Method Study of the Effect of the Demonstration Method on Students' Achievement in Financial Accounting. International Journal of Instruction, 11(4), 577-592. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1191665

article_title: Powerful Learning Conversations: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Cinzia Rienzo, Heather Rolfe and David Wilkinson. (2016). Powerful Learning Conversations: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Before a full-scale trial, define the intervention tightly and use paper-based outcome tests
description: The report draws two design lessons from this feasibility pilot. First, an under-specified intervention whose "distinctive features of feedback in sport were insufficiently defined" led to inconsistent implementation, so programmes should be clearly defined and less open to teacher interpretation before efficacy testing. Second, digital testing caused server glitches and school dropouts, so the report recommends that "paper-based tests are used" in any full trial. Both lessons come from the pilot's own process and outcome data.
requirements: A clearly specified programme with defined underpinning concepts and a manual or resource pack for teachers
constraints: The recommendation about paper-based tests arises from technical difficulties specific to the digital Access Maths Test in this pilot, including a software glitch limiting test time to 30 minutes instead of 45
target_learners: Year 9 secondary school pupils
target_learning_goals: reliable measurement of attainment outcomes in evaluation trials
examples: Four schools were unable to complete the digital Maths test after the test provider's server failed, contributing to a 45% attrition rate for Maths and unbalanced groups
key_sources: Cinzia Rienzo, Heather Rolfe and David Wilkinson. (2016). Powerful Learning Conversations: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581274

article_title: Examining Family-School Engagement in a Randomized Controlled Trial of the Family Check-Up
citation: Garbacz, S. A., Stormshak, E. A., McIntyre, L. L., & Kosty, D. (2019). Examining family-school engagement in a randomized controlled trial of the family check-up. School Psychology, 34, 433–443. https://doi.org/10.1037/spq0000284
title: Developmental–ecological model of family-school engagement with four primary dimensions
description: The article grounds family-school engagement in a developmental–ecological model in which children develop within concentric systems: home and school are microsystems, and "the mesosystem consists of connections between microsystems, such as home–school collaboration". Within this frame, family-school engagement is multidirectional and transactional and "includes four primary dimensions: family-school engagement at home, family-school engagement at school, family-school collaboration, and family-school communication". The study measures the home and school dimensions and treats collaboration and communication as related but distinct.
requirements: Measures must distinguish the home and school dimensions of engagement, as the study did with the FIQ-E home-based involvement items and the PTIQ school items
constraints: The article notes many prior studies of family-school engagement were cross-sectional and correlational, so directionality of relations was often unclear
target_learners: kindergarten children and their primary caregivers in early elementary school
target_learning_goals: family support for children's academic skills and social–emotional competencies during the kindergarten transition
examples: The study operationalized the home dimension with seven FIQ-E home-based involvement items (α = .814) and the school dimension with six PTIQ items (α = .624)
key_sources: Garbacz, S. A., Stormshak, E. A., McIntyre, L. L., & Kosty, D. (2019). Examining family-school engagement in a randomized controlled trial of the family check-up. School Psychology, 34, 433–443. https://doi.org/10.1037/spq0000284

article_title: Site Selection in Experiments: A Follow-Up Evaluation of Site Recruitment in Two Scale-Up Studies
citation: Tipton, E., Fellers, L., Caverly, S., Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Sullivan, K., & Ruiz de Castillo, V. (2015). Site selection in experiments: A follow-up evaluation of site recruitment in two scale-up studies. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Discuss generalization during study design rather than delaying it until after the evaluation
description: The article argues that generalization should be built into experiment design and recruitment rather than handled by post-hoc statistical adjustment alone. It reports that delaying generalization discussions "until after the evaluation is complete" brings "increased standard errors and, often, limits to bias reduction", motivating the third research stream that improves generalization through design and recruitment strategies.
requirements: Early definition of an inference population and eligibility criteria
Recruitment strategies targeted at strata of the inference population
constraints: Even design-based plans faced real-time recruitment problems, including districts willing to join only one of the two experiments
target_learners: Schools and districts in scale-up evaluations of instructional programs
target_learning_goals: Causal effect estimates that generalize to a well-defined inference population
examples: The OCR and EM studies defined inference populations of current curriculum users from developer data and stratified eligible non-user districts for recruitment
key_sources: Tipton, E., Fellers, L., Caverly, S., Vaden-Kiernan, M., Borman, G., Sullivan, K., & Ruiz de Castillo, V. (2015). Site selection in experiments: A follow-up evaluation of site recruitment in two scale-up studies. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs

article_title: Influence of Conflict Resolution Training on Conflict Handling Styles of College Students
citation: Abel Gitimu Waithaka, Shante' Moore-Austin, Priscilla N. Gitimu. (2015). Influence of conflict resolution training on conflict handling styles of college students. Research in Higher Education Journal, 28. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Design conflict training sessions around the audience's age, life experiences, the nature of the conflict, and the training duration
description: The article's closing recommendation is that conflict training be tailored to who is being trained and how long the training runs. It states: "any conflict training session would be designed with consideration of the audience being trained on basis of their age, life experiences, nature of the conflict and the duration of the training." This follows from the study's null results, which the authors link to a one-time, short session delivered to adults with diverse life experiences.
requirements: Training should be planned for various levels of competence in conflict management, as the article states this is needed for effectiveness
constraints: The study's own one-time, short-duration training produced no significant change, so the principle is grounded in a null result
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: conflict resolution skills
conflict orientation
examples: The study delivered a one-time conflict handling video training to the experimental group only, with a one-week interval between pre- and post-testing
key_sources: Abel Gitimu Waithaka, Shante' Moore-Austin, Priscilla N. Gitimu. (2015). Influence of conflict resolution training on conflict handling styles of college students. Research in Higher Education Journal, 28. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html

article_title: The Effects of Portfolio Assessment on Writing of EFL Students
citation: Behzad Nezakatgoo. (2011). The Effects of Portfolio Assessment on Writing of EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p231
title: Defer grading and allow revision so students can internalize instruction before final evaluation
description: The article recommends postponing grades in writing courses: "the instructor postpones assigning grades until students have had time to internalize instruction", empowering students to rewrite and polish papers before selecting their best work for grading. The study's experimental condition operationalized this by recording no grade at submission, crediting revisions, and allowing continued work on papers until term's end.
requirements: Feedback delivered while students are still working on a paper rather than after grading
constraints: The recommendation rests on one quasi-experimental study with 40 students at a single college
target_learners: EFL freshman composition students
target_learning_goals: Improved writing performance under examination conditions
examples: Experimental-group students received written feedback by email within two days and could continue revising previously written papers until the end of the term
key_sources: Behzad Nezakatgoo. (2011). The Effects of Portfolio Assessment on Writing of EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p231

article_title: Effectiveness of E-Learning for the Teaching of English: A Study of Comparative Strategies
citation: Intakhab Alam Khan. (2016). Effectiveness of E-learning for the Teaching of English: A Study of Comparative Strategies. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.3p.125
title: Deweyan experiential philosophy as the pedagogic basis for e-learning with the teacher as facilitator
description: The article grounds e-learning in John Dewey's philosophy, arguing that e-learning "includes most of the pre-requisites of Dewey's philosophy" because Dewey stressed practicum, real experience and interaction. On this basis the teacher's role in an e-learning environment is "specified to a position of a 'facilitator'": the teacher participates in activities and facilitates learners rather than traditionally teaching them. The article uses this framework to argue for web-based curriculum design and hybrid online courses with field-based experiences.
requirements: Teachers need pre-service teacher training or professional development in the specified teaching area to carry out the facilitator role
constraints: Realization of the e-learning philosophy requires availability of resources, infrastructural facilities and human resource, as stated by the article
target_learners: Saudi EFL preparatory-year students at community colleges
target_learning_goals: English language skills (listening, reading, grammar, vocabulary) preparing for English for Specific Purposes
examples: The article proposes that Dewey would have encouragement for hybrid online courses allowing field-based experiences, activities and internships in teaching
key_sources: Intakhab Alam Khan. (2016). Effectiveness of E-learning for the Teaching of English: A Study of Comparative Strategies. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.3p.125

article_title: The Effect of Online Learning Environment Based on Caricature Animation Used in Science and Technology Course on the Success and Attitude of the Student for Humor
citation: Uğur Başarmak, Ahmet Mahiroğlu. (2016). The Effect of Online Learning Environment Based on Caricature Animation Used in Science and Technology Course on the Success and Attitude of the Student for Humor. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Design caricature animations according to students' individual differences and development level to support success
description: The article's forward-looking design recommendation is that caricature animations used as humorous elements in online learning should be matched to learners. The authors state that "the usage of caricature animations which are des igned according to the individual differences and development level of the students, shall increase the success of the students." This follows their finding that caricature animations raised success scores but not attitudes toward humor, and their view that visual materials help learning through entertainment.
requirements: Knowledge of students' individual differences and developmental level
Online learning environment capable of presenting caricature animations as education material
constraints: The attitude-toward-humor outcome showed no significant difference, so attitude gains should not be assumed
target_learners: 7th-grade secondary school students in online learning environments
target_learning_goals: Academic success in Science and Technology units
examples: The study's experiment-group environment embedded caricature animations as the final humorous activity under each subject title
key_sources: Uğur Başarmak, Ahmet Mahiroğlu. (2016). The Effect of Online Learning Environment Based on Caricature Animation Used in Science and Technology Course on the Success and Attitude of the Student for Humor. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1117641

article_title: Demonstration Technique to Improve Vocabulary and Grammar Element in Teaching Speaking at EFL Learners
citation: Muhammad Husnu. (2018). Demonstration Technique to Improve Vocabulary and Grammar Element in Teaching Speaking at EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(2). http://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p26
title: Demonstration technique for teaching speaking
description: Demonstration technique is a teaching technique in which the teacher shows the real object, shows pictures, and uses actions, facial expressions, and body language activities to teach vocabulary and grammar for speaking. The article describes it as giving "simple materials and practice," with learners guessing words and demonstrating them directly in front of the class, which trains learners to be brave to stand in front of their friends and reduces hesitation. The article states it provided a way to decrease anxiety and changed the classroom into a positive, active, and fun learning experience.
requirements: A teacher able to act out the materials and motivate students, with an attractive and pleasant classroom atmosphere
constraints: The article evaluates it specifically for the vocabulary and grammar elements of speaking at EFL learners
target_learners: EFL learners at the beginner level
target_learning_goals: vocabulary use in real practice
grammar in speaking
reduced anxiety and hesitation in speaking
examples: In the treatment, learners guessed words and demonstrated them directly in front of the class in every meeting.
key_sources: Muhammad Husnu. (2018). Demonstration Technique to Improve Vocabulary and Grammar Element in Teaching Speaking at EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(2). http://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p26

article_title: The Effects of the First Part of the CoRT Program for Teaching Thinking (BREADTH) on the Development of Communication Skills among a Sample of Students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan
citation: Wael Mohammad Alshurman. (2017). The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069
title: De Bono's account that thinking is a teachable skill developed through practice
description: The article's framing theory, drawn from De Bono, holds that thinking can be taught because it can be treated as a simple process, and that lateral thinking (hyperlink thinking) looks at problems from different angles instead of only one method, in contrast to straight thinking that moves through successive logical steps. Thinking means dealing with a conscious awareness of thinking patterns, whose tools should be used deliberately. The article states that "De Bono (1989) believes that practice or training leads to mastery or perfection in the development of thinking skills", comparing learning thinking skills to learning to ride a bike or swim, where initial confusion gives way to skill.
requirements: Training according to training programs in the field, since learning thinking skills is conducted through work and practice
constraints: At the beginning of learning, the learner feels confused since he thinks learning them is difficult, unnecessary and unnatural
target_learners: university students and learners generally
target_learning_goals: thinking skills and, indirectly, communication skills
examples: The study operationalized this account by training students on ten CoRT thinking tools and measuring an indirect outcome, communication skills.
key_sources: Wael Mohammad Alshurman. (2017). The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069

article_title: How to Implement an E-Learning Curriculum to Streamline Teaching Digital Image Processing
citation: Sándor Király. (2016). How to Implement an E-learning Curriculum to Streamline Teaching Digital Image Processing. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 9, Number 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2065-1430
title: Self-developed demonstration software and Excel tools for Fourier transforms, convolution and mathematical morphology
description: The curriculum includes purpose-built interactive tools: an Excel spreadsheet for defining and representing signals and their spectra; a flash program finding cosine functions similar to a given signal; a MATLAB program for frequency-domain filtering of JPEG files showing that increasing frequencies causes stronger edges and noises while decreasing them blurs edges; two convolution demonstrators (step-by-step convolution with different PSFs, and rank filters versus the smoothing filter) implemented for Windows and Android; a morphology program performing selected operations with a set structuring element and showing which pixels change; and Excel sheets demonstrating energy saving of DCT and WT.
requirements: Software implemented for both Windows and Android operating systems so students can run the demonstrations
target_learners: university students learning integral transforms, convolution and mathematical morphology
target_learning_goals: relational understanding of integral transforms, convolution and mathematical morphology, including 1D-before-2D sequencing of the Fourier transform
examples: Students used GIMP to apply learnt filters such as Sobel or Laplace on real pictures, and the Wavelet Toolbox of MATLAB to perform wavelet transforms on images.
key_sources: Sándor Király. (2016). How to Implement an E-learning Curriculum to Streamline Teaching Digital Image Processing. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 9, Number 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2065-1430

article_title: Effect of Demonstration Method of Teaching on Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science
citation: Daluba, Noah Ekeyi. (2013). Effect of Demonstration Method of Teaching on Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science. World Journal of Education, 3(6). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v3n6p1
title: Demonstration method of teaching
description: The demonstration method is a teaching approach in which the teacher is the principal actor while learners watch with the intention to act later. The teacher shows learners how to do something and explains the step-by-step process, serving as an attention inducer and powerful motivator that provides immediate feedback through students' own products and gives real-life situations of the course of study.
requirements: A skilled teacher who can carry out the demonstration effectively.
constraints: The article describes the method as requiring the teacher to be the principal actor, with learners watching before acting.
target_learners: Secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of practical skills and conceptual knowledge in agricultural science
examples: In the study, demonstration teaching was delivered over two months to 240 students across six schools.
key_sources: Daluba, Noah Ekeyi. (2013). Effect of Demonstration Method of Teaching on Students' Achievement in Agricultural Science. World Journal of Education, 3(6). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v3n6p1

article_title: Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools
citation: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581
title: Develop all components of cognitive independence as a whole rather than in isolation
description: The article argues that "Mastering new content of the subject area 'Informatics' is possible only when all components of cognitive independence develop as a whole." It therefore identifies informative, operational, motivational, emotional-volitional, and reflexive components and diagnoses each with dedicated indicators. The correlational finding that components were significantly interrelated in the experimental group supports treating them as interdependent.
requirements: Diagnostic materials covering every component, and teaching methods that purposefully address each component
constraints: Formulated in the context of Informatics teacher education
target_learners: Future Informatics teachers
target_learning_goals: Cognitive independence for continuous self-learning in a rapidly changing subject area
examples: The authors developed a set of indicators, control and ascertaining materials (tasks, tests) for all five components
key_sources: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581

article_title: The Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management Program: Outcomes from a Group Randomized Trial
citation: Wendy M. Reinke & Keith C. Herman & Nianbo Dong. (2018). The Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management Program: Outcomes from a Group Randomized Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-018-0932-3
title: Developmental epidemiological conceptual framework of baseline risk moderating universal prevention effects
description: The article applies a developmental epidemiological conceptual framework in which the presence of social, emotional, or behavioral problems interferes with a child's ability to adjust to classroom social demands and makes these problems more likely to escalate over the year without intervention. Within this lens, variation in universal prevention responsiveness is expected to be predicted by baseline behavioral or social emotional risk, so students with greater initial risk should benefit more. The trial's moderation findings are interpreted in these terms.
requirements: Moderation analyses testing treatment-by-baseline-risk interactions in universal prevention trials
constraints: The article notes effects of universal prevention programs may not be consistent across the full population of students exposed
target_learners: Kindergarten to third grade students in universal, whole-classroom interventions
target_learning_goals: Social emotional competence, behavior, and academic functioning
examples: The authors cite Good Behavior Game studies showing intervention effects were strongest among youth with high baseline antisocial behavior
key_sources: Wendy M. Reinke & Keith C. Herman & Nianbo Dong. (2018). The Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management Program: Outcomes from a Group Randomized Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-018-0932-3

article_title: Classmate Peer-Coaching: "A Study Buddy Support Scheme"
citation: Thalluri, Jyothi; O'Flaherty, Jackie A.; and Shepherd, Paul L. (2014). Classmate peer-coaching: "A Study Buddy Support scheme". Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 92-104. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/8
title: Design peer-tutor support systems specifically for the peer-tutor configuration rather than grafting them onto a standard classroom
description: Drawing on Colvin (2007), the article holds that peer tutoring succeeds only when the surrounding system is purpose-built: "the system must be designed specifically with peer tutors in mind", including training and support concerning the socialisation of students, teachers, and instructors. The article applies this in preparing the virtual classroom, where thought was needed to adjust resources and identify how best to engage participants.
requirements: Training and support systems for tutors, students, and instructors must be built into the design
constraints: The article warns peer tutors cannot be grafted onto a standard classroom configuration with automatic success
target_learners: university students participating in peer-tutoring schemes
target_learning_goals: effective peer-supported learning of course content
examples: Preparing the virtual classroom required converting Word documents to PDFs, supplying multiple-choice questions for polls, and creating multiple content layouts for different teaching sections.
key_sources: Thalluri, Jyothi; O'Flaherty, Jackie A.; and Shepherd, Paul L. (2014). Classmate peer-coaching: "A Study Buddy Support scheme". Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 92-104. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/8

article_title: Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill
citation: Rachmawati, E., Prodjosantoso, A. K., & Wilujeng, I. (2019). Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 299-310. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12120a
title: Developing and using models as a science practice in which models represent systems in four forms and are refined against evidence
description: The article defines models as "a representation of reality that describes the structure and order of a concept" displaying four forms: verbal or conceptual description, action or procedure steps, physical or virtual replica, and equations or formula. Developing and using models is one of the NGSS practices, letting students make abstract systems concrete via replicas, diagrams, mathematical formulas, analogies, and computer simulations. Students are expected to evaluate and refine a model through an iterative cycle, modifying it when new evidence cannot be explained. The study assesses this skill through using and developing aspects with printed indicators.
requirements: Skill assessment uses criteria derived from indicators for the Using aspect (describe, understand steps, obtain data, recognise weaknesses) and the Developing aspect (create replica, create questions, change variables, conclude relationships)
constraints: At the middle-school level the article lists emphases such as evaluating model limitations and developing or modifying a model based on evidence to compare what happens if a system variable changes
target_learners: Middle-school science students, here grade 8
target_learning_goals: Explaining natural phenomena with models
Modifying models based on evidence
Predicting and describing phenomena
examples: Students built a human respiratory system replica and used Charta and torso models as the developing and using components of the skill
key_sources: Rachmawati, E., Prodjosantoso, A. K., & Wilujeng, I. (2019). Next Generation Science Standard in Science Learning to Improve Student's Practice Skill. International Journal of Instruction, 12(1), 299-310. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.12120a

article_title: Different Modes of Digital Learning Object Use in School Settings: Do We Design for Individual or Collaborative Learning?
citation: Akpinar, Y. (2014). Different modes of digital learning object use in school settings: Do we design for individual or collaborative learning? International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology, 10(3), 87-95. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu/viewarticle.php?id=1747
title: Design learning objects for use in multiple study modes, individual and collaborative
description: The article concludes that learning objects developed for individual use may still help students working with peers, and that supporting both modes is essential: "designing and developing learning objects for the use of multiple modes is crucial". Since teachers already use individually designed LOs collaboratively, LOs should be built to function in either setting rather than a single intended mode.
requirements: LOs must remain usable when students share one computer and must agree on all system actions, as instructed in the collaborative condition
constraints: The comparison among study modes did not strongly favor either mode, so the principle rests on feasibility evidence rather than a demonstrated advantage of either mode
target_learners: seventh and ninth grade students in state schools
target_learning_goals: science units (pressure/buoyant force, work and energy, electricity) and geography map scales
examples: Four simulation-based LOs from a repository were studied by 127 students randomly allocated to individual or paired modes in school computer labs
key_sources: Akpinar, Y. (2014). Different modes of digital learning object use in school settings: Do we design for individual or collaborative learning? International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology, 10(3), 87-95. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu/viewarticle.php?id=1747

article_title: With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving
citation: Frederick, M. L., Courtney, S., & Caniglia, J. (2014). With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Decreasing-support grouping sequence across a task week
description: The study's tasks were administered with the level of student support decreasing each day, moving through group configurations of total class participation (TL), small group (SG), partners (P), and individual (I) work. This graduated release of support pairs a graphic organizer with progressively more independent grouping formats across a week of non-routine tasks. Groups of four were composed of one high, two average, and one low student based on prior-year state assessment scores.
requirements: Groups formed with heterogeneous ability composition based on prior assessment scores
constraints: Studied in sixth-grade geometry over nine weeks with the same teacher for both classes
target_learners: sixth-grade middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: initiating and completing non-routine problem solutions
geometry concepts
examples: Table 1 illustrates a set of geometry tasks administered during one week with the level of student support decreasing each day
key_sources: Frederick, M. L., Courtney, S., & Caniglia, J. (2014). With a Little Help from My Friends: Scaffolding Techniques in Problem Solving. Investigations in Mathematics Learning, 7(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1052936

article_title: A Qualitative Perspective: Pre-Service Teachers Discuss Educational Technology Online
citation: Spatariu, A., & Winsor, D. L. (2010). A Qualitative Perspective: Pre-Service Teachers Discuss Educational Technology Online. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov
title: Online discussions require both detailed instruction and constant, consistent instructor feedback with probing questions
description: The article concludes that quality online argumentation depends on pairing explicit discussion guidelines with regular, supportive, probing instructor interaction. Treatment groups received brief but regular instructor feedback that highlighted critical points and posed probing questions, while control groups received only minimal, vague, generic feedback. The authors state that "instruction during the use of educational technology platforms may require both detailed instruction; and constant and consistent feedback from the instructor."
requirements: Instructor feedback must be supportive, directed toward individual responses, and include probing questions that require groups to reflect on their knowledge and beliefs
constraints: The control group received feedback only once per group, generally vague and generic, void of positive comments, specific examples, and probing questions
target_learners: pre-service teachers in undergraduate educational technology courses
target_learning_goals: argumentation quality in asynchronous online discussion
critical thinking about controversial educational issues
examples: Treatment groups received structured week-1 instructions to post an initial position, a challenge to a group member, and a response to the challenge, with instructor posts modeling how to generate reasons and evidence for both sides
key_sources: Spatariu, A., & Winsor, D. L. (2010). A Qualitative Perspective: Pre-Service Teachers Discuss Educational Technology Online. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102777

article_title: Relieving of Misconceptions of Derivative Concept with Derive
citation: Kaplan, A., Ozturk, M., & Ocal, M. F. (2015). Relieving of misconceptions of derivative concept with derive. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(1), 64-74. http://www.ijres.net
title: Derive computer algebra system as an instruction tool for the derivative concept
description: Derive is a computer algebra system — software that performs numeric and symbolic operations and draws graphics — used in this study as the instruction tool for the experiment group. The authors selected it because it is easy to use and has features such as drawing graphs, solving equations, and taking derivatives and integrals. Students worked individually with it to re-solve examples and check their answers.
requirements: Students need individual access to the software during instruction
constraints: The article notes that necessary software and experienced staff do not exist in some schools
target_learners: 12th-grade secondary school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Resolving misconceptions in the derivative concept
examples: The subject was first presented without computers, then each student solved the same examples again with Derive and controlled their correctness on their own computer.
key_sources: Kaplan, A., Ozturk, M., & Ocal, M. F. (2015). Relieving of misconceptions of derivative concept with derive. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(1), 64-74. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105126

article_title: Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course
citation: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145
title: Desirable difficulty framework: spacing and interleaving make learning harder but more effective
description: The article designs its vocabulary enhancement activity using the desirable difficulty framework (Bjork, 1994), which holds that "desirable difficulties are desirable because they trigger encoding and retrieval processes that support learning, comprehension, and remembering". Spacing and interleaving were used to make learning more difficult and desirable, prompting students to generate answers. The article notes this reflects the characteristic of "slowing the rate of improvement during the learning process but may lead to long-term benefits".
requirements: The instructor must decide which technical words to target, offer timely help when a term is not used as in the native language, and guide attention to material beyond vocabulary
constraints: Difficulty must be calibrated: material should challenge students enough to avoid frustration from too difficult or boredom from too easy material
target_learners: accounting majors learning ESP technical vocabulary
target_learning_goals: retention of technical terms
deeper processing of accounting concepts
examples: Journal entry practice introduced new entries with planned review frequency based on the desirable difficulty framework
key_sources: Liju Xu. (2018). Learning and Retaining Technical Vocabulary with Enhancement Activities in an ESP Course. English Language Teaching, 11(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n10p145

article_title: Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446
title: Delay procedural fraction instruction until after the conceptual basis is established
description: The intervention included procedural instruction but delayed its introduction until after the conceptual basis for interpreting fractions was established, at lesson 22 of 36. This sequencing reflects evidence that conceptual knowledge has more generalized effects on new learning than procedural knowledge and tends to have a larger effect on procedural development than the reverse. As fraction calculations were addressed, concepts continued to be extended and integrated with procedures.
requirements: Conceptual instruction on fraction interpretation must be established before computation procedures are introduced
target_learners: at-risk fourth graders
target_learning_goals: fraction calculation procedures built on conceptual understanding
examples: Fraction computation was introduced in Lesson 22, after weeks of conceptual work on magnitude, comparison, and ordering.
key_sources: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446

article_title: Effect of Ability Grouping in Reciprocal Teaching Technique of Collaborative Learning on Individual Achievements and Social Skills
citation: Sumadi, I. N. S. Degeng, Sulthon, & Waras. (2017). Effect of Ability Grouping in Reciprocal Teaching Technique of Collaborative Learning on Individual Achievements and Social Skills. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education, 6(3), 216-220.
title: Form collaborative-learning groups deliberately, considering ability composition, because grouping type significantly shapes both achievement and social-skill outcomes
description: The article argues that forming and managing collaborative learning groups requires deliberate attention to member composition, since "The formation of groups based on personality attributes and capability of learners is the purpose of managing collaborative learning environment". Its quasi-experimental findings show that grouping composition significantly affects both individual achievement and social skills, with high homogeneous groups gaining most and low homogeneous groups least. The principle directs instructional designers to choose grouping compositions intentionally rather than by default.
requirements: Groups of approximately three members formed on stated ability or attribute bases, as the article describes small groups "consisting of three members for each group based on ability"
constraints: Findings come from a quasi-experimental setting with Indonesian pre-service primary teacher students; the low homogeneous group showed the smallest gains on both outcomes, which the article notes as a potential downside of homogeneous low-ability grouping
target_learners: Primary School Teacher Education Department students (pre-service teachers)
target_learning_goals: Individual achievement
Social skills development
examples: The study assigned students to high, middle, and low homogeneous groups and a heterogeneous group within reciprocal teaching of collaborative learning and measured pre-test to post-test gains.
key_sources: Sumadi, I. N. S. Degeng, Sulthon, & Waras. (2017). Effect of Ability Grouping in Reciprocal Teaching Technique of Collaborative Learning on Individual Achievements and Social Skills. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education, 6(3), 216-220. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1157151

article_title: Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers
citation: Geerts, W. M., Steenbeek, H. W., & van Geert, P. L. C. (2018). Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers. International Education Studies, 11(1), 64. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p64
title: Design patterns and pattern languages as structural units of situated teacher knowledge.
description: The article introduces design patterns as series of efficient interactions used as solutions to recurring problems, consisting of structures of heuristics. Pattern languages are clusters of design patterns used for a specific domain, such as the overarching pattern language 'Teaching' which includes subordinate design patterns like 'pedagogical action', 'dealing with personal characteristics', 'reflecting', 'giving instructions', 'guiding the learning process', and 'dealing with disorder'. Design patterns are instances of situated knowledge, not context-free potential actions.
requirements: Iterative cycle of analyzing the current situation, figuring out a solution, and evaluating results
constraints: Acquiring design patterns as declarative knowledge is relatively simple but of little use for improving concrete actions
target_learners: Pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of design patterns and pattern languages as situated knowledge
key_sources: Geerts, W. M., Steenbeek, H. W., & van Geert, P. L. C. (2018). Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers. International Education Studies, 11(1), 64. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p64

article_title: Effective Professional Development of Teachers: A Guide to Actualizing Inclusive Schooling
citation: Nishimura, T. (2014). Effective Professional Development of Teachers: A Guide to Actualizing Inclusive Schooling. International Journal of Whole Schooling, 10(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1055365
title: Desimone's conceptual framework for coaching-based professional development.
description: The article presents Desimone's (2009) conceptual framework for effective professional development related to coaching, delineated in Figure 1. The framework identifies critical components including "content focused" professional development with "Active Learning," "Coherence," "Duration," and "Collective Participation," which lead through increased teacher knowledge and changes in attitudes and beliefs to changes in instruction and improved student learning. The first critical component centers on content and active learning for teachers, characterized by "interactive feedback, collaborative discussions, and problem solving sessions."
requirements: Professional development must include collective participation with teachers from the same school and grade level.
Active learning must be characterized by interactive feedback, collaborative discussions, and problem solving sessions.
target_learners: In-service teachers participating in coaching-based professional development
target_learning_goals: Improving instructional practice and student learning through sustained professional development
examples: The article's IPD study applied this framework by providing weekly meetings and individualized coaching over eight weeks.
key_sources: Nishimura, T. (2014). Effective Professional Development of Teachers: A Guide to Actualizing Inclusive Schooling. International Journal of Whole Schooling, 10(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1016781

article_title: The Flipped Classroom Model to Develop Egyptian EFL Students' Listening Comprehension
citation: Ahmad, S. Z. (2016). The Flipped Classroom Model to Develop Egyptian EFL Students’ Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p166
title: Devote class time to active learning rather than lecturing in flipped EFL classrooms
description: The researcher recommends devoting class time to active learning rather than lecturing, based on the study's finding that the flipped classroom improved listening comprehension. In this study, class time was used for "student-centered active learning activities where they created, collaborated, and put into practice what they learned from the lectures they viewed outside class."
requirements: Instructors must prepare video content for students to view before class so class time is freed for active learning.
constraints: Evidence comes from a one-group pre-posttest design without a control group.
target_learners: third-year EFL university majors
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension
examples: The study used activities including 3-2-1, write-pair-share, debates, concept mapping, jigsaw, learning by teaching, fishbowl, and three-step interview during class sessions.
key_sources: Ahmad, S. Z. (2016). The Flipped Classroom Model to Develop Egyptian EFL Students’ Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p166

article_title: Enhancing Foreign Language Learning through Listening Strategies Delivered in L1: An Experimental Study
citation: Bozorgian, H., & Pillay, H. (2013). Enhancing Foreign Language Learning through Listening Strategies Delivered in L1: An Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Deliver listening strategy instruction in learners' L1 for lower-intermediate EFL students
description: The article recommends teaching listening strategies in the students' first language when learners lack target-language proficiency. The rationale is that "the lower intermediate students were not linguistically competent enough in the target language (English) to understand when and how to use the listening strategies." This aligns with Macaro's perspective that strategies cannot be taught at beginning or lower intermediate levels unless teachers shift to students' first language.
requirements: Teachers must be able to deliver instruction in the students' L1; strategies and materials must be translated and adapted for the learners' language context
constraints: Applies to beginning and lower intermediate proficiency levels; the article notes some teachers believe L1 should not be used as it may hinder learning
target_learners: Lower-intermediate EFL learners (e.g., Iranian language institute students aged 16-28)
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
examples: Five listening strategies (guessing, making inferences, identifying topics, repetition, note-taking) were translated into Persian and taught over 14 sessions
key_sources: Bozorgian, H., & Pillay, H. (2013). Enhancing Foreign Language Learning through Listening Strategies Delivered in L1: An Experimental Study. International Journal of Instruction, 6(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085363

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Social-Emotional Learning on Receipt of Special Education and Grade Retention: Evidence from a Randomized Trial of "INSIGHTS"
citation: McCormick, M. P., Neuhaus, R., Horn, E. P., O'Connor, E. E., White, H. S., Harding, S., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. (2019). Long-Term Effects of Social–Emotional Learning on Receipt of Special Education and Grade Retention: Evidence From a Randomized Trial of INSIGHTS. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419867290
title: Developmental cascades account for long-term SEL effects on educational service outcomes
description: The article frames long-term SEL impacts using developmental cascades theory: interventions at sensitive transitions like kindergarten entry can "lead to positive cascading effects by targeting competence in domains that are linked to functioning across other domains over time". SEL programs target social–emotional competencies such as self-regulation, which are linked to behavior and academic skills, potentially lowering referral likelihood. The article also invokes Bailey et al.'s (2017) contention that early programming provides "access to qualitatively different experiences for students".
requirements: SEL intervention implemented at a sensitive transition such as the move to kindergarten
target_learners: children in kindergarten and first grade
target_learning_goals: social–emotional competencies including self-regulation and behavior management
key_sources: McCormick, M. P., Neuhaus, R., Horn, E. P., O'Connor, E. E., White, H. S., Harding, S., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. (2019). Long-Term Effects of Social–Emotional Learning on Receipt of Special Education and Grade Retention: Evidence From a Randomized Trial of INSIGHTS. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419867290

article_title: Effectiveness of an AI-augmented teacher feedback model in improving medical students' clinical documentation skills: a retrospective cohort study.
citation: Hu Shuai, Du Fei, Fang Can, Zheng Xiyan, Shi Xianjie, Zhou Zheng. (2026). Effectiveness of an AI-augmented teacher feedback model in improving medical students' clinical documentation skills: a retrospective cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09953-7
title: AI-generated structured feedback reports based on DeepSeek V3
description: The AI feedback system was powered by DeepSeek-V3 and generated structured scoring and itemized feedback reports based on the Admission Record Writing Quality Evaluation Standard (2024 Edition). Reports included "scores and improvement suggestions across eight dimensions: basic writing requirements, general items, chief complaint, history of present illness, past medical history, physical examination, auxiliary examinations, and preliminary diagnosis." The system analyzed medical records through natural language processing and rule-matching algorithms.
requirements: Students enter their completed medical record text into the system with a structured scoring instruction
constraints: A stable model version was maintained for all scoring procedures
target_learners: medical interns
target_learning_goals: clinical documentation skills
medical record writing
key_sources: Hu Shuai, Du Fei, Fang Can, Zheng Xiyan, Shi Xianjie, Zhou Zheng. (2026). Effectiveness of an AI-augmented teacher feedback model in improving medical students' clinical documentation skills: a retrospective cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09953-7

article_title: National Consensus Catalog of Psychomotor Competencies for Brazilian Medical Graduates: a modified Delphi study - Part I.
citation: Nogueira Rodrigo de Melo, Dolci José Eduardo Lutaif, Fernandes Cesar Eduardo, Gonçalves Antonio José, Parreira José Gustavo, Colleoni Ramiro Neto, Menezes-Rodrigues Francisco Sandro, Tallo Fernando Sabia. (2026). National Consensus Catalog of Psychomotor Competencies for Brazilian Medical Graduates: a modified Delphi study – Part I. Revista da Associação Médica Brasileira. https://doi.org/10.1590/1806-9282.20261096
title: Define both competencies and expected performance levels to support competency-based curriculum development and assessment
description: The article argues that clearly defined psychomotor competencies paired with explicit expected competence levels constitute the foundation for competency-based medical education. By defining both the competency and the expected level of performance for each procedure, the catalog "provides a practical framework to support competency-based curriculum development, procedural skills training, and competency assessment in Brazilian medical schools". Explicit performance expectations may contribute to greater consistency in procedural skills training across medical schools.

description: The DeliA e-learning program is a German-language asynchronous online program on delirium for nurses in nursing homes, consisting of five modules covering "(1) Definition, complications and consequences; (2) Risk factors and causes; (3) Symptoms and diagnostics; (4) Prevention, therapy and management, and (5) Delirium in the dying phase." article_title: Deliberate practice: The cornerstone of microsurgical therapy.
citation: Velásquez‐Plata D, Burkhardt R. (2026). Deliberate practice: The cornerstone of microsurgical therapy. Clinical Advances in Periodontics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cap.70055
title: Deliberate practice: a structured, goal-oriented approach to maximize skill development
description: The article presents deliberate practice, building on Ericsson's 1993 definition, as "a series of activities structured to improve the levels of current performance." Activities target identified weaknesses, performance is monitored for feedback, and practice can only be sustained briefly because it is neither easy nor enjoyable. The article positions this framework as the foundation for microsurgical skill acquisition, replacing the older view that expertise is innate.
requirements: Structured activities must target identified weaknesses with monitored performance outcomes and feedback geared towards further improvement
constraints: Deliberate practice can only be sustained for a limited time since it requires extraordinary effort
target_learners: novice, intermediate, and expert microsurgeons in periodontics and implant dentistry
target_learning_goals: acquisition and refinement of microsurgical technical skills such as bimanual instrumentation and suturing
examples: Ericsson and Chase's memory study demonstrating cognitive gains through structured practice techniques coupled with immediate feedback

article_title: Deliberate practice: The cornerstone of microsurgical therapy.
citation: Velásquez‐Plata D, Burkhardt R. (2026). Deliberate practice: The cornerstone of microsurgical therapy. Clinical Advances in Periodontics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cap.70055
title: Four components define deliberate practice sessions
description: The article enumerates four components of deliberate practice: "structured approach, its effortful and challenging nature, continues feedback, and repetition." Each practice session follows a well-defined script with clear goals focused on a unique weakness or refinement of existing competencies, supported by timed trials, quantitative metrics, and repeated high-quality execution of fundamental skills to build automaticity.
requirements: A well-defined script curated by a microsurgical instructor with clear goals per practice session, and continuous feedback with measurable goals
constraints: Sessions are often shorter in duration due to the natural fatigue that accompanies intense focus and effort
target_learners: periodontal and implant microsurgery trainees at all career stages
target_learning_goals: microsurgical manual skills such as needle transfer, needle rotation, and suturing
examples: Needle transfer through closely spaced plastic hoops with timed trials, and fingertip-driven needle rotation using jewelry beads on blackberry drupelets

article_title: Deliberate practice: The cornerstone of microsurgical therapy.
citation: Velásquez‐Plata D, Burkhardt R. (2026). Deliberate practice: The cornerstone of microsurgical therapy. Clinical Advances in Periodontics. https://doi.org/10.1002/cap.70055
title: Four characteristics distinguish deliberate practice: purposeful, weakness-focused, fully attentive, improvement-seeking
description: The article defines four characteristics of deliberate practice: it is "purposeful and systematic, focused on weaknesses, demanding of full attention, and focus on constant improvement." The article explicitly contrasts deliberate practice with naïve practice, which involves repetition without a clear goal or feedback, and with a flow state of low attention demands, whereas deliberate practice is mentally strenuous.
requirements: Clear definition of objectives, strategically sound methods, self-awareness of vulnerabilities, and avoidance of distractions
constraints: Sustained dedication is required to avoid plateauing
target_learners: microsurgery practitioners seeking to move beyond automaticity
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of surgical skill beyond the competence plateau
examples: Picking up a microsurgical needle and securing it in the needle holder jaws, an exercise encompassing all four characteristic elements

title: Deliberate Practice as a cyclical skill-acquisition model for psychotherapy supervision
description: Deliberate Practice (DP) is a model of behavioral skill acquisition, adapted from performance fields such as sports and music, structured around a cyclical process of "identifying skill deficits, tailoring behavioral exercises, and rehearsing until it is time to reevaluate the deficit and redesign the next exercise." Its core components are direct observation of performance, concrete feedback, defining learning goals, repeated behavioral rehearsal, and ongoing assessment. The article argues DP prevents the plateauing of standard learning curves by breaking whole-skill practice into small sub-skills practiced with constant refinement, feedback, and repetition.
requirements: A supervisor able to observe performance directly (e.g., video recordings), give concrete feedback, and tailor practice difficulty to the trainee's level
