target_learning_goals: acquisition of specific therapy micro-skills such as validation, emotion regulation, and clinical decision-making
examples: Three supervision sessions with therapist Robert: session 1 chose a learning goal from video observation, session 2 rehearsed validation sub-skills, session 3 tied practice to case conceptualization via the Three Step Question

description: The article tests the longitudinal logic model of SEL interventions articulated by Taylor and colleagues (2017), under which "boosts in social–emotional competencies and self-regulation skills in childhood can set in motion positive developmental cascades" by improving children's relationships with teachers and peers and classroom engagement. In cascade models, early skill-boosting helps children tackle subsequent developmental challenges or access more protective socialization contexts, promoting later school adjustment. The REDI serial mediation findings instantiate this model, with preschool gains cascading through grade school adjustment and parent involvement to adolescent outcomes.
requirements: Testing the model requires longitudinal follow-up of randomized preschool SEL trials with repeated measures of social adjustment, parent involvement, and adolescent outcomes.

description: The article proposes that the impact and success of a death simulation are determined by three characteristics identified from the interviews: "the unexpected confrontation with the patient death, the AD and the debriefing". target_learning_goals: Preparing for patient death and end-of-life decisions

article_title: Learning deliberate reflection in medical diagnosis: does learning-by-teaching help?
citation: Kuhn Josepha, Mamede Silvia, van den Berg Pieter, Zwaan Laura, van Peet Petra, Bindels Patrick, van Gog Tamara. (2022). Learning deliberate reflection in medical diagnosis: does learning-by-teaching help? Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10138-2
title: Deliberate reflection procedure for diagnostic reasoning
description: Deliberate reflection (Mamede et al., 2008a) is a structured, stepwise procedure designed to counter biased, intuitive diagnostic reasoning on clinical cases. "The procedure requires the physician to first read a case and give an initial diagnosis. Subsequently, the physician goes back to the case and lists (1) findings that support the diagnosis, (2) findings that oppose the diagnosis, (3) findings that would have been expected if the diagnosis were true, but were absent." The physician then generates alternative diagnoses, applies the same analytical steps to each, and finally ranks the diagnoses in order of likelihood to choose a final diagnosis. Prior reviews cited in the article place it among the most consistently successful cognitive interventions for diagnostic accuracy, especially for complex cases or bias-inducing conditions.
requirements: Physicians analyse one diagnosis fully before moving to the next, and include expected-but-absent findings when falsifying a diagnosis
constraints: In this study it was applied without explicit reflection instructions at test, where it did not produce measurable gains over control reasoning
target_learners: physicians and physicians in training (general-practice residents, medical students)
target_learning_goals: diagnostic accuracy and unbiased clinical reasoning on complex cases
examples: In the learning phase, residents studied three worked-out deliberate-reflection examples on clinical cases, each analysing three plausible differential diagnoses, and ranked the diagnoses themselves
key_sources: Kuhn Josepha, Mamede Silvia, van den Berg Pieter, Zwaan Laura, van Peet Petra, Bindels Patrick, van Gog Tamara. (2022). Learning deliberate reflection in medical diagnosis: does learning-by-teaching help? Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10138-2

article_title: Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial.
citation: Whittall Jonathan P., Orkin Aaron M., Handford Curtis, Klaiman Michelle, Leece Pamela, Charles Mercy, Wright Amy, Turner Suzanne, Morrison Laurie J., Strike Carol, Campbell Douglas M. (2022). Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0270829
title: Include a debriefing session in simulation protocols used with non-clinicians to consolidate learning and elicit lived-experience feedback
description: The SOONER simulation protocol comprised a briefing, the simulated overdose, and a debriefing guided by the PEARLS framework adapted from healthcare learners. The debriefing allowed participants to self-assess, receive teaching, and share lived-experience insight, which the authors say "empowered participants to share insight which allowed researchers to identify gaps in the proposed resuscitation protocol".
requirements: A debriefing facilitation approach; the article adapted the PEARLS framework because no validated debriefing tool existed for non-clinicians who have witnessed overdose
constraints: No tool has been validated to lead a simulation debriefing with non-clinicians who have witnessed opioid overdose
target_learners: Non-clinicians at high risk of experiencing or witnessing opioid overdose
target_learning_goals: Opioid overdose bystander resuscitation skills, including naloxone administration and CPR
examples: The debriefing was led by evaluating clinicians, lasted approximately 5–10 minutes, and used facilitated discussion, affirmation of positive behaviours and teaching
key_sources: Whittall Jonathan P., Orkin Aaron M., Handford Curtis, Klaiman Michelle, Leece Pamela, Charles Mercy, Wright Amy, Turner Suzanne, Morrison Laurie J., Strike Carol, Campbell Douglas M. (2022). Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0270829

article_title: Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education.
citation: Driessen, E. P., Knight, J. K., Smith, M. K., & Ballen, C. J. (2020). Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(4), ar52. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-04-0068
title: Authors of biology education research should provide a cited definition of active learning and describe the strategies used
description: Because active learning is rarely defined and interpreted in many different ways, the article advocates that BER concerning active learning provide a cited definition and that authors define and describe the active-learning strategies used in experimental research. The article states: "we advocate for all BER concerning active learning to provide a cited definition." Providing definitions may aid increased fidelity and reproducibility of experimental outcomes.
requirements: Authors should follow a definition of active learning with a citation and give examples of the strategies they are using, with detail about application and frequency
constraints: The article notes the broad interpretation of active learning may discourage instructors from trying new practices and serve as a barrier to experimental replication
target_learners: Undergraduate biology students
target_learning_goals: Increased fidelity and reproducibility of experimental outcomes in biology education research
examples: The article suggests authors could say they used an active-learning instructional approach focused on student engagement using group work and clicker questions with peer instruction, followed by appropriate citations
key_sources: Driessen, E. P., Knight, J. K., Smith, M. K., & Ballen, C. J. (2020). Demystifying the Meaning of Active Learning in Postsecondary Biology Education. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(4), ar52. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-04-0068

article_title: Enhancing the one-minute preceptor method for clinical teaching with a DEFT approach.
citation: Savaria MC, Min S, Aghagoli G, Tunkel AR, Hirsh DA, Michelow IC. (2022). Enhancing the one-minute preceptor method for clinical teaching with a DEFT approach. Int J Infect Dis 115:149-153. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijid.2021.12.314
title: DEFT: a four-step clinical teaching framework (Diagnosis, Evidence, Feedback, Teaching) enhancing the one-minute preceptor
description: DEFT is a descriptive acronym — Diagnosis, Evidence, Feedback, Teaching, meaning skillful — that condenses the one-minute preceptor's five microskills into four steps and de-emphasizes the temporal 'one-minute' component. The article uses it as 'a potentially helpful reminder to improve the quality of interactions between learners and preceptors', illustrated with a pediatric respiratory infection vignette aligned to Bloom's taxonomy.
requirements: A preceptor interacting with a learner about a patient case, usable at admission, during hospitalization, or in the outpatient setting
constraints: The article presents DEFT as a proposed model; prospective studies are needed to validate it
target_learners: clinical-year medical students
residents/registrars
fellows
target_learning_goals: medical knowledge
clinical skills
diagnostic reasoning
examples: A sample preceptor-learner interaction about a 3-year-old hospitalized with suspected respiratory infection, mapped to revised Bloom's taxonomy levels in Table 1
